requestTitle: Topics in Adversarial Machine Learning (COSC 89.40 / 189.40), Dartmouth College
abstract: COSC 89.40 / 189.40, Topics in Adversarial Machine Learning, is a student-led seminar at Dartmouth College on how machine learning breaks when someone wants it to: backdoors, data poisoning, adversarial examples and adaptive attacks, training-data extraction, jailbreaks, and protections for artists against style mimicry. Twenty students, half graduate and half undergraduate, read one paper per class from the top security venues and run a small research project in groups of two or three, a new attack or defense, a measurement study, or a reproduction with an extension, written up as a paper. The projects train and attack models: backdoored classifiers, adversarially trained networks, open-weight 8-billion-parameter language models, and text-to-image models. Student laptops and free notebook sessions cannot hold these workloads, so groups shrink their questions to fit. NAIRR Classroom GPU resources give each group an A100 and a hosted notebook with open-weight model access for the Fall 2026 and Winter 2027 offerings, so every student in the class can pick the question first.

abstract: New York City College of Technology (City Tech, CUNY) requests NAIRR Classroom resources to support CET4973: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, an upper-level undergraduate course in Computer Engineering Technology. The course is being redesigned to provide students with a hands-on progression from foundational artificial intelligence and machine learning concepts to contemporary generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic AI systems. Students will complete guided computational labs, three scaffolded AI application projects, and an open-ended final project addressing a problem of academic, professional, entrepreneurial, community, or personal relevance. NAIRR Classroom resources will provide equitable access to consistent notebook-based computing environments, GPU resources, and modern AI development tools while reducing barriers associated with local software installation, limited personal hardware, and individual access to AI infrastructure. The project will also support practical AI literacy, responsible AI practices, system evaluation, and the ability to select appropriate AI approaches for real-world problems. deepC: Learning Diffusion Priors for Carbon Emissions at 1km via High-resolution Numerical Simulations
abstract:
Verifying greenhouse gas emissions at policy-relevant spatial scales remains a critical bottleneck in climate mitigation. Traditional atmospheric CO2 inversions rely on sparse observations and coarse transport models that cannot resolve neighborhood-scale patterns or sector-specific signatures in urban domains. Recent advances in machine learning offer promising pathways to bridge this gap, but require high-resolution, physically consistent transport simulations spanning multiple seasons to train robust inversion systems. Building on our recent benchmark demonstrating successful neural network emission inference from kilometer-scale transport fields, this project will produce the first year-scale, 1 km GHG transport dataset explicitly designed for generative inversion development. We request 120,000 service units on TACC Frontera to simulate approximately 600 model-days across five high-emission, mixed urban-suburban-natural regions in the United States. These simulations will capture diverse meteorological regimes, changing background CO2, and seasonal shifts in transport and biospheric fluxes essential for learning long-trajectory dynamics.

The simulations will enable modeling of the joint distribution of CO2 emissions, column concentrations, and surface concentrations over long timescales at 1 km resolution. Long-trajectory simulations spanning multiple seasons are critical for learning inversions across regime shifts, capturing varying biogenic and anthropogenic effects, and accounting for evolving background CO2. This directly supports training of a diffusion-based generative prior that, through data assimilation techniques, will incorporate sparse but high-resolution satellite and sensor observations to guide the posterior toward high-quality, physically-consistent inversion estimates. The resulting framework will be validated across seasonal regime shifts with rigorous ensemble-based uncertainty quantification. All processed datasets and preprocessing scripts will be publicly released, establishing a new benchmark for ML-driven atmospheric inverse modeling at urban scales.

Advancing Tuberculosis Care with AI
abstract:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains the world's deadliest infectious disease despite being curable, with over 1.3 million deaths annually. Adherence to TB treatment is undermined by stigma, mental-health comorbidity, and limited access to care outside clinic hours. 

This project advances how AI-based conversational agents can deliver safe, clinically grounded support to TB patients and translate patient–agent conversations into structured signal for healthcare providers. We are developing and evaluating a multi-agent, LLM-based conversational system that provides patients with continuous, evidence-based adherence and mental-health support which will be integrated with the deployed patient and provider portal.

requestTitle: Long-Range Biological Reasoning with Hypergraph Foundation Models
abstract:
Higher-order reasoning, modeling interactions among arbitrary groups of entities, not just pairs, remains a fundamental challenge in AI. Existing hypergraph models either encode only local neighborhood aggregates or project onto pairwise graphs, discarding the multi-arity structure that makes hypergraphs expressive and causing long-range dependencies to collapse under depth. We introduce HyperFoundation, a family of foundation-scale hypergraph models built on Hypergraph Laplacian Positional Encodings (HyLapPE), a positional encoding derived from hypergraph Laplacian eigenvectors without pairwise projection, injecting global structural context before message passing begins. We construct large-scale biological hypergraphs integrating genes, diseases, drugs, pathways, side effects, and microbiome interactions; pretrain HyperFoundation across distributed multi-GPU NAIRR systems; and evaluate on a progressive pipeline from disease-gene association to mechanistically grounded drug repurposing.

The scientific contribution is threefold: (1) a spectral characterization of structural position ambiguity in hypergraph networks; (2) HyLapPE, enabling global structural awareness without topology modification; and (3) HyperFoundation, an open pretrained model family with datasets, checkpoints, and training pipelines released publicly. This project advances the NAIRR Pilot's focus on AI powered scientific discovery, foundational AI capabilities, and open infrastructure for the research community.

requestTitle: Leveraging Curiosity for Knowledge Acquisition in Complex Environments
abstract:
The goal of this request for computational resources is to enable a deeper exploration into systems which
perceive, reason and act in complex environments to obtain knowledge.
Existing work in this domain relies on human supervision or dense reward signals, preventing the agent
from ‘losing itself’ in the vast state space of a complex environment. However, complex environments
are often dynamic: robots may be placed in unseen rooms, web agents may be deployed on novel pages,
and coding agents may be asked to work on freshly written code bases. Strategies that rely on human
demonstration are poorly situated to deal with such dynamic environments. We propose a general solution
paradigm that enables knowledge acquisition in complex environments without any human supervision:
the cultivation of intrinsic curiosity. A ‘curiosity-driven agent’ seeks novel experiences in its environment
of operation. While such methods have shown promise in traditional RL settings, their application to
Language Model agents remains unexplored. This project will build on two independent components, which explore the same problem from different perspectives: discovering API functionality with Coding Agents, and Unsupervised Task Acquisition in Visual Environments. In both cases, we have obtained promising initial results using our previous ACCESS allocation; however we are bottlenecked by computational limitations, and would require access to more powerful instances for a more thorough exploration.

By providing broad, hands-on exposure to generative AI methods, this project aims to build practical AI/ML skills among students in Hawai'i, an institution and region historically underrepresented in large-scale AI research computing.

requestTitle: Modernizing Operating Systems Education through Hands-On KV-Cache Management for Large Language Models
abstract:
This project will modernize undergraduate and graduate operating systems education by introducing students to the management of the Key-Value (KV) cache in large language model (LLM) inference. The project will be integrated into CSC341, an undergraduate Operating Systems course, and CSC541, a graduate Operating Systems course. KV-cache management provides a timely and concrete application of fundamental operating systems concepts, including memory allocation, paging, caching, cache replacement, memory sharing, scheduling, resource allocation, and distributed resource management.

Students will use GPU-based computational resources to study how the KV cache is created and grows during autoregressive LLM inference and how it affects GPU memory capacity, latency, throughput, and scalability. Through hands-on programming assignments, students will build simplified KV-cache managers, implement and compare allocation and replacement policies, investigate cache reuse and prefix sharing, and evaluate the impact of context length, concurrent requests, and memory constraints. Graduate students will additionally investigate KV-cache-aware request and model placement in multi-GPU environments.

The proposed activities emphasize understanding AI infrastructure rather than training large foundation models. Students will use pre-trained open-source language models and lightweight open-source software environments to conduct realistic systems experiments. NAIRR Classroom resources will provide access to the GPU computing capabilities needed to observe and measure real KV-cache behavior under LLM inference workloads. The project will help students connect foundational operating systems principles with emerging AI infrastructure and prepare them for research and careers in AI systems, GPU computing, and large-scale computing.

requestTitle: Interactive Robotics Motion Planning via NRP JupyterHub
abstract:
Our institution requests access to the National Research Platform (NRP) Nautilus Cluster / JupyterHub resource to support an undergraduate Computer Science course, CS 341: Introduction to Algorithmic Robotics and Motion Planning. This course introduces students to core algorithms in configuration spaces (C-space), graph-based search (A*, Dijkstra), sampling-based motion planning (PRM, RRT, RRT*), and kinematic trajectory optimization.

We expect approximately 15–28 undergraduate students to utilize this browser-accessible JupyterHub environment for interactive programming assignments, algorithm visualization, and performance benchmarking. By eliminating local software setup barriers (e.g., C++/Python dependencies, ROS/simulator configurations) and utilizing open-source containers, this resource will significantly enhance practical, hands-on learning and ensure equitable computational access for all enrolled students.

requestTitle: Scaling Trustworthy Evaluation for Latently Verifiable AI Agents with Frontier Models
abstract: This project aims to scale trustworthy evaluation for AI agents on latently verifiable tasks, where success is objective but difficult to verify automatically. Building on the InEx framework, we combine an intrinsic evaluator that checks whether an agent’s trajectory supports its final answer with Azure-hosted extrinsic verification for hard cases that require additional evidence. AWS resources will support training open-source intrinsic evaluators from verified traces, synthetic hard negatives, and confidence-weighted feedback. We will compare this evidence-grounded approach with final-answer matching, generic model-as-judge methods, and frontier-only evaluation, focusing on calibration, false-positive success labels, and failure recall. The project will also test whether evaluator outputs provide better reward signals for downstream web-agent training.

requestTitle: Self-Evolving Agentic Systems for Long-Horizon Tasks
abstract: Agentic systems, in which multiple large language models (LLMs) with specialized roles form workflow-style architectures, are increasingly expected to perform long-horizon tasks, where completing a single query may take hours or even days and can involve dozens or hundreds of calls to LLMs and external tools. Developing such systems introduces three core challenges: longer trajectories, higher evaluation cost, and a larger design space. Existing approaches typically rely on outcome-based rewards, but in long-horizon settings, these suffer from reward sparsity and prohibitive trajectory sampling costs. In the proposed project, we address these challenges by applying self-evolution methods, which use self-evaluation to generate training signals without human annotation, to three components of agentic system development: workflow optimization, model training, and co-evolving synthetic training data generation. A key advantage of self-evaluation is that it can be applied at intermediate stages of a trajectory, enabling dense, stage-level rewards and finer control over computational cost without requiring full trajectory execution.

requestTitle: Software Engineering of AI-Enabled Real-Time Systems
abstract:
A cloud-based learning environment for a Software Engineering course in which students learn to design, build, deploy, and evaluate AI-enabled real-time software systems. Students work in teams to develop distributed applications that acquire and process real-time human-centered sensing data, including EEG, eye tracking, posture, gestures, and physiological signals, using event-driven communication. AI is introduced as a component of larger software systems, allowing students to explore model development and real-time inference to trigger behaviors in interactive and robotic systems, while focusing on the software engineering challenges of integrating AI into reliable applications.

Throughout the 15-week course, students gain hands-on experience with cloud computing, containers, APIs, databases, automated testing, continuous integration and deployment, observability, and cyber-physical system integration.

NAIRR Pilot resources provide a shared computational environment where students can deploy, integrate, and operate these systems. Through this environment, students experience the complete lifecycle of AI-enabled systems—from real-time data acquisition and processing to AI-driven behavior—while applying software engineering practices throughout their development and operation.

requestTitle: Principled Royalty Distribution in Music Generative AI
abstract: Music generative AI is rapidly becoming widely deployed, raising growing questions about the use of copyrighted recordings in model training and the appropriate compensation of content creators. These developments underscore an urgent need for principled royalty distribution mechanisms that fairly compensate stakeholders. Recent advances in data attribution have made it possible to estimate the contribution of training data to generated outputs, opening the door to attribution-based royalty schemes. However, two fundamental challenges remain unaddressed. First, in text-to-music systems, generation is jointly driven by training data and a user-supplied text prompt, but existing attribution methods do not account for this dual source of influence, which makes it unclear how to allocate credit between training-data contributors and prompt-providing users. Second, a tempting alternative—attributing credit directly from prompt content (e.g., assigning credit to an artist whenever a user requests “a song in the style of [artist]”)—may be trivially gamed by users who paraphrase or describe the same target without naming it. This proposed research will address these two challenges by (1) developing and empirically validating a joint attribution framework that simultaneously credits training data and user prompts in text-to-music systems, and (2) systematically auditing and hardening prompt-content-based attribution mechanisms against paraphrase-style gaming attacks. If successful, the project will lay technical and empirical foundations for sustainable royalty distribution in music generative AI.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot: Towards Reproducible Deep Learning Research via Code Generation
abstract: Almost all scientific and engineering fields are exploring deep learning methods for domain breakthrough. However, it is intractable for domain scientists to keep up with the deep learning research pace, given the exponentially increasing number of preprints on ArXiv. Although many papers come with GitHub repositories, the reproducibility cannot be guaranteed. It is infeasible for domain scientists to filter and select candidate methods for their problems. In this project, we aim to enhance the reproducibility of deep learning papers with the aid of large language models. We formulate the reproducibility problem as a problem of code generation from papers. We will leverage open large language models such as Qwen3-Coder-30 and CWM-32B with a curated dataset with over 700 paper-code pairs. We will examine the techniques of LLM fine-tuning, in-context learning, retrieval augmented generation, chain-of-thoughts reasoning, and a multi-agent system. We expect the resulting model to be capable of generating correct and executable code on NAIRR Pilot GPU resources for those papers without code. For papers with incomplete or erroneous code, the resulting model will be able to automatically debug the code and deploy it for execution.

Efficient Multimodal Long Context Reasoning via Parameter Generation
abstract: Modern AI systems increasingly rely on multimodal data such as text, images, and audio, but current methods convert all inputs into long token sequences, leading to inefficiencies and loss of structural information. This project proposes a new paradigm, multimodal parameter synthesis, which directly maps multimodal inputs into lightweight model parameters that can be dynamically injected into large language models, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning without expanding context length. The project will develop methods for generating, integrating, and sharing such parameters across inputs and AI agents, and evaluate them on standard multimodal and multi-agent benchmarks to demonstrate improvements in performance, scalability, and computational efficiency. By reducing the resource demands of multimodal AI and enabling more scalable reasoning systems, this work aligns with NAIRR’s goal of broadening access to advanced AI capabilities, and all resulting models, tools, and benchmarks will be released publicly to support the research community.

requestTitle: A Scalable MARL Framework for Multi-Player General-Sum Games
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents, they increasingly interact in complex, competitive environments requiring negotiation and strategic decision-making. However, training LLMs for these multi-agent, general-sum games using traditional reinforcement learning methods creates massive computational bottlenecks. This project addresses these limitations by developing a highly scalable, open-source Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework specifically designed for multi-billion parameter LLMs. The research pioneers three key innovations: an efficient dynamic batching system using LoRA adapters to manage multiple opponents without excessive resource drain, a modular GPU-accelerated self-play pipeline, and a memory-efficient, critic-free training approach utilizing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). By resolving severe memory and compute constraints, this project will democratize access to large-scale AI agent research. All findings, codebases, and frameworks will be publicly shared to advance the open-science community and accelerate the deployment of capable, interactive AI ecosystems.

requestTitle: ECLIPSE: Multimodal Immune Landscape Profiling of BRCA1 Pre-Cancer Using Contrastive Learning
abstract:
Background and Clinical Significance
Individuals with pathogenic BRCA1 mutations face cumulative lifetime risks of breast and ovarian malignancies reaching 72% and 44%, respectively. Currently, clinical risk reduction relies disproportionately on irreversible prophylactic surgeries, such as oophorectomy and mastectomy. This is because existing diagnostics cannot distinguish between pre-malignant tissue that is under effective immune surveillance and tissue where that surveillance has already silently failed. This immune failure in BRCA1-associated pre-cancers is driven by active dysregulation of the immune tumor microenvironment (iTME) —creating a biologically silent but clinically dangerous state of immune tolerance.
Project Objectives and Methodology
To address this diagnostic gap, this project develops ECLIPSE (Embedding-based Contrastive Learning for Immune Pre-malignancy State Evaluation). ECLIPSE is a contrastive learning framework that resolves the full continuum from immune control to immune failure before malignancy develops. Using data from the uniquely structured Gray BRCA Pre-Cancer Atlas, the framework co-projects four complementary biomedical data modalities into a unified latent manifold:
•	Pathology images 
•	Spatial transcriptomics 
•	Somatic mutation profiles 
•	Structured clinical metadata 
Unlike traditional models that predict a single discrete label, ECLIPSE learns a continuous immune-state representation. This enables an interpretable comparison of immune behavior across different patients and lesion severities.
Resource Utilization and Training Strategy
This project is executed through the Sustainable Research Pathways (SRP) program, engaging a cohort of five student researchers and a faculty mentor. The team requests an allocation of 270,000 Service Units (SUs) over 12 months on the Indiana University Jetstream2 platform. Jetstream2’s OpenStack-based cloud platform provides critical on-demand GPU instance availability, avoiding the batch queue delays of traditional HPC systems. Access to 80GB GPU memory (NVIDIA H100) is a strict requirement, as the multimodal architecture must process high-resolution images, transcriptomic embeddings, and clinical encodings simultaneously in a single forward pass. This resource will serve as a dedicated rapid-iteration development environment, enabling all five students to simultaneously build, debug, and validate their models.
Expected Outcomes and Broader Impacts
The successful completion of this NAIRR Pilot project will deliver several key assets to the cancer prevention research community:
•	A Unified Multimodal Latent Space: A validated embedding space that aligns clinical, morphological, mutational, and molecular data to capture the immune failure trajectory.
•	Open-Source AI Tools: The public release of the ECLIPSE codebase, pre-trained encoder weights, and four standalone CLIP-aligned encoder modules for community reuse.
•	Novel Biomarkers: The identification of spatial and transcriptomic features that correlate with immune failure, pinpointing the earliest detectable markers of immune tolerance to lay the groundwork for future immune-based interception strategies.

requestTitle: Start-Up: Nathan Szymanski, University of California, Los Angeles
Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Participant-level Modeling of Individual Differences in Cognitive Reserve
abstract:
Alzheimer’s disease shows large differences across individuals: patients with similar levels of brain degeneration can experience very different patterns of cognitive decline. This variability is often attributed to cognitive reserve, the ability to maintain cognitive function despite underlying brain pathology. However, most current machine learning approaches focus on broad diagnostic categories and do not capture these individual differences.

This project develops a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates brain MRI with clinical and biological data, including cognitive tests, demographics, genetic risk factors, and fluid biomarkers. By learning shared representations across these data sources, the model aims to identify latent factors that explain why Alzheimer’s disease progresses differently across individuals.

The resulting models will help characterize heterogeneous disease trajectories and provide new tools for studying cognitive reserve. All models and code will be released as open-source resources for the research community.

requestTitle: Start-Up: Chen Yang, Texas A&M University
Contamination-Resistant Datasets for Fair and Accurate LLM Benchmarking
abstract: This project develops a new way to make AI benchmarks more trustworthy. Today, many large AI models may have already seen parts of common test datasets during training, which can make their scores look better than their real abilities. We propose creating benchmarks that can still be used to test AI systems but are much harder to copy, memorize, or accidentally include in training data. The project will build and test an early prototype of this idea across different AI models and benchmark types, with the goal of supporting fairer and more accurate evaluation of future AI systems.

requestTitle: Photographic Memory: Long-Horizon Egocentric Vision
abstract: Human memory is fallible: people forget half of what they learn within an hour. Smart glasses can now record our daily lives, opening the possibility of AI companions that remember on our behalf, helping recall a name, a medication name, or where we left our keys. But no practical system today turns continuous first-person video into a memory that is accurate, useful, and privacy-respecting. This project builds the foundations of memory augmentation. We are developing LOCI, a system that decides in real time which moments are worth remembering and organizes them into a memory users can query in plain language. To keep costs and privacy risks low, LOCI runs a lightweight model on the user's phone and calls larger cloud AI only for the small fraction of moments that matter. We are also creating EpisodicVQA, the first dataset pairing day-long smart-glasses recordings with human memory diaries, letting us directly compare what people remember with what AI captures. Because humans and AI tend to forget different things, we expect the two to be most powerful when combined.

Investigating Collective Intelligence and Controlled Emergence in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: We request NAIRR computational resources to conduct large-scale experiments on collective intelligence and controlled emergence in decentralized AI systems composed of 100–500 large language model (LLM) agents. The proposed study requires approximately 45,000 node-hours (180,000 GPU-hours), distributed orchestration infrastructure, and model-access credits to support 2.75 million agent inference operations across multiple communication topologies, task domains, and random seeds. These resources will enable systematic evaluation of coordination, robustness, and safety in large-scale multi-agent systems that exceed the capabilities of local computing infrastructure. The project will produce open-source evaluation infrastructure, datasets, and benchmarks for the broader decentralized AI research community.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot Project Request: Factorized One-Step Video Generation for Efficient On-Device and Streaming AI
abstract: This project will develop a more efficient approach to video generation for streaming and future on-device AI systems. Current video generation methods often require many repeated neural network evaluations to produce each frame, which increases compute cost, memory use, latency, and energy demand. This project will explore a factorized video-generation pipeline that separates temporal reasoning from pixel rendering. A compact semantic and motion representation will be predicted over time using an autoregressive model, and a one-step Pixel MeanFlow decoder will then render video frames from that predicted state. The project will evaluate whether this design can reduce computation and memory while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments will use public video datasets and report both generation quality and efficiency metrics, including latency, peak memory, forward passes per frame, and GPU-hours. The expected outcome is an open, reproducible benchmark and software release for efficient video generation, supporting future research in low-cost generative AI, streaming video models, and deployment-aware machine learning.

requestTitle: Scalable Data Selection for Efficient Foundation Model Adaptation
abstract: This project will develop and evaluate Target-Conditioned Trajectories, a compute-efficient data selection method for adapting open foundation models. Public instruction datasets contain millions of examples, but training on all available data is expensive and can reduce task-specific performance when data are noisy, duplicated, or irrelevant. We will scale a completed 3,000 GPU-hour pilot into a focused NAIRR study across representative open models, task families, and candidate data pools up to approximately one million examples. The project will compare target-conditioned selection against random, retrieval, quality-filtering, diversity, and feasible gradient-attribution baselines. Expected outputs include an open-source data-selection toolkit, reproducible configurations and selected-subset artifacts where licenses permit, a best-practices report for efficient data curation, and a manuscript on compute-efficient foundation model adaptation.

requestTitle: Geometry-Aware MeanFlow and FAST-DeepONet for Operator Learning on Arbitrary Physical Domains
abstract: This project develops fast, structure-preserving learning methods for robotic and physical systems by combining two research directions: SE(3)-MeanFlow for robotic grasp generation and FAST-DeepONet for efficient operator learning in PDE-governed domains. The common goal is to reduce inference costs while preserving the geometry, uncertainty, and physical structure of the target problem.

requestTitle: An Active Learning Approach to Selective Ligand Design for Targeted Immunotherapy
abstract: Achieving selectivity between highly homologous proteins with identical binding pockets is a fundamental challenge in drug design, one where differential binding arises largely from protein dynamics, rendering conventional docking ineffective. A critical example is folate receptor beta (FRβ) and its near-identical homolog folate receptor alpha (FRα): selective FRβ targeting is essential for cancer immunotherapy, as FRβ marks immunosuppressive tumor-associated macrophages while FRα is expressed on epithelial cancer cells and healthy tissues like the kidneys. Because static structures cannot distinguish these receptors, physics-based relative binding free energy (RBFE) simulations are required to capture the dynamic signatures of selectivity. Building on a completed NAIRR Start-Up allocation (NAIRR260042), we propose an active learning workflow in which an initial diverse set of candidate ligands is evaluated using RBFE calculations and analyzed using DiffNet, a graph-based maximum likelihood inference algorithm that integrates pairwise simulation data into consistent per-ligand selectivity estimates. These estimates then train a surrogate machine learning model that selects the next ligands to simulate, balancing predicted FRβ selectivity, model uncertainty, and chemical diversity. The most promising candidates will be prioritized for synthesis and in vitro and in vivo validation in our laboratory.

requestTitle: INTERACT: Intent-Driven Human–Vehicle Interaction with Constraint-Aware Control
abstract: Autonomous driving systems have achieved strong performance in perception, localization, and control, yet they remain limited in their ability to systematically incorporate human intent into autonomous decision-making. Driving is inherently a cooperative process that requires interpreting human intent, negotiating priorities, and adapting behavior under dynamic constraints. Existing autonomy architectures typically optimize predefined objectives in isolation, lacking a principled mechanism to translate human intent into executable planning directives. This gap leads to brittle behavior, limited interpretability, and difficulty aligning autonomous actions with human expectations. This project proposes DIRECT (Driving Intent–Integrated Reasoning and Constraint Translation), an edge-deployable framework for integrating human driving intent into autonomous control systems through structured intent translation and context-aware constraint compilation. DIRECT decomposes intent integration into two complementary components: an Intent-to-Instruction Translator (I2IT) and a Context-Aware Constraint Compiler (CACC). I2IT translates multimodal human intent expressions into a structured, planner-agnostic Intermediate Instruction Representation (IIR), capturing task-level intent and behavioral preferences without binding them to execution context. CACC then grounds the IIR within hard and soft constraints to produce a Driving Intent–Integrated Representation (DIIR) that can be directly consumed by existing planning stacks. The framework is designed to support large-scale training and efficient edge deployment via teacher–student distillation, enabling low-latency, on-device intent-aware autonomy. A proof-of-concept evaluation in high-fidelity simulation demonstrates that human driving instructions can be reliably translated into executable constraints and successfully realized by standard autonomous planners. By providing a modular, interpretable, and deployable pathway from human intent to autonomous execution, DIRECT advances human-aligned autonomous driving under real-world constraints.

requestTitle: A Multimodal, Hierarchical Cyberattack Simulation Suite for Water Infrastructure
abstract:
Cyberattacks increasingly threaten critical infrastructure. However, most disaster simulators, built for natural hazards, miss the fast-evolving cyber-physical threats. 
Advances in large language models (LLMs) lower simulation barriers and costs, replicate expert reasoning, and detect anomalies in domains such as water management and network security. Large language models (LLMs) may help improve these simulations. They can combine threat information and create realistic cyberattack scenarios. However, current LLM-based tools still cannot simulate cyber-related disasters on a large scale, especially for critical water infrastructure.
We propose  Prophetess, a multimodal, hierarchical cyberattack simulation suite for critical water infrastructure. Our project pursues two goals: (1) construct a historical, multimodal cyber-event graph paired with a domain-tailored cybersecurity LLM; and(2) develop a knowledge-guided simulator that links sociocultural decision processes with detailed adversarial behavior exercised in cyberattack testbeds. \ProjectName produces system logs, narrative timelines, and testbed executions to support vulnerability discovery, threat assessment, incident-response planning, and resilience testing—ultimately advancing national preparedness for cyber-physical disasters.

requestTitle: An Open H100 Benchmark for Resource-Efficient Neuro-Symbolic AI Systems
abstract: Neuro-symbolic AI combines neural perception with symbolic reasoning to support interpretable and trustworthy reasoning. However, researchers lack an open H100-scale benchmark that shows how neuro-symbolic workloads use memory, which operators dominate runtime, and how compression changes the latency-memory-accuracy tradeoff on modern AI accelerators. This project will create that public benchmark on SDSC Expanse AI, using representative neuro-symbolic models, operator microbenchmarks, H100 profiling traces, and reproducible scripts.

requestTitle: HypoOrchestra: Agentic Scientific Discovery with Statistical Evidence and Error Control
abstract: Agentic AI systems can now mine large-scale biomedical databases to generate scientific hypotheses at a speed that would be infeasible for individual researchers. However, a critical barrier to deploying these systems in high-stakes environments is their propensity to confidently report false discoveries. This occurs because agents inevitably surface the most striking patterns in the data, which are subject to selection bias; moreover, reusing that same data to compute evidence would severely overestimate confidence and inflate false discoveries. We propose \textbf{HypoOrchestra}, an open-source, model-agnostic multi-agent framework that bridges hypothesis generation and evidence quantification. It not only generates data-driven scientific hypotheses from multimodal biomedical databases, but also pairs agent-generated hypotheses with statistically valid evidence and formal false discovery rate (FDR) control. HypoOrchestra contributes (i)~an \emph{information-governance layer} that partitions summary-level data into independent blocks so generation agents can explore adaptively while untouched blocks are reserved for validation; (ii)~an \emph{evidence layer}, built on our prior POPPER framework, that produces per-claim e-values and FDR-controlled discovery sets with failure-aware abstention; and (iii)~\textbf{HypoBench}, a benchmark for evaluating data-driven hypothesis generation under shuffled relationships and decoy injection, thereby separating genuine data mining from memorized knowledge for transparent assessment of agentic scientific hypothesis generation. The project is executable over the next 12 months and is constrained primarily by research-resource access rather than by a need for large-scale model training. The primary need is sustained OpenAI-compatible model access through NAIRR-supported channels, complemented by substantial CPU resources for orchestration, data processing, simulation, and large-scale evaluation, and modest GPU resources for open-source baselines and supporting experiments. The outcome will be an open-source framework for agentic scientific discovery that attaches formal statistical guarantees to AI-generated hypotheses, and a transparent benchmark for evaluating the false discovery rates of agentic scientific discovery systems.

requestTitle: A Comprehensive Suite for 4D Spatio-temporal Intelligence
abstract:
Humans exhibit powerful spatio-temporal intelligence: from continuous sensory input, we construct an internal 4D model of the world that tracks who is where, how things move, what may happen next, and how our actions will alter the scene. Despite rapid progress in computer vision, it remains unclear whether today’s AI systems can develop such capabilities, because existing datasets and benchmarks primarily target static 3D scenes. Even when dynamic content is included, it is often synthetic, short in duration, or captured with a narrow field of view, yielding only fragmented motion segments rather than a coherent 4D representation of the world evolving over long time scales.

To this end, we aim to build a comprehensive 4D suite that reconstructs dense scene geometry all around and captures long-range dynamics all the time, providing the continuous 4D supervision required for long-horizon spatio-temporal understanding. Our key insight is to turn to a natural yet underexplored data source—in-the-wild long 360° videos—which provide complete scene coverage, realistic motion, and effectively eliminate out-of-view failures. Such panoramic capture allows us to observe long-range dynamics and interactions that are impossible to recover from narrow field-of-view or short-duration videos. For each 360° video sequence, our pipeline produces a comprehensive, high-quality 4D reconstruction comprising: (i) a dense, globally consistent 3D reconstruction of static structures; (ii) long-range, temporally coherent 4D trajectories for dynamic entities; and (iii) high-level semantic annotations, including instance masks and text descriptions that link geometry and motion to language. Together, these multi-level annotations provide the full stack of information required to understand real-world 4D scene dynamics.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot: An LLM-Driven Framework for Agentic Lossy Compression of Scientific Data
abstract: The overarching goal of this project is to develop a unified, end-to-end auto-tuning cyberinfrastructure for selecting best-fit configurations for lossy compression of extreme-scale scientific datasets, such as those arising in astrophysics and climate simulations. Modern scientific applications routinely generate petabyte-scale outputs; storing, moving, and analyzing these datasets is increasingly constrained by I/O bandwidth, memory capacity, and long-term storage costs. Lossy compressors can significantly reduce data volume, but configuring by trial-and-error is challenging, error-prone, and increasingly difficult, due to the diverse post-hoc analysis requirements, and ever increasing compression algorithms.  This project proposes AgenticLC, an intelligent, data-driven decision-support system that helps scientific users navigate this complex configuration space, reducing manual tuning effort while preserving application-level quality.

requestTitle: Comparing LLM Inference Workloads Across Computer Architectures
abstract:
This project will integrate National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) classroom infrastructure into ISC 2073: Secure Computer Architecture, a required undergraduate course for cybersecurity and information systems majors at The University of Texas at San Antonio, a Hispanic-Serving Institution where 44% of undergraduates are first-generation college students. The initiative expands access to GPU-enabled computing by allowing students to investigate how modern computer architectures support large language model (LLM) inference through hands-on experimentation using shared cloud-based GPU resources.

Students will compare the performance and energy characteristics of identical quantized open-weight language models executing on two computing platforms: an ARM-based Raspberry Pi and a fractional NVIDIA A100 GPU hosted on Indiana University's Jetstream2 through a browser-based JupyterHub environment. By collecting and analyzing measurements including inference throughput, power consumption, and energy efficiency, students will connect architectural concepts such as parallelism, memory bandwidth, and specialized AI accelerators to the practical behavior of modern AI systems.

Beyond performance evaluation, the project examines the security, governance, and societal implications of AI infrastructure. Students will investigate aspects of edge and cloud-based inference, including multi-tenancy, side-channel risks, supply-chain complexity, and energy economics of large-scale AI computing, before discussing the architectural tradeoffs that influence the deployment of trustworthy AI systems. 

The project will also demonstrate a scalable classroom model for delivering GPU-enabled AI education through shared JupyterHub environments that require no specialized local hardware. Outcomes from the pilot will inform future computer architecture and cybersecurity curricula while providing equitable student access to advanced computing resources and workforce preparation in AI-enabled and secure-by-design systems.

requestTitle: Project-Based Education in Graduate Course
abstract: Tennessee Tech University’s (TnTech) course entitled Anomaly and Intrusion Detection Systems is a graduate-level course. This course investigates and implements current advances in this ever-growing field. The application of anomaly detection to a wide range of domains, including fraud, insider threats, and time-series data are investigated in depth, as well as network attacks and the systems for detecting oddities such as network intrusions and denial of service attacks. This course not only covers the subjects through readings, but the students are required to collect data and implement models for the purpose of detecting anomalies as part of a semester-long project. requestTitle: The AI Sandbox: A Pedagogical Online Platform for Designing, Developing, and Playtesting Game AI Agents
abstract: How do you learn to build artificial intelligence for games? At the University of Arizona, students in INFO 426/526 (Game AI) learn by building it - and by watching their creations compete, cooperate, and converse. Over a 15-week online course, each student designs and programs AI agents for two games: a tactical wargame, where agents are judged on how well they play, and a village role-playing game, where they are judged on how believably they behave. At the heart of the course is the Game Sandbox, an online platform  that provides two leaderboards for each assignment: one scored by the machines, one by human peers playing with or against their classmates' agents. NAIRR Pilot resources make this shared experience possible, hosting the platform and powering the GPU-based inference that brings student-trained agents to life. requestTitle: Start-Up: Anyi Liu, Oakland University
Start-Up: Yueqi Chen, University of Colorado, Boulder
Measuring Security Risks in AI-Agent-Generated Environment Configuration Artifacts
abstract:
AI coding agents are increasingly used to generate deployment artifacts such as Dockerfiles, Docker Compose files, and Terraform templates. Because these artifacts directly control software build and cloud deployment behavior, security errors in them can lead to vulnerable images, excessive permissions, unsafe bootstrap logic, and unnecessary network exposure. However, there is still no systematic framework for measuring the security risks of AI-agent-generated environment configuration artifacts at scale.

This project will build a benchmark and evaluation framework for assessing the security of deployment artifacts generated by six AI agents across 300–400 real-world repositories. We will measure functional validity, scanner-detectable vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, and higher-level risks that existing tools often miss, such as unnecessary privileges and intent-inconsistent exposure. The expected outcome is a reusable benchmark, new detector components, and an empirical characterization of security failure modes in AI-generated deployment artifacts.

requestTitle: CyberSAFE-AI Classroom: Reproducible, Hands-On Education in LLM Security, Privacy, and Responsible Deployment
abstract:
This request will transform CSE 6392, a graduate seminar in large language model (LLM)
security, privacy, and ethics, into a reproducible computational classroom in which every student can safely
investigate how AI systems fail, how failures are measured, and which defenses preserve utility. Students
will use instructor-managed NAIRR resources to complete a sequence of controlled laboratories on adversarial machine learning, privacy leakage, jailbreaking, prompt injection, retrieval-augmented generation, agentic tool use, guardrails, multimodal manipulation, and insecure code generation. The unifying pedagogy is
attack→measure→mitigate→reflect: each activity requires an explicit threat model, quantitative evaluation, a
defense or control, and a responsible-use analysis. The project will deliver a deployment-ready course, measurable
AI-workforce outcomes, and a reusable, openly licensed instructional package designed for adoption by educators
across the United States.

abstract: CS 460 (Fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence) at the University of Alabama at Birmingham is a newly redesigned course that aims to familiarize students with algorithms and concepts underlying modern artificial intelligence systems. Topics include deep learning and large language models, reinforcement learning, and (briefly) classical search and planning algorithms. This proposal requests access to classroom compute resources for student assignments and projects. Projects and several assignments will involve fitting deep neural networks and the use of local, open-weight large language models. The required compute will exceed usual student laptop resources. Access to readily available compute will allow projects to reflect more realistic use cases and will thus provide students with more practical experience implementing and assessing AI workflows.

requestTitle: Security and Privacy in Machine Unlearning
abstract:
Machine unlearning—the process of making a model "forget" specific training data—is essential for data privacy and regulatory compliance, such as the "right to be forgotten." However, current MU methods face significant security and privacy vulnerabilities.

Our research aims to develop and evaluate novel frameworks for secure, private, and verifiable machine unlearning. To empirically validate our proposed algorithms, we require significant computational power for repeatedly training, unlearning, and testing large-scale deep learning models.

requestTitle: Rapid Prediction of Image-Based Molecular Biomarkers for Precision Oncology
abstract:
This NAIRR Pilot Project advances AI methods for scientific discovery while improving interpretability, security, and trust by developing a clinically deployable platform for rapid prediction of molecular biomarkers from routine histopathology images. The goal is to reduce diagnostic latency and improve treatment decisions using foundation model–driven computational pathology.

Building on our NAIRR Startup project (NAIRR250502), we established scalable infrastructure on the Purdue Anvil system, hosting 2,220 high-resolution slides (847 GB) from CPTAC-LSCC and CPTAC-LUAD. We deployed the BiomedParse foundation model and our ClinSegAI pipeline, enabling efficient single-cell segmentation via Slurm. Over 100 slides have been processed with significantly improved speed, demonstrating feasibility for large-scale analysis.

The project will (1) enhance cell-level segmentation and feature extraction by fine-tuning BiomedParse and ClinSegAI and further improve both the vision and language modules through targeted model fine-tuning on domain-specific pathology data; and (2) develop a high-performance molecular prediction framework for biomarkers such as PD-L1, DNA mutations, and gene fusions. Preliminary results show improved accuracy (0.93 vs. 0.41) and reduced inference time (15 seconds vs. 12 minutes). This work will deliver a scalable, interpretable AI platform that accelerates biomarker discovery and supports precision medicine.

abstract: CS 789, "AI-Powered Cyber Attacks and Defenses," is a graduate course at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas examining generative AI in cybersecurity across three themes: vulnerabilities of AI systems (adversarial AI), the use of AI to conduct attacks (offensive AI), and the use of AI to strengthen defenses. Students gain hands-on skills that exceed personal hardware: parameter-efficient fine-tuning of open-weight language models, running large local LLMs for inference, building retrieval-augmented generation pipelines with vector and graph databases, and constructing AI agents that orchestrate security tools. requestTitle: SCALE Course for GPU Hours
abstract:
The Swarm Coordination and Autonomous Learning for Emerging Researchers (SCALE) project seeks to expand access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) education and autonomous systems research for students from underserved and EPSCoR institutions. Through immersive classroom instruction, field-based experimentation, and collaboration with national laboratories, the project trains undergraduate and graduate students in cutting-edge topics including federated learning, explainable AI, reinforcement learning, autonomous drone coordination, privacy-preserving machine learning, and secure distributed systems.

The project combines hands-on drone experimentation with scalable cloud and GPU-enabled AI infrastructure provided through the NSF NAIRR Pilot ecosystem. Students develop and evaluate AI models for autonomous vehicle swarms, secure communications, environmental monitoring, and distributed decision-making in real-world environments. The curriculum integrates advanced AI workflows using TensorFlow, PyTorch, OpenMined, ROS2, and reinforcement learning frameworks while exposing students to large-scale GPU computing resources.

SCALE also supports collaboration with Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) and partner institutions including the University of New Mexico (UNM), New Mexico State University (NMSU), and Navajo Technical University (NTU). These partnerships create pathways for internships, undergraduate research, and workforce development in AI, cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and national security applications.

By combining inclusive education, high-performance computing, and real-world autonomous systems experimentation, the SCALE project aims to develop a diverse next-generation workforce capable of advancing trustworthy and privacy-preserving AI technologies for scientific, industrial, and national security applications.

requestTitle: Cloud-Enabled NLP and AI Workflows for Workforce Readiness in Data Science Education
abstract: Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) and large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for both computational resources and practical artificial intelligence (AI) skills. However, many students lack access to the infrastructure required to gain hands-on experience with modern AI systems. This project addresses this gap by providing scalable, cloud-based resources and mentorship to support student-led NLP projects using techniques such as prompt engineering and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The primary goal of this initiative is to strengthen AI workforce readiness by enabling students to design, build, and evaluate real-world applications while developing industry-relevant technical skills. Through participation in project-based learning environments, students gain experience with modern AI workflows, including model integration, evaluation, and deployment. By expanding access to advanced computational tools and structured learning opportunities, this project supports the development of a highly skilled AI talent pipeline across institutions and regions in the United States. This work aligns with NAIRR’s mission to expand access to advanced computing infrastructure and contributes to national priorities in strengthening the AI workforce and advancing U.S. competitiveness in artificial intelligence.

requestTitle: Enhancing Faithfulness of Medical Reasoning and Knowledge Understanding in LLMs
abstract: Clinical decision support requires reasoning that is faithful, interpretable, and safe, yet today's large language models exhibit failure modes unacceptable in care: fabricated citations, confidently incorrect doses, and inability to reconcile conflicting evidence across electronic health records (EHR), peer-reviewed literature, and structured ontologies. This 12-month project builds a trustworthy clinical reasoning system combining three innovations: (1) retrieval-augmented reasoning over MIMIC-IV, PubMed Central, and medical ontologies (UMLS, SNOMED-CT, RxNorm, ICD-10, DrugBank) via a hybrid dense-sparse pipeline; (2) a multi-agent architecture in which a Causal Validator grounds proposed clinical relationships in the PC algorithm, NOTEARS, and do-calculus on real EHR cohorts, and a Safety Verifier cross-checks outputs against contraindication tables and adversarial probes; and (3) uncertainty-aware inference-time scaling, where token-level perplexity, semantic self-consistency, and conformal prediction trigger escalation to deeper reasoning only on hard cases. The pipeline is provider-neutral: routine inference and ablations run on locally-served Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, MedAlpaca-13B, and BioMistral-7B on NCSA DeltaAI GH200 nodes, while frontier reasoning escalation, synthetic data generation, and LLM-as-judge evaluation use DeepSeek-R1, MiniMax M2, DeepSeek-V3, and Llama 4 Maverick via SambaCloud. Validation spans knowledge benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, MMLU-Med), MIMIC-IV outcome prediction (in-hospital mortality, 30-day readmission, sepsis onset), and faithfulness and safety metrics including hallucination rate, counterfactual robustness, and adversarial safety violation rate. Deliverables include an open-source four-agent framework, a public synthetic rare-condition dataset, an evaluation harness, and at least two peer-reviewed publications, with reproducibility tracked through Weights & Biases. The project advances NAIRR Pilot focus areas in safe and trustworthy AI, large-scale model exploration of complex clinical datasets, and cyberworkforce education.

requestTitle: IT7075 - Training Applied AI for Cybersecurity
abstract: This request supports Applied AI for Cybersecurity (IT 7075), a redesigned graduate course at the University of Cincinnati's School of Information Technology, serving 35 students. The course teaches students to build and operate AI for defensive cybersecurity: hosting local large language models, retrieval-augmented generation over security frameworks, and orchestrated autonomous agentic workflows (LangChain, LangGraph, and the Model Context Protocol) that carry out cybersecurity tasks against isolated lab targets. Two capabilities exceed a personal laptop and drive this request: a GPU-backed environment to host a capable LLM that orchestrates multi-step agentic tasks, and multiple virtual machines per student, an attacker/analysis VM and deliberately vulnerable targets, on an isolated network. We request GPU compute roughly 100 GB of persistent storage per student, accessed via SSH. All datasets are public and all software open source, with offensive activity confined to instructor-provisioned lab networks.

requestTitle: Advanced Prompt Engineering for Cyber Professionals - USCGA
abstract:
This classroom allocation will support a fall undergraduate course that prepares cadets of the US Coast Guard Academy to use large language models and generative AI tools effectively, safely, and critically in cyber operations and C5I professional contexts. 

The course emphasizes practical AI fluency rather than model-training theory. Students will complete hands-on labs in prompt engineering, document-grounded generation, retrieval-augmented generation, AI-assisted code development and debugging, structured output generation, agentic AI concepts, and professional communication products such as executive summaries, vulnerability reports, and technical briefings.

NAIRR Classroom resources will provide a common, controlled computing environment for all students. This is needed to avoid unequal reliance on personal AI accounts, to support repeatable notebook-based labs, and to allow students to work with shared public or instructor-created technical documents, code examples, and evaluation artifacts. 

The course will emphasize verification discipline, recognition of AI failure modes, operational-security awareness, and appropriate human oversight of AI-assisted workflows.

requestTitle: Scale-Aware Generative Models for Physical Dynamics
abstract: Physical systems exhibit rich multiscale dynamics across space and time. Turbulent flows, weather systems, biological motion, and many other scientific phenomena contain coherent structures spanning a wide range of spatial and temporal frequencies. However, most modern generative video models treat all frequencies uniformly during training and generation, without explicitly modeling the scale structure inherent in physical data. The goal of this project is to develop scale-aware generative models for physical dynamics by extending our preliminary work in scale-invariant diffusion models on images. In our preliminary work, we demonstrated that organizing diffusion processes across frequencies enables hierarchical coarse-to-fine reconstruction and improves the modeling of self-similar image statistics. These results provide initial evidence that scale-aware diffusion processes can effectively model multiscale structure, which motivates us to extend this framework to spatiotemporal generative modeling, where both spatial and temporal scales play central roles.

requestTitle: Language Models as Rubric Judge, Jury, and Executioner
abstract: Current efforts to train AI agents at scale rely heavily on “playgrounds” whose tasks have well-specified notions of success, such as mathematics and code. Yet many economically and scientifically important tasks do not admit a clear executable definition of correctness.  For example, in deep research, agents must perform multi-step information gathering and produce long-form, well-attributed answers, but the desiderata for a good response are often underspecified and difficult to evaluate automatically (Shao et al. 2025). This proposal requests computation for basic research on rubric-grounded judges and feedback models: evaluation systems that take as input segments of an AI agent’s behavior, relevant context, and judgment instructions, and produce structured assessments along specified dimensions. More accurate and efficient rubric-evaluator models would expand the range of tasks on which AI systems can be trained using reinforcement learning, and make long-horizon agent learning more practical by providing scalable oversight for trajectories even in the absence of simple, verifiable outcomes. The models resulting from this project will support research on reinforcement learning in non-verifiable domains by making feedback signals cheaper, more reproducible, private, and easier to inspect. We will train and evaluate new rubric-judge models, iterating on both data and methods. The efforts described here serve a longer-term goal: developing feedback signals for learning agents in domains where task success cannot be reduced to a simple verifier.

abstract: CS383: Data Science and Machine Learning at York College, CUNY, is being developed and piloted as part of our new Undergraduate AI Online Certificate through the CUNY Tech Futures initiative. In this course, students work through the complete data science workflow, including data cleaning, exploratory data analysis, supervised and unsupervised machine learning with Scikit-Learn, and neural network development using TensorFlow and PyTorch. As students move into the deep learning and final project components, the computational requirements quickly exceed what most student laptops can support. Without access to shared computing resources, students would be limited to using small, simplified datasets rather than working with data that more closely reflects real-world applications. Access to the NAIRR Pilot Classroom resources would allow students to use JupyterLab to train and evaluate models on larger datasets, giving them practical experience with modern AI and machine learning workflows while strengthening the implementation of this new certificate program.

requestTitle: NAIRR AI in Education with Pilot Classroom Resources
abstract:
This project will pilot the integration of National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) classroom resources into undergraduate and graduate computing courses (CSS382 and CSS566) at the University of Washington Bothell. The initiative leverages the Vocareum AI Notebook platform to provide students with scalable, cloud-based access to GPU-enabled environments for hands-on artificial intelligence and machine learning education.

In CSS382: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, students will engage in guided laboratories, programming assignments, and project-based learning activities to develop practical experience in natural language processing using industry-relevant tools and workflows. Topics include introduction to machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI techniques supported through interactive notebook-based experimentation.

In CSS566: Software Management, Vocareum AI Notebooks will be integrated with collaborative software development and project management platforms such as GitHub and Jira to support project-based software engineering and AI application development. Students will gain experience with team-based development workflows, version control, cloud-based AI deployment environments, and agile project management practices relevant to modern AI-enabled software systems.

The project will further explore reproducible and scalable classroom deployment models for AI education, including shared datasets, collaborative development workflows, cloud-based resource provisioning, and managed GPU access. Outcomes from the pilot will inform broader adoption of NAIRR-supported infrastructure in computing curricula while expanding equitable access to advanced AI education and workforce preparation opportunities in higher education.

requestTitle: Introduction to Humanoid Robotics: Human-Robot Interaction, Kinematics, and Autonomy
abstract:
At the University of Minnesota Duluth — a research-emerging institution serving a large rural and first-generation student population — access to advanced AI computing infrastructure has historically constrained what students can build. This course changes that.
CS 4452/5452, Introduction to Humanoid Robotics: Human-Robot Interaction, Kinematics, and Autonomy, is a 4-credit, project-based community-engaged learning course in which undergraduate and graduate students assemble and program Hiwonder AiNex humanoid robots using the Robot Operating System (ROS), train AI vision models using PyTorch and OpenCV, and deploy their systems at real community partner sites — nursing homes, assisted living facilities, adult day care centers, and mental health organizations across the Duluth region.
NAIRR Classroom resources provide the GPU compute that makes this course possible at scale. Students work in teams to fine-tune deep learning models for face detection, gesture recognition, object recognition, and human activity classification — tasks that require concurrent GPU training infeasible on local instructional machines. NAIRR's JupyterHub environment also supports a structured Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) study embedded in the course: students design and conduct empirical studies at community partner sites, measuring how residents and staff respond to the AiNex robot on dimensions of trust, comfort, and anthropomorphism. Findings from these studies directly shape robot behavior design for community deployments.
The course emphasizes that technically capable AI systems can still fail when the humans around them are not comfortable, informed, or well-served. This human-centered framing — grounded in real community relationships, real data, and real ethical stakes — prepares students for careers in AI and robotics that extend beyond technical competence to social responsibility.
By making advanced AI infrastructure accessible at a rural-serving institution, NAIRR enables a replicable model for community-engaged AI education that other research-emerging institutions can adopt.

requestTitle: Start-Up: Jadelynn Dao, Stanford University
End-to-End 3D Reconstruction for Organ-Level Maize Tassel Phenotyping Using Close-Range Aerial RGB Imagery
abstract:
This project develops and validates a scalable, reproducible pipeline for organ-level 3D reconstruction and phenotyping of maize tassels using close-range aerial RGB imagery. While neural field-based reconstruction methods have demonstrated strong performance in controlled environments, there is a lack of open, field-realistic, organ-level datasets that enable systematic benchmarking and downstream scientific analysis. 

The proposed work reconstructs tassel geometry from multi-view UAV imagery using neural field methods initialized with structure-from-motion camera poses and refined through mixed-precision training on H100-class GPUs. Reconstruction is performed over spatially localized tiles, followed by isolation of individual tassel instances and extraction of biologically meaningful morphometric traits. Reconstruction quality and phenotyping validity are evaluated using image-based metrics, repeatability analyses across replicate flights, and robustness studies under view subsampling and environmental variability.

All outputs, including curated datasets, standardized metadata, open-source workflows, and evaluation benchmarks, will be released under permissive open licenses. By producing AI-ready data resources and validated workflows, this project directly supports the NAIRR Pilot mission to expand equitable access to advanced AI infrastructure and accelerate open scientific discovery.

requestTitle: Reimagining Education with AI: An Open Framework for Interoperability and Learning
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used by students for coding and learning tasks, yet its role in education remains largely unstructured and difficult to evaluate. This project proposes an open-source, web-based AI assistant framework integrated directly into computational learning environments to provide structured support for programming education. Rather than replacing instruction, the system offers context-aware hints, debugging assistance, and explanations within the coding workflow. The framework is designed to be modular and extensible, enabling integration with multiple AI models and tools to support diverse instructional needs. By enabling controlled deployment and evaluation, this project investigates how AI-assisted interactions influence problem-solving strategies, debugging behavior, and learning outcomes. The expected outcome is an open, reusable research framework and empirical insights that can guide the effective and responsible integration of AI into education.

Data Management and Business Intelligence MBA Course
abstract: Data-driven decision making has become a critical competency for modern business leaders. The course Data Management and Business Intelligence introduces MBA students in the Business Intelligence and Analytics concentration to the foundations of data management, database systems, and analytical decision support. Through a hands-on learning environment based on Jupyter Notebooks, students develop practical skills in organizing, querying, and analyzing business data using SQL, SQLite, and Python-based analytical tools. The course emphasizes the complete lifecycle of business data, from database design and data modeling to querying, reporting, and business intelligence applications. Students work with realistic business scenarios and datasets to learn how organizations transform raw data into actionable insights that support strategic and operational decision making. Topics include relational databases, entity-relationship modeling, SQL querying, data integration, data quality, business reporting, and introductory analytics. Computational resources are requested to provide students with cloud-based Jupyter Notebook environments that support interactive exercises, assignments, and projects throughout the course. These resources will enable students to access a consistent computing platform regardless of their personal hardware capabilities while gaining practical experience with industry-relevant tools and workflows.

requestTitle: Reliable LLM Pipelines for Extracting Housing Outcomes, Service Trajectories, and Longitudinal Summaries from De-identified Street Outreach Case Notes
abstract: This project develops trustworthy AI methods for extracting useful information from de-identified homelessness outreach case notes. Working with data from Breaking Ground, a nonprofit that provides street outreach and homelessness services, we will use open-weight large language models to identify housing outcomes, service trajectories, and barriers from free-text records, and to generate longitudinal client summaries. The research focuses not only on model accuracy, but on interpretability and trust: we will study calibrated uncertainty, ensembling, hallucination detection, targeted correction, and learning from nonprofit and expert edits so that outputs can  be reviewed and used more reliably. The project will produce both a research-ready  dataset derived from unstructured notes and reusable methods for trustworthy measurement and summarization from sensitive-domain text.

requestTitle: Fine-Tuning Evo2-40B Genomic Foundation Model for Long-Read Microbial Classification
abstract: This project will fine-tune Evo2-40B, a 40-billion-parameter genomic foundation model developed by the Arc Institute, on long-read microbial metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) to improve phylogenetic placement, phenotype prediction, and taxonomic classification of gut microbial sequences. The 40B model's extended context length (1,048,576 bp) is uniquely suited to long-read assemblies that span megabases, a regime where smaller 1B and 7B models underperform.

requestTitle: Attack Provenance in LLM-Powered Agentic Systems
abstract: LLM-powered agentic systems, including Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and LLM-based agents, have become a transformative computing paradigm, yet their expanding attack surface leaves them vulnerable to adversarial manipulation that existing defenses cannot reliably prevent. This project tackles a complementary and underexplored problem: attack provenance, the post-hoc task of tracing a misgeneration event back to the specific compromised component that caused it. We propose a unified algorithmic foundation that traces adversarial influence in RAG and LLM-based agents, achieving high detection accuracy with low inference cost. The project advances the security and transparency of agentic AI by pinpointing the root causes of adversarial misgenerations.

requestTitle: Graph-Matched Swarm Intelligence for Lifelong Video Agents
abstract: Video is an information-rich modality central to applications such as surveillance, autonomous systems, and scientific sensing, yet current video understanding systems remain limited by static architectures, one-shot inference, and weak long-horizon reasoning. This project proposes a new paradigm for video intelligence: lifelong swarm intelligence for video agents. We develop a multi-agent framework in which task-specific collaboration structures are dynamically constructed through graph matching between video-task requirements and agent capabilities, followed by swarm-based reasoning and continual learning. The proposed system enables adaptive coordination, memory-augmented reasoning, and explicit, domain-grounded explanations, allowing agents to reason over long-duration videos while continuously improving over time. By integrating graph-structured coordination, uncertainty-aware collaboration, and verbalized reasoning, this work advances the foundations of collective AI and enables scalable, interpretable, and resilient video understanding systems.

requestTitle: Trustworthy Vision-Language Models via Minimal Sufficient Captions for Faithful Image Generation
abstract:
Vision–language models often generate hallucinations fluent but incorrect statements about objects, attributes, or relations that are not actually present in the image undermining reliability in safety critical settings such as medical imaging, autonomous systems, and misinformation detection. Existing work can detect hallucinations or refine captions to be more complete, but it does not explicitly optimize the trade off between caption length and visual fidelity, nor does it provide principled tools to derive concise, grounded descriptions that are just sufficient for faithful image reconstruction. This gap limits both trustworthiness and efficiency, as long, redundant captions increase compute and still leave room for ungrounded content.
This project develops a trustworthy vision–language framework that detects, localizes, and corrects hallucinations by learning minimal sufficient captions, defined as the shortest captions that still support faithful reconstruction of the source image above a target fidelity threshold. The approach combines reconstruction guided recaptioning, semantic claim extraction, knowledge graph aware verification, and iterative caption pruning and addition to enforce visual groundedness while preserving answer quality. Planned outputs include a vision hallucination benchmark suite, a two stage detector–corrector pipeline, and open source code, datasets (where licenses permit), evaluation prompts, and reproducible NAIRR runbooks for deployment on national GPU resources.
