requestTitle: Scalable Bug and Fix Trajectory Synthesis for Training AI Software Engineering Agents
abstract: Software systems underpin cloud platforms, critical infrastructure, and large-scale digital services. Ensuring the reliability and security of these systems requires tools that can automatically detect and repair defects. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled new forms of AI-driven software engineering agents capable of reasoning about code and debugging complex programs. However, progress in training such agents is limited by the lack of large-scale datasets containing realistic software defects and verified repair processes. This project proposes SWE-SYNTH, a scalable framework for generating synthetic software defects and repair trajectories using LLMs, enabling the creation of large training corpora for AI-driven debugging agents and advancing research on code repair.

requestTitle: Open-World Robustness in Foundation Models via Generative Continual Learning
abstract: Large foundation models achieve strong performance across language and vision tasks but rely on static training assumptions that do not hold in dynamic, open-world environments. In practice, models must handle evolving data streams, open-vocabulary concepts, and adversarial prompt manipulations. This project proposes a unified meta-learning framework that treats adversarial prompt ordering and semantic manipulation as a continual learning problem. Instead of static filtering or one-shot fine-tuning, we develop modular generative architectures with shared encoders and concept-specific branches to enable expansion without catastrophic forgetting. We further introduce a meta-reinforcement learning approach to adapt inference-time data management strategies, such as filtering, ordering, and replay, under shifting threat distributions. The framework also supports modality-incremental adaptation, aligning new input modalities while preserving prior safety guarantees. Together, this work establishes a scalable and principled foundation for robust inference in open-world foundation models.

requestTitle: Computational Redesign of S. pombe Poly(U) Polymerase Cid1 for Selective Poly(G) and Poly(C) Synthesis Using AI-Driven Protein Design
abstract: Template-independent poly(U) polymerases (PUPs) catalyze non-templated addition of UTP to RNA 3′ ends. The S. pombe homolog Cid1 (PDB: 4FH5) has crystal structures with all four NTPs (UTP: 4FH5, ATP: 4FHV, GTP: 4FHW, CTP: 4FHY), yet incorporates UTP with ~30× selectivity over ATP and negligible GTP/CTP activity. We will computationally redesign the Cid1 nucleotide-binding pocket to selectively incorporate GTP (poly-G polymerase) and CTP (poly-C polymerase) while abolishing UTP activity. This is part of an ongoing effort to engineer orthogonal template-free polymerases for programmable RNA synthesis. Redesigning selectivity requires reconfiguring (1) central domain residues to satisfy the distinct heavy-atom patterns of guanine (O6, N1-H, N2-H₂, N7) or cytosine (O2, N3, N4-H₂) rather than uracil (O2, N3-H, O4), and (2) the H5 helix geometry to accommodate modified nucleotide contacts. We employ a multi-stage pipeline: RFdiffusion for backbone remodeling, LigandMPNN for sequence design/scoring, AlphaFold3 for structure prediction, and AMBER MD for binding validation (Fig. 1).

requestTitle: Rubric-based Reward Modeling for Efficient LLM Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for writing, coding, and question answering, but they often produce unnecessarily long, repetitive explanations. This “overthinking” increases response time and cost because most LLM services are priced by the number of generated tokens, and longer outputs do not always improve correctness. This project will develop a rubric-based reward modeling approach to make LLM reasoning more efficient. We will design clear, human-interpretable rubrics that score responses on correctness, conciseness, and non-redundancy, and use these rubrics to generate preference-style supervision for training a reward model. The resulting reward model will be used to steer LLMs toward shorter, higher-information answers while preserving accuracy. Success will be measured by reductions in output length and repetition, and by maintaining task performance on public benchmarks. We will release rubric specifications, an anonymized dataset of prompts and rubric-derived labels, and reproducible evaluation code to support broader community use.

requestTitle: Attention Via Convolutional Nearest Neighbors
abstract: The shift from Convolutional Neural Networks to Transformers has reshaped computer vision, yet these two architectural families are typically viewed as fundamentally distinct. We argue that convolution and self-attention, despite their apparent differences, can be unified within a single k-nearest neighbor aggregation framework. The critical insight is that both operations are special cases of neighbor selection and aggregation; convolution selects neighbors by spatial proximity, while attention selects by feature similarity, revealing they exist on a continuous spectrum. We introduce Convolutional Nearest Neighbors (ConvNN). a unified framework that formalizes this connection. Crucially, ConvNN serves as a drop-in replacement for convolutional and attention layers, enabling systematic exploration of the intermediate spectrum between these two extremes. We validate the framework's coherence on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 classification tasks across two complementary architectures: (1) Hybrid branching in VGG improves accuracy on both CIFAR datasets by combining spatial-proximity and feature-similarity selection; and (2) ConvNN in ViT outperforms standard attention and other attention variants on both datasets. Extensive ablations on k values and architectural variants reveal that interpolating along this spectrum provides regularization benefits by balancing local and global receptive fields. Our work provides a unifying framework that dissolves the apparent distinction between convolution and attention, with implications for designing more principled and interpretable vision architectures.

requestTitle: Curriculum-Driven RL for Generalizable Multimodal Agents
abstract: This project aims to advance \textbf{reinforcement learning (RL) for multimodal agents} that must perceive, reason, and act across long-horizon, multi-turn interactions. Our central goal is to develop and evaluate curriculum-driven learning strategies that help agents progressively acquire skills, while also improving their ability to internalize environment dynamics i.e., learn an actionable world model that supports planning, generalization, and recovery under ambiguity. The outcome is a reproducible training-and-evaluation pipeline and benchmark suite for multimodal RL for multi-turn embodied settings.

abstract: This project conducts the first large-scale empirical study of emergent unfaithfulness in safety-aligned large language models — the phenomenon whereby the most capable LLMs silently alter their outputs on faithfulness-critical tasks when source content conflicts with alignment objectives. We will map emergence thresholds across 20+ model configurations, develop mitigation methods and release an open-source benchmark dataset for evaluating safety, faithfulness, and capability trade-offs in LLMs.

requestTitle: Stable Multi-turn RL for Reliable Computer-Use Agents
abstract:
Training reliable computer-use agents via online reinforcement learning remains a fundamental challenge due to instability in long-horizon, multi-turn interaction. While recent large language models demonstrate strong reasoning abilities, they often fail in grounded execution, particularly under dynamic GUI environments where small execution errors compound over time. The lack of stable and reproducible reinforcement learning pipelines for interactive agents has limited systematic progress in this domain.

We propose a hierarchical Brain–Body architecture for stable multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning. The architecture decouples high-level strategic reasoning (Commander) from low-level grounded execution (Pilot), enabling structured optimization across distinct levels of abstraction. We introduce a three-stage training framework: (1) supervised perceptual grounding with calibrated abstention to stabilize action execution; (2) structured strategic alignment with state-consistency regularization to reduce plan–execution divergence; and (3) large-scale online iterative reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to address long-horizon credit assignment and self-correction. 

This project delivers an open-source OSWorld agent and a reproducible VeRL-based reinforcement learning stack, establishing a scalable and transparent framework for studying stable multi-turn RL in real GUI environments.

requestTitle: Proactive Validation to Detect and Diagnose Silent Errors in Deep Learning Training
abstract:
Large-scale deep learning training is now foundational to artificial
intelligence research and deployment, enabling unprecedented advances in
society. However, modern training pipelines are complex, making them vulnerable to silent training errors. These errors can invalidate weeks of computation and consume vast computational resources before being detected, if they are detected at all. Current practices rely on coarse signals such as loss or accuracy, which are often insufficient to detect these failures early or to explain their root causes. 

This project proposes a proactive approach to improving the reliability and
efficiency of large-scale deep learning training by continuously validating
training correctness during execution. Building on our preliminary work,
the project develops and evaluates new techniques to automatically derive
training invariants, efficiently check them at runtime, and provide automated
diagnosis after error detection. By reducing wasted computation and improving trust in training results, this work will contribute to reliable and efficient AI infrastructure.

requestTitle: Diagnosing Predictions of Scientific Foundation Models
abstract: Scientific foundation models (SciFMs) are increasingly deployed across a wide range of scientific domains. A central challenge is determining whether a specific model output should be trusted. Existing uncertainty quantification methods provide calibration guarantees only in aggregate and fail to address the query-level questions most relevant to scientific decision-making. This project develops practical, query-level output quantification diagnostics for pretrained scientific foundation models using internal network representations. Leveraging recent advances in statistical learning theory and the spectral analysis of deep neural networks, we propose a suite of lightweight, interpretable diagnostic metrics that characterize how individual inputs propagate through a model. These metrics capture complementary aspects of internal representations and provide a compact characterization of whether a given query is likely to produce an unreliable output. The proposed approach will be evaluated on open-source large language models for reasoning tasks and on scientific foundation models applied to partial differential equation benchmarks and earth-system prediction datasets. The project aligns directly with NAIRR Pilot goals by advancing trustworthy and interpretable AI methods for scientific discovery while enabling efficient use of shared national computing resources through post hoc, compute-light diagnostics rather than large-scale retraining.

requestTitle: Hands-on AI Safety and Security Education for the AI Workforce Using Classroom-Scale LLM Resources
abstract:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming part of education, software development, cybersecurity, business, public policy, and everyday decision-making. However, students often learn to use AI tools without enough hands-on experience in understanding how these systems fail, how they can be misused, and how they should be evaluated before deployment. This project will support a classroom resource allocation for AIP290/CS290, Ethics, Safety and Security of AI, a core course in the new BS program in AI+ at Southern Illinois University Carbondale. The course will prepare undergraduate students to understand the ethical, safety, and security challenges of modern AI systems and to evaluate AI tools responsibly.
NAIRR classroom resources will be used to add a practical computing component to the course. Students will use a shared Jupyter-based environment and GPU-supported language model inference to complete selected hands-on activities on LLM prompting, hallucination and verification, prompt injection and AI security risks, and zero-shot application development with code security review. Students will work with selected open-source language models to explore how modern AI systems behave in realistic settings and to evaluate issues related to reliability, security, and responsible deployment.
The project will broaden access to practical AI safety and security education by giving students reliable classroom-scale access to computational resources that may not be available through personal laptops or free tools. Students will complete lab notebooks, short risk-analysis reports, AI-generated code review exercises, and a final team project. These activities will help students connect technical AI behavior with ethical reasoning, security analysis, and governance considerations. The resulting instructional materials will be reusable in future offerings of the course and will contribute to building an AI-ready workforce prepared to develop, evaluate, and deploy trustworthy AI systems.

abstract: CSE 587: Deep Learning for Natural Language Processing at The Pennsylvania State University teaches graduate students to build, train, and analyze modern language models from the ground up. Through hands-on programming assignments, students implement a Transformer from scratch, fine-tune a reasoning model with reinforcement learning, write a high-performance GPU kernel, and complete a team project. A NAIRR Pilot allocation gives roughly 35 students the computing resources to train and experiment at realistic scale, while introducing them to national research cyberinfrastructure and preparing them for careers in AI research and engineering.

requestTitle: Sparse-to-Dense 3D Brain Image Generation and Neural Circuit Instance Segmentation
abstract: We propose an expert-in-the-loop data flywheel comprising three tightly coupled model components that iteratively improve one another. (1) A 3D instance segmentation model that takes raw high-resolution neuron volumes and produces per-neuron instance masks. This is a particularly challenging problem: 3D instance segmentation for neuron imaging remains underexplored, and neuron morphology is highly deformable, making standard architectures insufficient. Developing effective models requires extensive experimentation and compute-intensive iterative training. (2) Promptable refinement models that accept expert spatial prompts to refine predicted instance boundaries. These serve as the interactive backend through which neuroscientists correct segmentation outputs. (3) A generative augmentation model based on latent diffusion that learns the 3D neuron data distribution from fewer than 100 labeled samples and synthesizes realistic training volumes, expanding the effective dataset by up to two orders of magnitude. The flywheel operates as follows: the instance segmentation model produces initial predictions, experts refine them through the promptable models, and the refined annotations retrain the segmentation model and condition the generative model for higher-quality synthetic data. Each cycle improves all three components.

requestTitle: Agent Audit: Scalable Security and Trust Evaluation Infrastructure for LLM Agent Systems
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used in coding, retrieval, enterprise automation, scientific workflows, and decision support. In these settings, failures often arise not only from model weights, but from the surrounding software stack, including unsafe tool execution, prompt injection surfaces, exposed credentials, insecure subprocess usage, over-privileged deployment settings, and misconfigured Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. This project scales Agent Audit, an open-source security analysis system for LLM agent applications, into a broader research infrastructure for security and trust evaluation of agent systems. The project will expand agent-security evaluation from a small benchmark to a larger open benchmark spanning repositories, configuration artifacts, and synthetic vulnerability cases. It will also combine static analysis with model-assisted red-teaming and remediation analysis using both open-weight LLMs on GPU systems and major commercial model APIs. The resulting open-source tools, benchmarks, reports, and reproducible workflows will support safer and more trustworthy development and deployment of LLM agent systems.

requestTitle: Principled Generative AI for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have demonstrated promising potential for automated scientific discovery. Large language models (LLMs) have already been used to assist or automate discovery in diverse domains, including mathematical optimization, physical systems modeling, and molecular design. These systems typically generate candidate hypotheses, algorithms, or programs that are evaluated by external tools such as simulators, theorem provers, or experimental pipelines. Our recent work DeltaEvolve explores this paradigm by combining LLM-based proposal generation with evolutionary search. While such approaches have shown promising empirical results, current methods largely rely on heuristic evolutionary algorithms, and there remains a fundamental gap in understanding how to design principled search and sampling strategies for scientific discovery with LLMs. This project aims to develop principled generative AI frameworks for autonomous discovery, focusing on both algorithmic foundations and large-scale empirical validation.

requestTitle: Evaluating Alignment of Privacy Norms and Preferences in LLMs
abstract:
As LLM agents increasingly complete tasks on behalf of users with little to no user intervention, LLMs must determine what user information is acceptable to disclose to a service provider and what information is private. 
In making this determination current LLMs focus primarily on privacy norms (what the majority considers appropriate), but individual privacy preferences are not adequately considered. Relying on societal privacy norms reduces the need for an agent to repeatedly request for user intervention to make this determination. The goal of this proposal is to understand how LLMs make privacy decisions when conditioned on three distinct levels of personalization: (1) general norms, (2) user privacy preferences and (3) privacy personas (archetypes of users with shared preferences).  Evaluating on these three levels of personalization quantifies how well they capture human privacy expectations-- either collectively (privacy norms) or individually (individual privacy preferences). This insight is vital for scenarios where the agent lacks sufficient privacy preferences from a user to make confident privacy decisions. Hence, the agent must contextually weigh general norms against preferences or personas. The OpenAI API credits provided by the NAIRR Pilot are essential for this study.

Leveraging Self-Supervised Transformers to Build a Foundation Model of 4D Mitochondrial Dynamics and Cancer Drug Action
abstract: This project leverages foundation-scale Vision Transformer architectures and expansive 4D microscopy data to create a self-supervised semantic latent space linking cellular phenotypes to drug action in cancer cells. Existing high-content screening methodologies are limited to two dimensions, missing the critical information residing in the fast three-dimensional interplay of drugs with cellular organelles. Our lab utilizes adaptive optics lattice light-sheet microscopy (AO-LLSM) for real-time 4D (x,y,z,t) imaging, generating a massive 50TB multichannel dataset of Cal27 cancer cells under the influence of 26 different drugs. We aim to combine state-of-the-art transformer architectures with our existing self-supervised deep learning frameworks to derive an interpretable latent space that links mitochondrial dynamics to drug action at the foundation scale. Achieving this requires 75,000 GPU hours on the DeltaAI GPU cluster, utilizing its GH200 nodes to handle the immense computational and high-speed NVMe storage demands of our 50TB dataset. Successful completion will establish the first latent space embeddings of high-content LLSM cancer drug screening data, forming the basis for next-generation approaches that will transform drug discovery.

requestTitle: Uncovering the Power of Unified Multimodal Models for World Modeling
abstract: Unlocking the full potential of foundation models—AI systems capable of understanding and generating content—requires empowering them to seamlessly interact across multiple modalities, such as text, images, and actions. This capability is critical for advancing applications in fields like robotics, autonomous systems, and healthcare. Emerging unified generative models, such as Bagel, represent a promising step toward achieving this multimodal intelligence by enabling the generation of both text and images in a cohesive and interleaved manner. However, these unified models still fall short in performance compared to specialized models like large language models or advanced image-generation systems. Our research aims to bridge this performance gap by leveraging reinforcement learning, a powerful technique that enables systems to continuously improve through trial-and-error learning. We will systematically evaluate existing reinforcement learning algorithms on unified models to identify their strengths and limitations, and we will develop a novel algorithm tailored specifically to the unique structure of unified models. This research will not only advance the algorithms but also demonstrate their practical value through applications in robotics, focusing on navigation tasks where multimodal intelligence can make a significant impact. Additionally, we are committed to fostering broader progress in this field by open-sourcing our results, including the implementation of our algorithm, model checkpoints, and evaluation tools. By doing so, we seek to accelerate the development of unified multimodal intelligence and its transformative applications across diverse industries.

requestTitle: Next-Generation Multi-Modal Protein Language Models for Controllable Protein Design
abstract: This project will develop next-generation AI models for protein design that jointly learn from protein sequences and three-dimensional structures. Current protein language models often treat proteins primarily as one-dimensional amino acid strings, limiting their ability to capture the structural and biophysical information that governs function. We propose a unified multimodal framework that combines two discrete protein representations developed in our lab: one for 3D structure and one for high-level sequence semantics. These representations will be integrated into a single autoregressive transformer model for controllable protein generation and optimization across tasks, including de novo design, inverse folding, binder design, and property-guided sequence editing. Using large public resources comprising more than 3 billion sequences and roughly 800 million structures, we will train and benchmark foundation-scale models while also studying scaling behavior with respect to data, model size, and representation design. The project aligns with NAIRR by leveraging advanced AI, large-scale biological data, and national computing infrastructure to create broadly useful methods for scientific discovery and biomedical innovation.

requestTitle: Generating Highly Performant Code via Multi-modal Representation and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Due to the rapid growth of data-intensive and AI-driven applications, there is an increasing demand for software that can fully exploit modern High-Performance Computing (HPC) systems. This project proposes a comprehensive framework for automatically rewriting sequential programs to run efficiently and reliably on multicore and manycore architectures. By combining advanced program analysis with reinforcement learning techniques, the framework gains a deep understanding of program structure and semantics to identify and generate parallelizable code while preserving intended functionality. It employs a graph-based multimodal contrastive learning approach that integrates LLVM intermediate representation graphs with source-level code, leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) to learn intrinsic parallel characteristics and directly produce parallelized programs without manual annotations. Generated programs will be validated using differential testing across diverse inputs and configurations to ensure output consistency with the original code. In addition, scalable validation techniques will be employed to verify array and algebraic transformations, including reduction parallelization common in HPC applications.

requestTitle: Physics-Constrained and Compressed AI for Radiance and Photon Flux Estimation from Hyperspectral Data
abstract: Hyperspectral imaging measures reflected or emitted light across hundreds of narrow wavelengths, providing rich information about atmospheric conditions, clouds, and Earth system processes. However, the extremely high data volume makes storage, transmission, and analysis computationally expensive, limiting its widespread use in large-scale monitoring. This project develops physics-constrained and computationally efficient AI methods to estimate radiance and photon-flux–related quantities from hyperspectral imagery while dramatically reducing data dimensionality. Using our publicly available (and expanding) dataset of radiometrically calibrated cloud imagery containing 462 spectral bands, we will investigate whether the essential information can be represented by a small number of learned spectral channels without sacrificing accuracy or interpretability. The approach combines physically informed constraints with neural network compression techniques to produce compact models that require less computation and energy. By enabling faster processing of hyperspectral data on shared national AI infrastructure, the project supports scalable atmospheric analysis and contributes to the broader goal of making advanced environmental sensing technologies more accessible and efficient.

requestTitle: Vulnerability Exploration and Mitigation for Safe Reinforcement Learning in Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) are increasingly integrated with intelligence to operate autonomously in complex environments. Safe Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been widely used to synthesize control policies that maximize task performance while satisfying safety constraints. As neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, the deployment of safe RL policies may cause safety violations in real-world CPS. This project aims to secure safe RL policies in CPS. We propose an end-to-end solution that spreads from identifying vulnerabilities in safe RL to its mitigation, covering both training and inference time. Our vulnerability exploration methods will generate effective and stealthy attacks for safety violation, while our mitigation methods will enhance the robustness of safe RL control policies. Using the requested computing resources, we plan to train, test, and deploy our solution using various high-fidelity simulators. We expect that our solution will significantly improve safety of safe RL enabled CPS in an adversarial setting.

requestTitle: Building High-Fidelity Digital Twins of Older Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment for Accelerating Conversational AI Development Against Dementia
abstract: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is a common prodromal stage of dementia, yet scalable and clinically grounded interventions remain limited. The I-CONECT clinical trial demonstrates that structured conversational engagement can reduce dementia risk and provides a uniquely valuable longitudinal dataset of cognitively meaningful spoken interactions. Meanwhile, large language model (LLM)–based conversational agents offer promise for supporting older adults with MCI, but their evaluation and alignment are hindered by ethical, logistical, and methodological barriers to large-scale human studies. This proposal aims to build high-fidelity digital twins of I-CONECT participants—fine-tuned LLMs that preserve clinically relevant cognitive signals, individual response patterns, and interaction dynamics—and to use them as a pre-deployment testbed for generative AI systems targeting cognitively vulnerable populations. We address key challenges in medical-fidelity transcription of disfluent clinical speech, modeling individualized conversational response mechanisms, and ensuring digital twin fidelity at both clinical and individual levels. The resulting framework will enable rigorous, low-risk evaluation of conversational AI for MCI and advance understanding of language, cognition, and interaction in aging.

requestTitle: Distilling Multimodal World Knowledge for Self-Driving
abstract: The goal of this NAIRR Pilot project is to develop and validate a practical framework for distilling “world knowledge” from multimodal large language models (MLLMs) into real-time self-driving planning models. While MLLMs trained on web-scale vision–language data can capture rich semantic and commonsense information (e.g., road topology, interaction intent cues, risk-relevant context), directly deploying an MLLM as a driving policy is often infeasible due to latency and compute constraints. Our objective is therefore to transfer useful MLLM capabilities into a lightweight camera-based planner that preserves real-time inference while improving reliability in complex and safety-critical scenarios.

requestTitle: Extraction of genetic variants from scientific fulltext document
abstract:
Abstract: As often in medicine, medical geneticists employ multiple nomenclatures and informal shorthand to describe genome variants (DNA mutations), so genetic variants are described inconsistently in scientific text, which makes automated extraction in software highly difficult (Wei et al, Bioinf 2018). However, during rare-disease diagnosis, one of the most critical steps is determining whether a genetic variant has ever been reported previously (criteria “PS1/PS4” in the American College of Medical Genetics’s diagnostic rulebook). In addition, with over 4,000 biomedical articles published per day, and at the very least tens of thousands of new publications annually containing genetic variant mentions, complete manual curation is impossible. Existing commercial solutions rely on labor-intensive curation of selected journals or outdated rule-based natural language processing (NLP) of selected publications, leaving a large fraction of genetic variants of the biomedical literature unindexed.
Our prior system, AVADA (Birgmeier et al., Genetics in Medicine 2023), demonstrated that automated extraction of variant evidence at diagnostic quality is feasible. AVADA has been deployed on the UCSC Genome Browser, where the resulting “variant-literature” track has become increasingly popular, at several thousand users per year. Recently, we re-implemented the variant extraction pipeline using an improved extraction workflow that allows regular, reproducible updates of the variants database based on mentions in scientific publications. The updated system has already been deployed on the UCSC Genome Browser by the same lead software engineer who built the original AVADA infrastructure. While the system currently shows promising recall (sensitivity), the precision (specificity) of extractions is quite low. Early tests show that adding an LLM-based component to verify extracted variants  substantially increases specificity, but realizing this gain requires processing ~2 million full-text articles containing variant mentions in diverse human-readable notations.
Here, we propose to run an LLM-enhanced pipeline across this full corpus of full-text articles using NAIRR HPC GPU resources. The outcome will be a comprehensive, freely available mapping of genetic variants to the scientific literature, deployed through the UCSC Genome Browser-an environment supported by staff with over two decades of experience in large-scale data management, curation, and stable production services. This resource will meaningfully accelerate variant interpretation in clinical genetics and rare-disease research.

Geometry and Training Dynamics of Representations in Large Language Models
abstract:
This project investigates the geometry and training dynamics of layerwise hidden representations in large language models (LLMs), through the lens of feature compression and linear steering. Linear steering methods modify model behavior by injecting directions into hidden representations, yet their effectiveness varies substantially across layers and models. A key open question is which geometric properties of representations make a layer more steerable, and how these properties emerge during training.

Building on our prior work on representation geometry and steering methods , we will analyze the geometric structure of hidden states across layers and relate these properties to the success of steering interventions for various concept. In addition, we will conduct controlled training experiments to study the dynamics of representation formation, examining how meaningful semantic directions and concept subspaces gradually emerge during training and how their formation relates to model capabilities such as generalization, reasoning, and grokking-like transitions.

Vision-Language-Guided Adaptive Control of Autonomous Search-and-Rescue Quadrupedal Robots
abstract:
Disaster environments—such as collapsed buildings, debris-filled corridors, and unstable terrain—require robotic systems capable of navigating, perceiving, and physically interacting with complex surroundings. Quadrupedal robots equipped with manipulator arms provide a powerful platform: they can traverse rough, unstructured terrain beyond the capability of wheeled systems while performing manipulation tasks such as opening doors, clearing debris, and activating equipment. However, current approaches treat locomotion, perception, manipulation, and planning as separate modules, creating brittle pipelines that fail when conditions change or new objectives arise. What is missing is a unified intelligence layer that jointly reasons about perception, instructions, and the robot’s physical capabilities

The goal of this project is to develop an intelligent quadrupedal robotic platform for autonomous search-and-rescue (SAR) operations that tightly integrates Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with embodied locomotion, perception, and decision-making. The proposed platform will leverage large-scale multimodal foundation models to interpret high-level natural language instructions (e.g., mission objectives, safety constraints) and formulate them into context-aware representation. These representations will be used for further terrain adaptation, victim identification, and manipulation. Existing VLMs provide powerful semantic understanding but remain limited for robotics because they lack real-time inference capability, robust grounding in dynamic physical environments, and reliable integration with low-latency control loops required for embodied decision-making. By coupling VLM-driven semantic reasoning with real-time control, mapping, and planning algorithms, we bridge the gap from high-level language-grounded perception to low-level torque commands that coordinate four
legs and an arm in real time.

requestTitle: Ensemble LLMs for Explainable Autonomous Maritime Navigation
abstract: Autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) are increasingly used in transportation, environmental monitoring, and maritime safety. These systems must safely navigate complex waterways while complying with international maritime regulations known as the COLREGs. Ensuring that autonomous vessels not only follow these rules but also explain their decisions is critical for safety, regulatory approval, and public trust. This project investigates the use of ensemble large language models (LLMs) to enhance high-level decision-making in autonomous maritime navigation. Multiple language models will operate in parallel, with their outputs combined through voting or consensus mechanisms to improve robustness and reliability. The system will be systematically evaluated across all 41 COLREGs rules using high-fidelity maritime simulations under diverse traffic conditions. By improving rule compliance, transparency, and scalability, this research advances trustworthy AI for safety-critical environments and supports broader applications in autonomous transportation systems.

requestTitle: An Efficient Absolute Visual Localization for UAV Navigation and Surveillance in GPS-Denied Environments
abstract: Objective: This project will develop a lightweight, drift-free Absolute Visual Geo-Localization (AVGL) framework for near real-time UAV localization and navigation in GPS-denied environments using passive vision-only sensing. The core scientific goal is to continuously re-localize the UAV against absolute georeferenced visual context rather than propagate pose estimates over time, thereby achieving consistent global positioning without reliance on GPS or active RF emissions. Expected outcomes include: (i) a robust hybrid AVGL pipeline combining large-scale retrieval with fine-grained geometric verification, (ii) quantitative evaluation across multiple UAV/satellite datasets using recall@K, average precision, mean localization error, and runtime, and (iii) publishable results and reusable benchmarking artifacts.

requestTitle: Fast Rotation Measure Synthesis using Simulation-Based Inference
abstract: Rotation measure (RM) synthesis is fundamental to understanding cosmic magnetism through radio polarimetry. Current methods face critical limitations. RM synthesis is computationally expensive and cannot automatically identify multiple Faraday components. Conversely, QU fitting requires manual component specification and provides no rigorous uncertainty quantification. We propose a novel approach using simulation-based inference (SBI) combined with deep learning for automated model selection. Our proof-of-concept demonstrates that neural posterior estimation can rapidly (~1 second per source) recover RM parameters with well-calibrated uncertainties. A 1D CNN classifier achieves 95% accuracy in distinguishing single versus multi-component sources. This 12-month pilot will extend the framework to the full astronomical RM range (-2000 rad/m/m to 2000 rad/m/m), develop 3--5 component models, and incorporate Faraday-thick depolarization physics. We will validate the complete pipeline on MeerKAT and VLA survey data from galaxy clusters. Success will enable automated probabilistic RM analysis for next-generation surveys (SKA, ngVLA) detecting millions of polarized sources.

requestTitle: Automated and Verified Migration of Legacy eBPF Programs to Rust
abstract: This proposal aims to develop an automated, agentic framework for translating legacy C-based eBPF programs into memory-safe Rust, addressing the growing national imperative for secure systems software. While eBPF is central to modern networking, observability, and security, most existing programs rely on unsafe C code that cannot fully prevent memory-related vulnerabilities. The project introduces a pipeline that combines large language models, formal verification, symbolic execution, and iterative repair to generate Rust programs that satisfy both Rust’s ownership rules and the Linux kernel’s eBPF verifier. Preliminary experiments successfully translated a subset of programs, and we now seeks substantial compute resources to scale the approach to 165 real-world eBPF programs using multiple proprietary and open-source LLMs. The work leverages prior NSF-funded research, and results—including tools, datasets, and evaluations—will be disseminated to the research community within one year.

requestTitle: Empirical Security Analysis and Defense Mechanisms Against Jailbreak Attacks in Large Language Models
abstract: This project aims to deploy OpenAI API (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini) to examine how models of different architectures and scales respond to adversarial prompts, analyze the stability and failure modes associated with inference-time attacks, and identify structural factors that influence vulnerability. We then aim to develop practical defense mechanisms that can effectively protect LLMs against these threats, with a specific focus on addressing the most prevalent jailbreak attacks. As LLMs continue to expand across resource-constrained platforms, such as edge devices, IoT systems, and mission-critical cyber-physical infrastructures, the need for transparent and scientifically validated security evaluation and defense mechanisms becomes increasingly urgent. Using systematic experimentation, we will quantify attack success rates and uncover empirical patterns that inform the design of multi-modal defense strategies. The scientific contribution of this project is threefold: (1) generating reproducible results on the security of emerging LLMs, (2) developing lightweight and practical defense mechanisms that enhance model security without imposing significant computational overhead, and (3) producing publicly accessible evaluation protocols and datasets that enable reproducible scalable security benchmarking across various models. These outcomes directly support the NAIRR Pilot focus area of trustworthy AI by providing advanced lightweight defense techniques for emerging widely deployed LLMs.

requestTitle: Risk-Controlled Test-Time Adaptation for Event-Driven Distribution Shifts in Geospatial and Environmental Imaging
abstract: Modern ML systems deployed for disaster response and environmental monitoring face distribution shifts after deployment. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can improve performance under benign shifts, but it introduces a distinct reliability hazard: the act of updating can itself cause harm. We propose a reliability-centered framework that makes \emph{update risk} measurable, predictable, and controllable. First, we build a regime-aware \emph{Update-Risk Map} that quantifies harm distributions and tail risk across appearance vs.\ mechanism shifts. Second, we develop a tiered, structure-aware \emph{verifier} that estimates the probability of harmful updating using bounded-cost evidence. Third, we wrap existing TTA rules with \emph{risk-controlled guardrails} (trust-region gating + rollback) to enforce explicit harm budgets. We will validate on event-driven benchmarks including SpaceNet8 flood mapping, seafloor change, and wildfire imagery, and release an open reporting toolkit and guardrail library.

requestTitle: SplitMind: Multimodal AI via Split Learning for Privacy-Critical Visual Intelligence
abstract: This project develops new methods for training artificial intelligence (AI) systems on sensitive data without requiring that the data be centralized in one location. Modern AI models that combine images and language, such as systems that answer questions about medical images, typically require large amounts of computing power and centralized datasets, which can raise privacy concerns. This project advances a “split learning” approach in which parts of the AI model operate locally, while only compressed intermediate information is shared for collaborative training. In addition, the project introduces a novel mechanism to selectively reduce unnecessary information before transmission, improving both privacy and computational efficiency. Using publicly available medical visual question answering datasets, the research will systematically evaluate how well these privacy-preserving architectures maintain performance while resisting data reconstruction and inference attacks. The resulting methods, software, and evaluation tools will be released openly to support broader adoption of trustworthy, privacy-aware AI systems. By enabling secure collaboration for multimodal AI development, this project contributes to advancing responsible and scalable AI for healthcare and other sensitive domains.

requestTitle: Towards Stable and Scalable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving into autonomous agents capable of multi-step interaction with complex environments. However, agentic reinforcement learning (ARL) remains unstable, difficult to reproduce, and highly sensitive to implementation details, limiting the scalability of LLM-based agents.
We propose to develop a standardized and stability-focused framework for agentic reinforcement learning. Specifically, we will build ARLArena, a reproducible testbed designed to isolate algorithmic behavior from engineering confounders, and conduct systematic analyses of policy optimization design choices in long-horizon, multi-turn settings. Building on these insights, we will develop Stable Agentic Multi-turn Policy Optimization (SAMPO) to improve training robustness and scalability. 
This project aims to provide open-source infrastructure, validated design principles, and large-scale empirical evaluation that support stable and reproducible research on LLM-based agents, advancing long-horizon reasoning and real-world interactive AI systems

requestTitle: Agentic AI for Maximizing Photocurrent Via Optimization of Instrumentation and Materials
abstract: This project proposes, for the first time, an artificial-intelligence–driven experimental system that simultaneously optimizes both optoelectronic materials and the optical measurement setup used to study them. The AI system automatically adjusts experimental components and selects promising materials to maximize photocurrent, a key signal for next-generation sensing and electronic technologies. By learning directly from real experiments and physics-based simulations, the platform can explore complex choices that are difficult and time-consuming for humans to tune by hand. The approach demonstrates how national-scale computing can enable smarter, more efficient scientific experiments.

requestTitle: Stable and Scalable Contextual Reinforcement Learning for Nonstationary and Networked Systems
abstract: Real-world autonomous and networked systems, such as power grids, robotic swarms, and cyber-physical infrastructures, operate in fundamentally nonstationary environments, where dynamics, costs, sensing, and even communication topology change over time. Yet most reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-agent RL methods assume stationarity and fixed interaction structures, making them brittle or unsafe under regime shifts and topology reconfiguration. This project proposes a new stability-aware paradigm for contextual reinforcement learning that integrates online switching control with formal stability guarantees into RL, enabling agents to adapt in real time to changing contexts while maintaining provable safety and performance. We will develop and evaluate this framework for both single-agent and multi-agent systems with time-varying communication graphs, using large-scale robotics and power-system benchmarks enabled by NAIRR computational resources. The project will deliver open-source algorithms, benchmarks, and peer-reviewed publications, establishing a new foundation for safe, adaptive, and scalable learning-enabled control in nonstationary and networked environments.

requestTitle: Reinforcing Reasoning through Self-Distilled Process Supervision from References
abstract:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently enabled major advances in AI reasoning, allowing large language models to solve problems in math and programming by checking whether answers are correct. However, many real-world tasks—such as personalized recommendations, planning, or medical question suggestion—do not have clear, verifiable outcomes, limiting the applicability of existing RLVR methods.

This project aims to extend RLVR to these open-ended tasks by developing a new reward modeling approach that learns from reference answers rather than strict correctness checks.

Ambient models for understanding continuous data streams beyond context window
abstract:
A missing piece in contemporary language models is the ability to consume extremely long streams of data, which fundamentally limits their potential to reasoning beyond their context window length. Scale can get one so far by simply increasing the context length during pre-training, but it incurs huge memory and time costs during training and inference, and ultimately cannot solve the problem. For example, coding agents today, which consume the entire repository in context and long execution traces from runtime interaction, can easily hit the context limit and are forced to perform a manual context compression regularly, abrupting the ongoing interaction and inevitably impacting reasoning capabilities after compression.

This research develops a new class of language models, ambient models (AMs), that considers streaming inputs as first-class inputs. Compared to existing language models that receive request-based inputs with careful prompt-engineering, ambient models are always-on, consuming a long stream of data at the scale of 100x or 1000x the pretraining context window. This allows AMs to monitor events non-stop and reason holistically over everything relevant from the past, not only in the matter of days, but in weeks and months, enabling new downstream applications like persistent personal AI, real-time news monitoring, and log abnormality detection. Our work aligns directly with the NAIRR Pilot’s focus on accelerating AI and AI-powered discovery and innovation, and discovering new and transformative paradigms that advance the capabilities of AI, as directed by Winning the Race: America's AI Action Plan.

Graph-Structured Long-Term Memory for Trustworthy Large Language Model Agents
abstract: The reliance of large language model (LLM) agents on unstructured, ever-expanding context windows is a primary source of untrustworthiness, leading to factual hallucinations, opaque reasoning, and prohibitive computational costs. This proposal pioneers a new foundation for agentic memory using dynamic, explicit graph structures to directly confront these limitations. This project extends the PI's NSF CAREER research on foundational graph learning to the computationally intensive domain of agentic AI, a scope requiring dedicated large-scale resources. Our core innovation is an end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) pipeline that trains an agent to act as a principled knowledge manager, learning to autonomously edit, traverse, and prune its memory graph. This approach ensures long-term factual consistency, provides an auditable reasoning trail, and maintains computational efficiency. We will validate our framework against complex agentic benchmarks like BrowseComp and GAIA, specifically measuring improvements in long-term reliability and interpretability over current baselines. The requested $25k A100-equivalent GPU hours and $5k in  OpenAI API credits are essential for this large-scale training and rigorous evaluation. Success will provide a blueprint for building AI agents that are fundamentally more trustworthy, auditable, and efficient.

This project extends the PI's NSF CAREER research on foundational graph learning to the computationally intensive domain of agentic AI, a scope requiring dedicated large-scale resources. Our core innovation is an end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) pipeline that trains an agent to act as a principled knowledge manager, learning to autonomously edit, traverse, and prune its memory graph. This approach ensures long-term factual consistency, provides an auditable reasoning trail, and maintains computational efficiency. We will validate our framework against complex agentic benchmarks like BrowseComp and GAIA, specifically measuring improvements in long-term reliability and interpretability over current baselines. The requested $25k A100-equivalent GPU hours and $5k in  OpenAI API credits are essential for this large-scale training and rigorous evaluation. Success will provide a blueprint for building AI agents that are fundamentally more trustworthy, auditable, and efficient.

requestTitle: Core Capabilities for Multimodal Musical Intelligence
abstract: Music is a challenging and important frontier for multimodal artificial intelligence. Musical recordings (audio) and scores (images) hold enormous scientific and cultural value, but most of that information is not readable by modern AI systems that could help us navigate it. This proposal requests computation for basic research in automatic music transcription (AMT) and optical music recognition (OMR), methods that transform recordings and scores, respectively, into textual representations. Improvements to the accuracy and efficiency of AMT and OMR methods would unlock large-scale access to the world’s recorded and written music for search, analysis, education, and accessibility. These tasks are also a stress test for modern multimodal AI models because they require precise symbol grounding, long-range structure understanding, abstraction to musicological concepts, and robustness to noise, polyphony, and performance variation. We will train and evaluate new multimodal models, iterating on both data and methods to move these problems forward.  The efforts described here serve a longer-term goal of granting AI systems multimodal musical intelligence:  the ability to converse naturally and accurately about musical content in any form, in support of scholars, musicians, listeners, and learners.

requestTitle: LLM Scaling Laws
abstract:
As Large Language Models (LLMs) become central to modern AI infrastructure, the ability to accurately predict their performance and resource requirements is critical for both efficiency and capability planning. However, while existing scaling laws (e.g., Chinchilla [1]) have provided rough guidelines for model sizing, they rely on rigid, pre-defined power-law assumptions [2] that often fail to capture complex, non-linear interactions between training hyperparameters. We seek to transcend these static approximations by leveraging a data-driven framework for boosting symbolic regression [3]. Unlike traditional curve-fitting or opaque neural network predictors, our approach constructs an ensemble of interpretable mathematical expressions [4] that iteratively minimize prediction error. By modeling validation loss not just as a function of parameter count and dataset size but also incorporating dynamic training hyperparameters like learning rate, critical for stability across scales [5] and epoch count, we generate precise, "white-box" laws that explain performance variability. This is vital for three reasons. First, it allows for granular resource allocation, predicting the exact compute needed to achieve a specific performance target. Second, the symbolic nature of our output provides direct theoretical insights into how hyperparameters interact, moving beyond empirical observation to mathematical understanding [6]. Third, our boosting framework incorporating adaptive Huber loss [7] and diversity regularization is explicitly designed to be robust against the noise and outliers inherent in large-scale training logs. Preliminary experiments using PySR [3] and gplearn [8] demonstrate that this boosting strategy significantly reduces Root Mean Squared Error and improves R-squared compared to standard Chinchilla baselines.

requestTitle: Diffusion Prior based Randomized Exploration Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Sequential decision-making problems, such as bandits and reinforcement learning, are central to many AI applications, including recommendation systems, robotics, games, and personalized healthcare. A key challenge is designing exploration strategies that balance exploiting high-performing actions with exploring uncertain ones. Existing approaches often rely on strong assumptions about reward distributions, function approximations, or task-specific structures, limiting their scalability and real-world applicability. This project seeks to develop efficient, theoretically grounded algorithms for diverse reinforcement learning settings by leveraging randomized methods and diffusion models. Through this NAIRR start-up award, the PI will gain experience applying advanced computing resources to the proposed research. We will conduct a scaling study using standard RL benchmarks to evaluate the computational requirements of our methods, laying the foundation for a subsequent full-scale research request.

requestTitle: DiagHOI: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Human–Object Interaction in Multimodal Foundation Models
abstract: Human–object interaction (HOI) understanding enables AI systems to recognize not only objects in images, but also how people interact with them, such as riding a bicycle or repairing a vehicle. This capability is essential for applications in robotics, assistive technologies, embodied AI, and safety-critical human-centered systems. Recent multimodal foundation models have shown strong generalization ability, yet existing benchmarks were not designed to systematically evaluate their reasoning about interactions. Current datasets primarily support leaderboard comparison and lack diagnostic structure for analyzing model strengths, weaknesses, and failure modes. This project will develop DiagHOI, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating interaction reasoning in multimodal foundation models. The benchmark will combine curated real-world images with carefully generated synthetic samples to provide balanced evaluation across diverse interaction categories. By enabling structured analysis of robustness, compositional generalization, and failure patterns, DiagHOI will help researchers design more reliable and interpretable AI systems for real-world human-centered environments.

requestTitle: Continuous Embodied Reasoning
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that reason through discrete chain-of-thought tokens suffer from error propagation, hallucination, and irrevocable commitment to faulty steps. We propose a "Thinker–Actor" architecture that instead performs implicit planning in a continuous latent space via diffusion before generating actions. The Thinker iteratively refines a multimodal plan, embedding conditioned on visual observations and task instructions, enabling global deliberation without discrete token constraints; the Actor then generates motor actions conditioned on this continuous plan. We will train at two scales (~300M and ~1B parameters) using supervised distillation on open-source robot data, followed by RL fine-tuning with action-aligned rewards, and evaluate on standard benchmarks. All code, weights, and evaluation frameworks will be open-sourced.

requestTitle: AI-powered Automation of Multidimensional Data Mining and Modeling in Evolutionary Biology
abstract:
Multifunctional ``magic traits'' that simultaneously mediate ecological adaptation and mate choice are thought to play a disproportionate role in species divergence, yet their macroevolutionary origins remain poorly understood. In insects, cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) represent a powerful model system: they function both as critical desiccation-resistance traits and as key chemical signals in mating communication. Despite decades of CHC research, existing data remain fragmented across species and studies, limiting large-scale evolutionary synthesis.

This project leverages artificial intelligence to automate the extraction, integration, and modeling of multidimensional CHC data across insect diversity. We will develop an LLM-driven agentic pipeline to systematically mine the literature and construct the first standardized cross-species CHC database. We will then integrate chemical, ecological, and phylogenetic information using multimodal machine learning to identify macroevolutionary patterns and quantify environmental effects on CHC composition through phylogenetically informed meta-analysis. By combining AI-driven data mining with evolutionary theory, this project will generate a unified framework for understanding how multifunctional traits evolve under interacting natural and sexual selection, while establishing scalable tools for large-scale comparative biology.

requestTitle: Multi-Agent System Coordination Optimization in the Open-World
abstract:
By integrating the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) with agent coordination, multi-agent systems (MAS) have attracted broad attention with a wide range of applications including intelligent diagnosis, website services, and code generation. Despite current progress, developing multi-agent systems for AI-as-teammate under evolving and unreliable open-world environments is highly challenging. Existing approaches are fundamentally constrained by their reliance on a template graph modification paradigm with a predefined set of agents and hard-coded interaction structures, significantly limiting their adaptability to task-specific requirements over time.

Hence, the communication topology, which regulates how information flows among different agents, plays a fundamental role in enabling effective multi-agent collaboration and coordination, requiring careful design in practice. In essence, the communication topologies of multi-agent systems can be modeled as graphs, where agents are represented as nodes and edges indicate communication between agents. In this proposal, we aim to develop new MAS coordination methods from the lens of agent communication topology design, in order to create more adaptable and reliable MAS that can thrive in open-world environments.

requestTitle: Feedback Self-Distillation for Robust Reasoning and Text Generation
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are becoming the default interface
for reading, writing, and asking technical questions, yet they can still fail badly on reasoning tasks. A model may solve a math or science problem correctly in one setting and then give an overconfident, wrong answer on a small variation. We need methods that both improve reliability and provide simple diagnostics that non-specialists can track. This project lies squarely in the NAIRR focus areas of trustworthy AI and AI for science.
Our technical focus is feedback self-distillation: a smaller student model is trained to imitate a stronger teacher model. This is attractive for NAIRR because many powerful foundation models already exist, but retraining them from scratch is out of reach for most research groups. Self-distillation instead uses a fixed teacher to generate teaching signals and trains a cheaper student that is easier to deploy and iterate on. In our project, we add an extra feedback signal derived from the teacher’s own uncertainty and from simple summaries of its singular values (spectral statistics). These statistics help us identify when the teacher’s representation appears stable, and we encourage the student to learn more aggressively from those examples

requestTitle: Enhancing Long-Horizon Structured Reasoning Capabilities in LLM Agents
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate complex workflows in areas like scientific research, personal assistance, and software development. Yet they struggle in long-horizon reasoning, tasks requiring substantial interdependent steps to complete. We attribute this to the limitation of linear reasoning, which fails to efficiently manage state dependencies over long trajectories. First, linear processing hinders accurate search; agents fail to reason structurally, and essential intermediate states get lost in the long context. Second, unstructured generation is inefficient; agents often overthink and generate redundant tokens that exhaust the context window. Finally, linear history lacks robustness; agents cannot effectively backtrack to correct early errors, leading to error propagation. This project will benchmark these failure modes, propose a structured reasoning framework to address the limitations of linear long-horizon reasoning, and validate its effectiveness.

requestTitle: Causal Fairness for Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract:
Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems have achieved unprecedented success, with models transforming how information is processed at scale. Yet despite this progress, challenges for broader adoption still exist, including those related to the trustworthiness and fairness of generative AI.
In this context, causal inference provides a principled framework for reasoning about fairness, as it links observed disparities to the underlying mechanisms that generate them, and aligns naturally with human intuition.
The goal of this project is to build causal foundations for fair generative AI. The generative AI setting is markedly more complex than the standard machine learning setting because generative models can sample from arbitrary conditionals over any set of variables, implicitly constructing their own beliefs about all causal mechanisms, rather than just learning a single predictive mechanism. Key challenges are addressed through three specific aims of the project: (1) Bias Detection in Generative AI, which develops new methodology for understanding the mismatch between the model and the real world along different causal pathways; (2) Causally Fair Generation at Inference Time, which leverages causal retrieval and prompt augmentation to achieve fairness at generation time without fine-tuning; and (3) Causally Fair Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Fine-Tuning, which incorporates causal reasoning directly into model representations via fine-tuning on structured CoT sequences, enabling models to internalize fairness principles.

requestTitle: Reducing Hallucinations in Multimodal Models: Building Transparent and Safe Vision Encoders from Open Data
abstract: Multimodal models that combine images and language are increasingly used in everyday tools, but they still hallucinate objects or facts that are not actually present. This project aims to make such systems more trustworthy by building transparent vision encoders trained entirely on open data. We will first assemble a large, balanced image corpus that covers everyday scenes, documents, diagrams, user interfaces, and scientific figures. Using OpenAI models, we will automatically label images with domain, layout, and safety information and generate additional images to cover rare or safety-critical cases. On top of this resource, we will train new vision encoders and simple diagnostic heads that expose what the model believes is in the image and allow us to detect and reduce hallucinations while maintaining accuracy. All datasets, models, and evaluation tools will be released openly, providing the community with a safety-focused visual backbone for building more reliable multimodal systems.

requestTitle: VULCAN-AI: Multi-Agent AI for Volcanic and Wildfire Hazard Intelligence
abstract: VULCAN-AI is a hierarchical, LLM-driven multi-agent system for real-time volcanic and wildfire hazard intelligence. Deep learning models extract structured signals from thermal and optical imagery, geophysical measurements, and environmental data, which LLM-based scientific agents interpret within their physical context. A higher-level Coordinator Agent fuses these multi-modal assessments inside a Dynamic World Model, performs scientific chain-of-thought reasoning, and generates transparent narrative summaries. The system also integrates the NSF Sage Edge Computing Platform to run distilled LLM agents directly on sensor nodes, enabling rapid, bandwidth-efficient anomaly detection in remote locations. Local multimodal agent development and perception-model training are supported by an existing ACCESS allocation (Jetstream2 CPU/GPU/Storage). NAIRR resources are requested solely for LLM API credits, which are essential for high-quality LLM reasoning, multi-agent dialog, narrative generation, and large-scale volcanic and wildfire scenario evaluation.

requestTitle: Training AI to Think Like a Botanist: Using Text-Based Trait Profiles for Interpretable Species Identification in Hyperdiverse Plant Communities
abstract: Tropical forests harbor most of Earth's terrestrial biodiversity and provide critical ecosystem services, including climate regulation, carbon sequestration, and water cycling1,2. Despite their ecological and economic importance, tropical forests face significant threats from deforestation, habitat fragmentation, and climate change3,4. Understanding, monitoring and predicting how tropical ecosystems respond to these challenges fundamentally relies on precise species identification because each species occupies and performs different roles and functions in the ecosystem5-7. However, achieving species-level identification remains a major hurdle8. Botanists often rely on vegetative morphological traits (e.g., leaf arrangement, margin type, venation patterns), which, while diagnostic, are often subtle and variable. As a result, field-based identification is time-consuming and reliant on highly specialized expertise that is not widely accessible in day-to-day ecological monitoring or restoration work. Additionally, in hyperdiverse tropical forests, many species are naturally rare and thus remain underrepresented in image-based training datasets, constraining model scalability. There is a clear need for approaches that integrate the structured botanical knowledge used by taxonomists themselves. This proposal represents a fundamental departure from image-centric AI identification methods, instead leveraging the rich taxonomic knowledge encoded in centuries of botanical literature as the primary reasoning foundation, with imagery serving as complementary validation. This knowledge-driven approach offers the potential for far more interpretable, scalable, and generalizable species identification.

requestTitle: Detecting Rust Safety Violations Using Large Language Models
abstract: Memory safety vulnerabilities continue to pose significant security threats, with major tech companies reporting that 70\% of their security issues stem from memory-related bugs. While Rust, a memory-safe programming language, offers strong safety guarantees, its dual architecture of safe and unsafe code introduces potential security risks. Our analysis reveals that 19\% of Rust packages contain unsafe code, and approximately 50\% of Rust's security vulnerabilities are linked to unsafe code usage. This project aims to develop an innovative approach using Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect safety violations in Rust programs. We will create a first-of-its-kind bug detection system that leverages LLMs to generate and verify safety invariants for unsafe operations. By fine-tuning LLMs on Rust's safety requirements and existing vulnerability patterns, our system will provide a more comprehensive and adaptable solution compared to traditional rule-based approaches. The success of this research will not only enhance Rust's security landscape but also demonstrate the potential of AI-driven program analysis in improving software security across different programming languages.

requestTitle: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Dynamic Visual Planning in Embodied Agents
abstract: This project aims to develop a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate vision-language models (VLMs) on their ability to perform complex planning tasks in dynamic, visually rich environments. Unlike existing benchmarks that focus on static scenes or language-only inputs, our benchmark will test models’ capabilities to reason and plan in settings where the environment changes over time due to interactions by multiple agents. By creating diverse synthetic and simulated tasks reflecting real-world challenges, we will assess how well VLMs integrate visual perception with sequential decision-making under dynamic conditions. This evaluation will provide critical insights into the strengths and limitations of current models and guide future research toward more robust embodied AI systems.

requestTitle: TRAIL: Trustworthy Reasoning and Integration of Language Models for Hardware Design
abstract: The increasing complexity of semiconductor systems demands intelligent, explainable, and trustworthy automation in hardware design. Traditional electronic design automation (EDA) flows depend heavily on manual expertise for generating, verifying, and optimizing hardware description language (HDL) code, limiting scalability and design agility. To address these challenges, this project proposes TRAIL — Trustworthy Reasoning and Adaptive Integration of Large Language Models for Hardware Design Automation. TRAIL introduces a unified framework for reliable AI-driven hardware synthesis through three integrated research tasks. Task 1 benchmarks commercial and open-source LLMs across languages (Verilog, SystemVerilog, C++/HLS) and applies low-rank fine-tuning (LoRA) to enhance code correctness and power–performance–area (PPA) efficiency. Task 2 integrates graph-based reasoning using Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) and data-flow graphs (DFGs) to enable architectural understanding and interpretable hardware generation. Task 3 develops a trustability and evaluation framework that quantifies syntax, functionality, and security correctness, producing a “trustability index” to guide reliable AI-assisted design. Supported by OpenAI API access via NAIRR Copilot, TRAIL will deliver an open-source, cloud-deployable system for explainable, reproducible, and high-quality LLM-driven hardware design, accelerating innovation in EDA and semiconductor automation.

requestTitle: Surgery-TRACE: A Provenance-First, Guideline-Grounded Clinical Reasoning Engine for Surgical Decision Support
abstract: Surgery-TRACE (Transparent, Reproducible, Auditable Clinical Explanation) develops a provenance-aware clinical reasoning engine to improve surgical decision-making. The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation with constrained chain-of-thought reasoning to produce guideline-grounded, auditable, and reproducible recommendations for complex surgical cases. This pilot leverages model and inference credits from multiple private-sector partners to evaluate and validate the system using deidentified retrospective cases and simulated multidisciplinary planning sessions, enabling safer human-in-the-loop workflows and reproducible outputs for research and education.

Uncertainty Evolution in Large Language Model Reasoning
abstract: We investigate how uncertainty evolves during multi-step reasoning in large language models and how it changes with model size. We will trace token-/span-level uncertainty and model disagreement, align uncertainty peaks to reasoning stages, and use controlled counterfactual tests to separate semantic uncertainty from surface-form effects. We then evaluate how these uncertainty signals improve reliability in test-time scaling, test-time adaptation, and on-policy distillation. We will release reproducible code and curated uncertainty traces for the research community.

requestTitle: Constructing Security-Feature Oracles for Critical-Data Identification
abstract: Software systems are essential to modern infrastructure and daily computing, yet growing complexity has made them increasingly vulnerable to security flaws. Many existing security tools either focus on high-level concepts such as authentication or on low-level software bugs, but rarely connect the two. This project uses large language models (LLMs) to automatically translate high-level security expectations into executable security checks that can be applied at scale. These checks are then used to identify security-critical program data whose corruption can silently undermine security. By automating expert reasoning with AI, this work accelerates security analysis across large software ecosystems and advances scalable, trustworthy computing.

requestTitle: Towards Effective and Robust Inference-time Knowledge Editing
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) face inherent challenges such as hallucination, sycophancy, and dishonesty, due to their training data and alignment processes. While knowledge editing has proven to be a viable post-hoc solution for addressing knowledge-related issues, existing research faces limitations, including suboptimal effectiveness and difficulties in simultaneously addressing critical aspects such as generalization, portability, and locality. To overcome these challenges, we propose an inference-time knowledge editing framework that is both effective and robust through two key tasks. The proposed framework is LLM-agnostic, making it compatible with existing knowledge editing techniques and enabling seamless integration. First, we jointly adapt advanced decoding strategies and activation editing, which adjusts model activations during inference by following specific directions across a limited number of attention heads, as an inference-time enhancement to improve the effectiveness of knowledge editing. Second, we propose a framework utilizing noise-adaptive decoding to address knowledge conflicts arising from multiple contexts across various modalities.
