requestTitle: A Comprehensive Understanding of Continual Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are rapidly redefining robotics by coupling perception, language grounding, and control, yet today’s models remain largely static: trained once and deployed without the ability to continually adapt as tasks, environments, and user needs evolve. This proposal targets the key bottleneck holding back progress in Continual Learning for VLA (CL-VLA): the field is fragmented across closed implementations, incomparable experiments, and inconsistent evaluation, making it difficult to determine what truly works, when, and why. We propose to bridge this gap by conducting the first comprehensive, systematic study of CL-VLA, underpinned by the development of the CL-VLA Library, a unified, modular, and open-source framework designed to standardize datasets, training, and evaluation pipelines with implementations of over 15 representative methods. We will rigorously benchmark these CL-VLA algorithms across benchmark and data regimes, while extending analysis to the continual adaptation of foundation VLA models (e.g., OpenVLA). This comprehensive study moves beyond simple success rates to quantify critical real-world deployment metrics, including adaptation time, computational overhead, and memory growth, ultimately validating these findings on physical robots. By releasing the library, baseline checkpoints, and a user guide for practitioners, this project will deliver compounding value: it will reduce duplicated compute across the community, accelerate method development, and establish trustworthy foundations for continually adaptive robotics.

requestTitle: Targeted Boltz-2 Screening of Food-Related Metabolites for GPCR Binding
abstract: Food-derived metabolites play important roles in metabolic regulation, in part through interactions with G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), yet systematic identification of these interactions remains limited by redundancy and bias in large-scale screening approaches. This project applies a diversity-driven computational strategy to identify informative metabolite–GPCR interactions relevant to metabolism, nutrition, and disease. Starting from food-related metabolites curated from the Human Metabolome Database, compounds are selected using molecular clustering and subclass-guided filtering to balance chemical diversity and biological relevance. Predicted metabolite–GPCR binding affinities and structures are evaluated using Boltz-2 and refined using structural confidence metrics, producing an interpretable interaction landscape to guide hypothesis generation and downstream experimental studies.

requestTitle: Resources for Deep Learning and Programming Foundations for Data Science courses for Biostatistics and Data Science Graduate Programs
abstract: This project integrates NAIRR Pilot computing resources into BIOS 6310: Deep Learning and Programming Foundations for Data Science, courses offered at The University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB). These courses are offered to graduate students in Biostatistics and Public health along with other postdoctoral fellows, healthcare professionals within the school of public and population health and other schools at UTMB. The deep learning course introduces basic concepts of deep learning and applications tailored to medical and public health professionals. The course will cover deep learning architectures (e.g. convolutional neural networks, multilayer perceptron, transformers, recurrent neural networks, multimodal models) in an intuitive manner, with hands-on exercises to develop and deploy modern neural networks on healthcare datasets. The programming foundations for Data science course introduce basics of programming in major languages such as R and Python and hands-on applications of learned programming skills in real-world datasets. The Vocareum AI Notebook platform, can provide access to required computational resources for the programming course while the Prototype National Research Platform (PNRP) Classroom platform access to GPUs for the deep learning course to work with real-world datasets and state-of-the-art frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow. These courses help gain students' necessary skill sets to be prepared for industry jobs as well as help them in presenting their class project work in various conference presentations and publish papers.

abstract: This project develops an autonomous AI system that continuously analyzes large-scale gene expression data to uncover molecular signatures linking diseases across populations and conditions. requestTitle: Aligning Large Reasoning Models via Safety-aware Post-Training
abstract:
Large reasoning models (LRMs) are a new generation of AI systems designed to solve complex problems by reasoning step by step, rather than producing short, direct answers. Their ability to process long conversational histories enables stronger performance in tasks such as scientific analysis, planning, and decision support. However, this same capability also introduces new safety risks: misleading or harmful content embedded earlier in a conversation can persist and subtly influence the model’s reasoning, potentially leading to unsafe outputs or unnecessary refusals to answer harmless questions.

This project aims to make large reasoning models safer and more reliable in realistic, multi-turn conversational settings. We will first systematically study how conversational histories can destabilize reasoning or expose new attack pathways that existing safety methods fail to address. Building on these insights, we will develop safety-aware post-training methods that explicitly teach models how to handle misleading or counter-aligned reasoning examples without sacrificing their usefulness.

By integrating these methods into widely used training pipelines, this research will produce practical tools for improving AI safety at scale. All code, evaluation benchmarks, and training recipes will be openly released, helping researchers, developers, and policymakers deploy reasoning-capable AI systems that are both powerful and trustworthy.

requestTitle: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves large language models (LLMs) by grounding responses in external knowledge but is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning attacks. This project aims to secure RAG through three thrusts: developing realistic attacks to reveal vulnerabilities, designing provable defenses to ensure robustness, and creating forensic tools to trace malicious content. We will develop and evaluate our methods using open-source RAG frameworks, public clouds, and HPC environments supported by NAIRR. The project will deliver generalizable tools, benchmarks, datasets, and evaluation pipelines to strengthen the security and reliability of RAG systems across diverse settings.

requestTitle: Bootstrap Embodied Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Robotic decision-making requires systematic reasoning about complex visual environments and decomposition of high-level commands into actionable steps. This proposal aims to develop a reinforcement learning framework that strengthens multi-step reasoning in vision-language-action models. Our approach consists of two stages: synthesizing multi-step reasoning traces through pre-trained generalist robot policies, followed by fine-grained step-wise RL optimization using generative reward models. We will rigorously compare process-based and outcome-based RL optimization strategies within robotics contexts. Evaluation will involve challenging out-of-distribution scenarios requiring spatial reasoning and complex instruction following, with validation on a variety physical robotic platforms to confirm real-world viability including manipulation, quadruped robot navigation, and self-driving. Collectively, this project will provide a scalable and generalizable framework for training robotics foundation models to perform complex multi-step reasoning in dynamic real-world environments without requiring additional robot training data or extensive human labeling.

requestTitle: Robust and Efficient Learning under Adversarial Environments
abstract:
Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse applications, but their deployment on resource-constrained devices—such as smartphones, embedded systems, and IoT platforms—exposes critical vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks. While randomized smoothing (RS) provides provable robustness against such attacks, its high computational cost limits practical deployment in real-time, low-resource environments.
This project aims to advance robust and efficient learning under adversarial settings. First, we propose an improved RS framework that drastically reduces computational overhead by leveraging more precise probability estimation and confidence intervals, enabling faster and more reliable robustness certification. Second, we introduce a hybrid framework that combines Bayesian neural networks with RS, providing theoretical robustness guarantees while improving uncertainty quantification and performance against adaptive adversaries.

requestTitle: Modeling Severe Weather Events with Latent Generative Models
abstract: Recent advances in data-driven weather forecasting have achieved remarkable progress. However, forecasts of severe weather within a 48-hour horizon still exhibit substantial uncertainty. In particular,  severe-event predictions are often derived indirectly from variable forecasts, introducing additional sources of error. This project aims to directly model the probability of such events within the forecasting system. The model developed from this project will improve probabilistic forecasts of severe weather events at 48-hour horizons. With the performance improvement, the methods developed from this project have the potential to enhance preparedness for severe weather events.

requestTitle: Open-Source Multi-Scale Language Models via Matryoshka Suite Training
abstract: We propose to develop and openly release a compact suite of multi-scale “Matryoshka” language models that share parameters across nested components, enabling efficient training and deployment of models at several sizes simultaneously. The overarching goal of the project is to contribute an openly accessible, reproducible, and easily extensible framework for training and analyzing modular language models. In addition, the architecture’s nested structure naturally supports intermediate predictions and multi-resolution analyses, offering secondary benefits for model transparency and interpretability. Using 10,000 GPU-hours on the Vista cluster, we will train a 1B-parameter Matryoshka suite, release all code and checkpoints, and provide documentation and evaluation tools for the broader research community.

requestTitle: Variability in LLM-Generated Personas: Method Comparison and Psychometric Assessment
abstract: This project advances the methodological rigor of mixed methods by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to transform qualitative insights into analyzable quantitative responses. Its core goal is to systematically examine response variability in LLM-generated synthetic personas to establish reliability for quantitative and psychometric augmentation. Specifically, the project evaluates response variability across persona generation methods, focusing on temperature, persona count, and prompt specificity. The findings will enhance data reliability and guide best practices for AI-based data augmentation in quantitative research.

requestTitle: Integrating Video AI Analytics in Symani Robotics Assisted Microsurgery
abstract: Symani Surgical System, approved by the FDA in 2024, provides robotics assistance in microsurgery and supermicrosurgery where vessels can be as small as 0.1mm in diameter. Microsurgery demands precision, dexterity, and stability – skills often limited by surgeon physiology, fatigue, and ergonomics. Symani offers enhanced motion scaling, tremor reduction, and visualization for sub-millimeter tasks such as microvascular and lymphovenous anastomoses. For lymphedema alone, 250 million people worldwide suffer from it but less than 600 surgeons perform supermicrosurgery. Despite growing enthusiasm for robotic microsurgery, there is limited research evaluating how well microsurgeons use Symani and whether Symani objectively improves surgical outcome, efficiency, surgeon learning curve and physiology. This first U.S.-based formal analysis on Symani aims to integrate AI-assisted case series analysis of intraoperative real-world microsurgery videos (e.g., on deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) microvascular anastomoses) to assess surgical outcome and surgeon performance. It will be the first AI research worldwide on Symani robotics.

requestTitle: Multi-Modal Agentic Social Network Modeling and Optimization
abstract: Social networks play a central role in shaping public discourse, information diffusion, and collective decision-making. Modern platforms are increasingly driven by rich multi-modal content, such as text and images, and by the growing presence of AI-powered agents that can actively participate in social interactions. However, existing social network models largely focus on network structure alone and treat social dynamics as passive processes, limiting their ability to analyze or guide complex, evolving online behaviors with agent-augmented dynamics. This project proposes a multi-modal and agentic framework for modeling and optimizing social networks. By integrating multi-modal representation learning with graph-based modeling and generative AI, the framework captures how individual human and AI agent behaviors evolve into collective social dynamics over time. The learned models are further optimized using reinforcement learning to support targeted interventions, such as influence modulation and toxicity reduction. The project will evaluate cross-platform applications linking online discussions to real-world outcomes and will release datasets, models, and tools to support responsible social computing research.

LiDAR and Thermal Situational Awareness Framework
abstract:
Public Overview: This project aims to develop BLLiT (Bootstrapping Language–LiDAR and Thermal for Situation Awareness), a robust multimodal framework designed to improve situational awareness in hazardous underground mining environments. Mining disasters such as collapses, explosions, and smoke blockages severely limit visibility, making it difficult for first responders to locate victims and make timely decisions. BLLiT addresses this challenge by fusing LiDAR data, which provides accurate 3D spatial mapping, with thermal imaging, which reveals heat signatures critical for detecting human presence or abnormal equipment activity. The system builds on the BLIP-2 architecture, enhanced with Point Transformer and Vision Transformer encoders, and employs a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) to align these sensor features with a large language model. This allows first responders to interact with the system through natural language and receive real-time, interpretable scene descriptions. By creating a novel multimodal dataset and advancing sensor fusion, this project seeks to enable safer, faster, and more effective disaster response operations.

abstract: Understanding how genetic variation influences gene expression is central to modern human genetics and biomedical discovery. Gene expression prediction models are widely used in applications such as drug target discovery, DNA variant prioritization, and disease mechanism discovery. While current deep sequence-to-function models have learned rich regulatory grammar, these models only consider a single copy of an individual’s DNA, rather than two, preventing the learning of certain nonlinear effects. requestTitle: Start-Up: Sandip Roy, University of California, San Diego
A Multimodal Unified World Model (muWM)
abstract: World models (WMs) promise interactive, controllable simulators that blend reasoning with high-fidelity visual rendering. However, many existing WMs behave primarily as pixel-level video generators and struggle with long-horizon logic, story/state consistency, and precise editing/alignment between user intent and visuals. We propose to train a Multimodal Unified World Model (muWM) that fuses language and action-level reasoning with state-of-the-art diffusion-based video generation. Our proposed design targets core hurdles of long-horizon & parallel world modeling, planning-aware generation, precise world editing/alignment, physical consistency/Real2Sim2Real, 3D awareness, and persistent memory. Our aim is to close the gap between existing open-source and state-of-the-art closed models. We will open-source our training dataset, codebase, and model to accelerate academic research in building world simulations.

requestTitle: NAIRR: Tuning the Pretraining Data Hyperparameters: a data-centric approach to optimizing AI foundation models
abstract: The term hyperparameter has traditionally been applied to a model architecture or training algorithm setting that influences model performance, such as the number of network layers or the optimizer learning rate. Hyperparameters have not been defined or discussed for training data. This omission is surprising since prior work has shown that choices about training data are as important – or perhaps more important – than choices about the model or optimizer.  In this project, we will establish hyperparameters for pretraining datasets in self-supervised learning, focusing on geospatial foundation models, where we can leverage natural geographic groupings to define dataset hyperparameters.

requestTitle: Traj-CLIP: Self-Supervised Representation Learning from  Molecular Dynamics Trajectories Using Transformers
abstract: Predicting protein function from structure remains a central challenge in computational biophysics. Protein Language Models (PLMs) have advanced our ability to relate sequence to function, yet they lack the physical and biophysical information necessary to fully capture dynamical protein behavior. To address this gap, we propose Traj-CLIP, a multimodal framework that integrates representations from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with those from PLMs. By leveraging short MD trajectories, we compute dynamic correlation matrices that describe protein flexibility, conformational changes, and allosteric communication. These are encoded using self-supervised vision transformers and aligned with PLM embeddings through contrastive learning, producing unified representations that couple static sequence features with dynamic biophysical information. Traj-CLIP enables downstream applications such as allosteric site prediction, assessment of mutational impacts, and inference of ligand binding, thereby extending the predictive power of sequence-based models into the domain of protein dynamics.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot: Making Sense – Retrieval-Augmented Ontology Generation from Video Tutorial Transcripts
abstract: Instructional videos are a popular way to learn hands-on skills such as ceramics and textiles, yet much of the practical knowledge they contain remains hidden in unstructured transcripts. This project uses large language models paired with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to transform that content into structured, searchable ontologies. By grounding model outputs in real-world video tutorials, we shift the focus from abstract or theoretical  workflows to the actual tools, materials, and techniques used in practice. These ontologies support interactive tools, including a contextual glossary, a badge system for tracking skill development, and a viewer that maps how making practices are connected. Together, these resources help learners, educators, and tool designers better access and apply practice-based knowledge.

This approach exposes students to practical challenges encountered in real-world HPC and AI workflows, where performance gains must be balanced against correctness and stability.

These resources will primarily support programming assignments and a milestone project conducted outside of class time, enabling equitable and scalable access to advanced computing infrastructure. No sensitive or proprietary data are involved.

By integrating hands-on GPU programming and mixed-precision computing into a graduate curriculum, this project directly advances NAIRR’s education and workforce development mission. It lowers barriers to experiential learning with advanced computing resources and prepares students with practical skills essential for careers in AI, high-performance computing, and data-driven scientific research.

requestTitle: Advancing Speech-Language Pathology Training with Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: This project proposes a novel application of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to transform workforce training for Speech-Language Pathologists (SLPs), practitioners of special education. Building on an initial research prototype, a 12-month investigation is proposed to explore how generative AI can support workforce training through two phases: (1) systematically evaluating MLLMs for generating and analyzing synthetic video data of speech intervention sessions that capture clients' relevant behaviors and therapeutic strategies, and (2) developing context-engineering mechanisms that produce personalized, evidence-based intervention recommendations tailored to individual clients' developmental profiles. Through human-centered evaluation with at least 50 practitioners, the project will assess the clarity, feasibility, and usefulness of AI-generated training materials. This work addresses a critical gap in applying generative AI beyond workload reduction to active workforce development, enabling SLPs to rapidly explore individualized therapeutic approaches while the project produces publicly available synthetic datasets, validated evaluation frameworks, and empirical evidence on how AI can augment professional decision-making in special education settings, with results disseminated through top-tier HCI venues and open-source tools.

requestTitle: Structured-Knowledge-Guided Agentic LLM Jailbreaking and Defense
abstract:
As GenAI systems become deeply integrated into our daily lives, ensuring their safety is a critical priority. Malicious users constantly try to ``jailbreak'' these AI models to produce harmful or dangerous content. While current safety filters are good at blocking obviously harmful questions, they have a major blind spot. Our research has identified a new, more subtle type of attack. Instead of asking one dangerous question, an attacker can ask a series of individually innocent questions. While each question appears harmless on its own, the answers, when combined, can provide the user with dangerous instructions for activities like cyberattacks or building weapons.

This project, supported by the NAIRR, has two goals. First, we will build an automated tool to test this ``multi-step'' vulnerability systematically across all major commercial LLM models. This will reveal how widespread this critical loophole is. Second, and more importantly, we will build the solution. We will develop a new generation of smart AI guardrails that don't just check one question at a time, but instead monitor the entire conversation. This new defense will be able to detect the subtle pattern of a multi-step attack and block it before any harmful information is revealed.

The outcome of this project will be a new set of open-source tools to audit AI systems and a new, more robust defense model, directly contributing to the development of safer and more trustworthy AI for the public.

abstract: The Machine Learning group, a key component of the Mathematical and Statistical Modeling initiative at Georgia Southern University, is spearheading the Computational Methods for Applied Mathematics and Data Analytics program. abstract:

requestTitle: Hands on Applied Machine Learning for Computer Science Education
abstract:
This proposal requests access to NAIRR Pilot classroom resources to support CSCI 484 – Machine Learning, a 400-level undergraduate course at Coastal Carolina University beginning in Spring 2026. The allocation will provide approximately 30 students per semester with hands-on experience using shared CPU and GPU computing resources to train and evaluate machine learning models. The instructional emphasis is on applied judgment: students will study how model behavior changes with dataset size, algorithm complexity, and computational constraints, and will practice responsible use of modern AI tools.

Course projects include face-recognition tasks using locally generated datasets and anomaly detection or segmentation using public datasets such as MVTec and Oceans11. Students will use open-source software (Python, scikit-learn, PyTorch, Jupyter, and related scientific libraries) and will access NAIRR resources primarily outside scheduled class time. Shared CPU nodes will support classical machine learning workflows, while selective GPU access will enable modest deep learning experiments.  No multi-node or large-scale distributed workloads are planned, and no proprietary, export-controlled, or regulated data will be used.

The project requires minimal support beyond standard classroom access. All participants will be U.S.-based students enrolled at Coastal Carolina University, and the course will be managed by the instructor.

With NAIRR Pilot support, students will gain authentic experience working within realistic computational limits, strengthening both technical competence and responsible practice in machine learning.

requestTitle: Start-Up: Zhu-Tian Chen, University of Minnesota
Reasoning-Driven AI for Expert-Enabled Inference and Adaptive Multimodal Data Collection
abstract:
Artificial intelligence has made remarkable strides in modeling and prediction when abundant data are available. Yet many of the most important scientific and engineering challenges do not involve passively collected, large datasets. Instead, they require interactive intelligence: deciding what data to acquire, when to acquire it, and how to fuse information across diverse modalities under conditions of uncertainty and resource constraints.

Existing machine learning models, including state-of-the-art deep learning, are fundamentally passive. They assume the data are already in hand, and their role is simply to fit predictive functions. This assumption is inadequate in domains where experiments are costly, sensing resources are limited, or expert decisions directly shape the data. Inference in such settings is both data-efficient and interpretability-driven, demanding new AI principles.

This project advances core AI methods to meet that challenge. Our goal is to develop algorithms that reason about data before it is collected, embedding expert knowledge into statistical models and enabling adaptive, uncertainty-aware sensing across multiple modalities. Therefore, our objective is to advance trustworthy, open, and high-impact AI that serves both science and society.

requestTitle: Start-Up: Mohammadhadi Amini, Florida International University
Accelerating Neurodegeneration Discovery with Agentic AI Systems in C-BRAIN
abstract:
Alzheimer’s disease research faces a critical challenge: despite decades of effort, more than 99% of drug candidates fail in clinical trials. This failure reflects a deeper problem in biomedical science - vital knowledge is scattered across millions of papers, complex datasets, and unpublished “dark data,” making it nearly impossible for a scientist to understand the complete picture.
The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN) is tackling this challenge by combining the expertise of leading scientists with cutting-edge Artificial Intelligence (AI). With support from the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) and Microsoft, we propose to develop and test three unique AI tools that mirror the way science works: generating hypotheses, testing them against data, and providing rigorous peer-review style critique. At each step, human experts will remain in the loop to guide, validate, and refine outputs, ensuring trust and scientific rigor.
Together, these AI tools will form the first open benchmark for “AI Scientist” systems; thereby, allowing the broader research community to compare and improve their own approaches. The proposed project will deliver a transparent, end-to-end pipeline that will accelerate discovery in Alzheimer’s and sets the stage for scalable, AI-enabled science across biomedicine. All results will be shared openly through publications, code, and data resources, consistent with C-BRAIN’s mission of advancing science for the public good.

requestTitle: Efficient Privacy-Preserving De-identification of Medical Text Using Distilled Language Models in Confidential Computing Environments
abstract: The HIPAA mandates strict patient privacy protection, requiring de-identification of Protected Health Information (PHI) in shared medical data. While LLMs can automate this, their high computational cost limits their adoption in resource-constrained hospital environments. Furthermore, cloud-based PHI de-identification is often restricted by HIPAA without robust privacy measures. To address this, we propose a novel, cost-effective, privacy-preserving pipeline that combines model distillation and confidential computing. Our approach involves fine-tuning a large LLM for PHI de-identification, distilling its knowledge into a computationally efficient Small Language Model (SLM), and deploying the SLM within a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). This ensures that de-identification can be performed securely and efficiently on a remote TEE, even in hospitals with limited GPU infrastructure, thus facilitating broader sharing of de-identified medical records. Our plan includes model development (LLM fine-tuning and distillation to an SLM), confidential deployment within TEEs, and privacy-preserving collaboration leveraging OpenMined’s Syft platform. Expected outcomes are a lightweight, secure de-identification model, a reusable confidential computing deployment framework, and peer-reviewed publications.

requestTitle: Detect Scams in the Wild: Towards Realistic Benchmarks and Victim-Centered Evaluation
abstract:
Many recent scam detection benchmarks use LLMs to generate synthetic attacker–victim conversations. This is scalable, but the resulting data often misses what real scams look like: emotional pressure, persuasive intent, messy language, and variation across channels. Models trained on such data overfit to clean patterns and perform poorly on real cases, and simple metrics like accuracy do not reflect victim-centered risks such as the likelihood of compliance.

Our goal is to create a benchmark that both exposes the gap between synthetic and real scams and
provides tools to address it. We collect and anonymize a corpus that covers multiple scam types and channels, including romance scams, email phishing, job scams, SMS scams, multi-agent LLM-generated scam dialogues, and large-scale consumer complaints from publicly available platforms (e.g., the Better Business Bureau across 20+ scam categories). Instead of focusing on a single scam format, we track shared manipulation and persuasion cues (e.g., urgency, authority, social proof) that recur across various scams. A hybrid annotation pipeline with LLMs, classifiers, and human verification produces input-level labels (manipulation strategy, realism) and task-level metadata (estimated compliance risk), enabling controlled evaluation of fine-tuned and zero-shot LLM detectors. This benchmark is designed to support victim-centered metrics and more useful, explanation-based defenses in real-world settings.

requestTitle: Hands-on AI Information Systems Lab Exercises in the Classroom
abstract:
This project establishes an AI-enhanced, cloud-based laboratory platform that delivers hands-on learning across database management, computer networking, and cybersecurity. Many institutions lack the on-premises infrastructure and staffing to support such labs; we address this by deploying reusable, containerized environments that can be launched in minutes each semester and replicated across multiple classes.
Students will engage directly with applied AI: training and evaluating models for anomaly detection in security logs, network traffic classification and QoS prediction, and AI-assisted query optimization and semantic search in databases. The platform also includes an AI-agent development environment where students build rule-based or LLM-driven workflow agents to automate tasks such as alert triage or data pipeline orchestration. GPU-enabled runtimes support model training and inference, while centralized orchestration provides secure, isolated access for every student.
The outcome is a scalable library of AI-integrated lab templates and notebooks that improves learning equity—giving all students access to advanced computational resources from any location—while reducing faculty setup time from weeks to hours. By aligning instructional goals with advanced compute needs, the project advances NAIRR’s mission to democratize AI education and creates a shareable framework other courses and campuses can readily adopt.

requestTitle: Pre-Training Large-Scale Foundation Models for Epidemic Dynamics
abstract: Infections such as flu and COVID-19 continue to pose major global and economic risks. Despite richer data, most existing models remain narrowly tailored to single diseases or regions and cannot fully exploit information from past outbreaks, diverse data sources, or contextual knowledge about affected communities. We propose the Foundation Epidemic Model (FEM), a general-purpose framework that learns shared representations from large-scale epidemic data and associated textual and contextual information. FEM will support multiple forecasting and situational-awareness tasks, adapt to new locations and pathogens, and provide interpretable outputs for decision makers. By unifying temporal, spatial, and contextual signals in a single adaptable model, FEM aims to significantly improve the accuracy, robustness, and usability of epidemic modeling for public health response.

requestTitle: Earth Foundation Model Fusion
abstract: This project aims to build a unified foundation model that fuses geospatial and atmospheric representations for Earth-system understanding. While recent advances in weather and climate models (e.g., FourCastNet, GraphCast, ClimaX) and geospatial models (e.g., Clay, Prithvi, AlphaEarth) have achieved remarkable progress within their respective domains, they remain largely disconnected. We propose to integrate satellite-derived surface embeddings with atmospheric reanalysis data to capture coupled land–atmosphere dynamics, improving the prediction and interpretation of phenomena such as vegetation stress, albedo change, and heat-wave amplification. The project will develop and compare multiple fusion strategies, including cross-attention and mixture-of-experts routing, and evaluate them on the WeatherBench-2 benchmark. The resulting model and dataset pipelines will be openly released to advance foundation model research for climate and Earth observation.

requestTitle: SmartWater -- River Network Water Quality Monitoring
abstract:
River water pollution has consequences for human and environmental
 health, economic prosperity, and water security. Recent advances in
 sensing and data science provide unprecedented opportunities for a
 step change in the approaches used to identify and understand sources,
 dynamics, and consequences of water pollution in complex landscapes.
 The proposed "SmartWater" project will generate innovations in
 experimental analytics, data science and mathematical modelling to
 yield new mechanistic understanding of the dynamic drivers of multi
contaminant pollution hotspots (locations) and hot moments (times) in a
 changing water world. SmartWater will integrate environmental
 sensing, machine learning, and mathematical modelling with
 stakeholders' catchment knowledge to transform the way we diagnose,
 understand, predict, and manage water pollution hotspots and hot
 moments. SmartWater will provide the basis for improved decision
support and water quality management frameworks, which will be
 developed with and implemented by partner stakeholders.

requestTitle: Sage Edge Computing Access Request
abstract: Climate change and natural hazards present significant dangers to both humanity and critical cyberinfrastructures (CI). In response, the Earth Sciences community has adopted a cross-boundary approach to monitoring and mitigating these threats by developing CI and workflows that encompass sensors, edge computing nodes, network backbones, and remote cloud data centers. Unfortunately, this cross-boundary approach is vulnerable to both physical (resiliency) and cyber (security) threats. Current state-of-the-art techniques for addressing these threats take a fragmented approach, focusing on specific resources and proving ineffective for the overall hazard workflow. This project proposes the HazardMon framework, which scales horizontally (from sensors to edge cloud to WAN backbones to remote cloud) and vertically (across all layers of the hardware and software stack) to combat these two threats. The project will open-source HazardMon, and results will be disseminated to the community. The broadening participation activities in this project will catalyze community engagement and experiential learning, resulting in a globally competitive workforce. The project will also collaborate with stakeholders, particularly the NSF SAGE project, to facilitate the practical implementation of these ideas.

abstract: Tribes in North America have lived with the land for centuries. Recent observations have raised concerns for a plant relative known to the Ojibwe as manoomin or wild rice. requestTitle: mCLM: A Function-Infused and Synthesis-Friendly Modular Chemical Language Model
abstract: Despite their ability to understand chemical knowledge, large language models (LLMs) are limited in designing novel, functional molecules that are also synthetically feasible. This limitation stems from their atom-level representations, which fail to capture the modular nature of both molecular function and modern automated synthesis. To address this, we propose mCLM, a modular Chemical Language Model that tokenizes molecules into functional building blocks—substructures that confer specific properties and are compatible with automated laboratory synthesis. mCLM learns a bilingual language, jointly modeling these molecular building blocks with natural language descriptions of their functions extracted from scientific literature. By reasoning at this modular level, mCLM can conduct complex chemical reasoning to iteratively refine molecular designs, ensuring the generated molecules are efficiently synthesizable while optimizing for multiple functional objectives. Our 7B parameter prototype has already demonstrated significant promise, successfully improving key pharmaceutical properties for 430 FDA-approved drugs and refining previously failed "fallen angel" drugs to overcome their shortcomings. This proposal seeks NAIRR resources to scale mCLM to 32B and 72B parameter models, trained on a comprehensive multimodal dataset. The resulting open-source foundation model will provide the scientific community with a powerful new tool to accelerate the discovery of novel medicines and materials. Furthermore, this project directly supports the NSF Molecule Maker Lab Institute (MMLI) Thrust 1 goal of developing new AI tools to solve complex chemistry problems.

requestTitle: Generalizable and Interpretable Deep Learning for Microarchitecture Performance Simulation
abstract:
The waning of Moore's law has cemented domain-specific computing as the prevailing path forward for performance scaling. This has led to a strategic shift by hyperscale companies like Google (Axion), Amazon (Graviton), and Microsoft (Cobalt) increasingly investing in custom CPU designs tailored to specific workloads. Evaluating the performance of potential architecture configurations is one of the crucial tasks during design and optimization. The need for advanced simulators that can flexibly address these competing demands has never been more pressing. Existing simulators, like gem5 and Sniper, each use different abstractions that balance multi-dimensional trade-offs among speed, accuracy, and detail. gem5, an industry-standard simulator, often requires weeks to months to evaluate performance across multiple potential microarchitecture configurations, making it impractical for rapidly evolving design requirements. Hybrid analytical and ML-based simulators like Concorde have been proposed to overcome the issue, but require significant effort to build the analytical model manually. Emerging DL-based simulations, like SimNet and TAO, have shown promise, achieving remarkably fast and comparable cycle-level accuracy, while achieving >1,000x higher throughput than gem5. But they hit two major roadblocks: they 1) lack generalization on unseen microarchitecture designs, and 2) offer limited interpretability for performance prediction. To address these challenges, we propose a framework that expands upon earlier ML-based microarchitecture simulations, structured around two pivotal thrusts.

Thrust 1 focuses on building a generalizable approach to performance prediction agents through large-scale training on a diverse set of both microarchitecture designs and benchmarks. Thrust 2 focuses on the critical challenge of interpretability in these models in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets. Using influence functions, we aim to explain its predictions relating to the inputs, determine a minimal sufficient training set to reduce simulation cost, and evaluate its generalization on unseen microarchitectures or programs. This work will produce an open-source, reusable framework along with key insights from large-scale training for ML-based simulation, providing a critical foundation to guide the future development of such tools for real-world applications.

requestTitle: Neural Compression of Large-Scale DNN Models using Hessian-Based Pruning with Bipartite Matching
abstract: We aim to substantially compress large-scale deep neural networks, e.g., the CNNs and Transformers without compromising accuracy by leveraging second-order information and graph-based optimization. Our approach builds on Hessian-based pruning to identify critical parameters. Unlike simple magnitude pruning, Hessian-guided methods evaluate the sensitivity of the loss to parameter removal, thereby better preserving model accuracy. We will compute approximate Hessian statistics for large models to guide the removal of filters and neurons with minimal accuracy loss and their selection will be guided by a bipartite matching combinatorial. We will showcase the efficiency of our compressed DNNs by evaluating them on real-world resource-constraints systems.

requestTitle: High-Resolution Multimodal Digital Twin Synthesis with Diffusion Models
abstract: This project develops artificial intelligence methods to generate realistic, privacy-preserving biomedical data across multiple modalities, including chest X-rays, CT scans, and electrocardiograms (ECGs). Using a novel framework based on cross-Modal cross-Attention Denoising Diffusion (xMADD), the team will create high-resolution “digital twins” that accurately reflect demographic, diagnostic, and physiological characteristics. These synthetic datasets will enable new opportunities in personalized diagnostics, digital health research, and privacy-preserving data sharing, while reducing barriers created by siloed or restricted medical data. Benchmarking and evaluation of the fidelity of generated data, will ensure that the models produce clinically meaningful results while protecting patient privacy. All software, models, and benchmarking tools will be released openly to foster transparency and accelerate scientific discovery. By scaling training across high-performance computing resources, this effort directly supports the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) goals of democratizing access to advanced AI tools, enhancing reproducibility, and advancing biomedical research through responsible innovation.

requestTitle: Fine-Tuning Open-Source Large Language Models to Support Real-World Patient–Clinician Communication in Laboratory Test Results Interpretation
abstract: Patient portals are widely used to access laboratory test results, yet many patients—especially older adults—struggle to interpret these results in the context of their unique medical history. Our ongoing AHRQ-funded LabGenie project addresses this gap through an AI-powered web application that delivers tailored lab visualizations and context-aware question prompts for patients and caregivers. However, no foundational large language model (LLM) has been specifically trained for answering laboratory test questions, which limits accuracy and contextual relevance in patient-facing explanations. We propose to fine-tune open-source models Llama 410, Gemma 311, OpenBioLLM12, and Meditron13 using two complementary, de-identified datasets: (1) a 22,283-pair LabTest Q&A corpus reflecting layperson inquiries and clinically grounded answers, and (2) an 11,973-sample Patient–Physician Dialogue dataset representing multi-turn, context-rich medical conversations. Fine-tuning will be conducted in two phases—first with the 11B model for feasibility and prompt refinement, followed by the 90B model for large-scale evaluation—leveraging Google Cloud GPU infrastructure. Model outputs will be assessed for clarity, accuracy, and clinical relevance through clinician review and user studies across diverse patient groups. This work will produce publicly available, domain-specific LLMs optimized for real-world patient–clinician communication about lab results, advancing health literacy, shared decision-making, and equitable access to high-quality health information.

requestTitle: DUNE2: A Physics-Informed Deep Learning Model for High-Resolution, Long-Lead ENSO Forecasting
abstract: DUNE2 is a physics-informed deep learning system for high-resolution, weekly ENSO forecasting up to 18 months ahead. Addressing limits of AI models trained on atmosphere-only reanalyses, DUNE2 proxies ocean forcing by using physically motivated atmospheric surface-flux as indices, i.e wind divergence over Niño-4 region, moisture flux  over Niño-1+2 region, and surface sensible heat flux over Niño-3.4 region as drivers. The model combines a patch-based spatiotemporal attention backbone inspired by video Vision Transformers with a UNet++ component to capture both long-range dependencies and localized dynamics at 0.25° resolution. Trained on weekly-averaged ERA5 fields, DUNE2 predicts SST anomalies across Niño 1+2, 3, 3.4, and 4. Skill will be benchmarked against CNN/UNet/UNet-LSTM baselines and operational dynamical systems (NOAA CFSv2, ECMWF SEAS5) using RMSE, ACC, and HSS. By unifying interpretable attention with physics-guided inputs, DUNE2 aims to deliver earlier and more reliable annual warnings of El Niño/La Niña events and to reduce false negatives for major ENSO transitions. Based on preliminary studies with an earlier version of DUNE without transformers, access to 4 A100's took ~12nours.

requestTitle: GUARD-AR: Generative AI Framework for Uncertainty-Aware, High-Resolution Diffusion Ensemble Forecasting of Atmospheric Rivers
abstract: GUARD-AR (Generative AI Framework for Uncertainty-Aware, High-Resolution Diffusion Ensemble Forecasting of Atmospheric Rivers) aims to revolutionize probabilistic weather forecasting by merging physics-based simulation with advanced generative AI. Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are responsible for most of the extreme precipitation and flooding events along the U.S. West Coast. Traditional ensemble forecasting of ARs is computationally expensive, requiring thousands of simulations. GUARD-AR introduces a diffusion-based generative model that can produce large, calibrated ensembles of high-resolution forecasts within minutes—reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude. Leveraging CW3E’s regional reanalysis and West-WRF ensemble datasets, the system will generate uncertainty-aware forecasts of precipitation and integrated water vapor that support water resource management, reservoir operations, and flood mitigation. The resulting models and datasets will be openly shared, accelerating AI-driven advancements in environmental prediction and decision support.

requestTitle: Securing LLMs against Prompt Injection Attacks
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as the backbone of real-world applications such as Google Search with AI Overviews and Microsoft Bing Copilot. Security history shows that when data and instructions are not properly separated within a system, injection attacks can emerge. For example, SQL injection attacks in traditional software. Similarly, due to the lack of a clear boundary between instructions and data in prompts, LLM-integrated applications are inherently vulnerable to prompt injection attacks. This project's novelties are twofold: (1) conducting a systematic study to deepen the understanding of such threats, and (2) developing new defenses to mitigate such attacks. Its broader significance and importance lie in establishing foundational security principles for the rapidly growing ecosystem of AI applications, which are now widely deployed across diverse societal domains. Moreover, the released code and materials produced by this project will not only help secure real-world LLM-integrated applications but also serve as valuable educational resources for undergraduate and graduate courses, fostering the next generation of researchers and practitioners in this emerging security area.

requestTitle: Graph Transformers for Estimating Protein Structure Model Accuracy
abstract:
Accurately estimating the quality of AI-predicted protein structures—known as estimation of model accuracy (EMA) or model quality assessment (QA)—remains a key unsolved challenge in computational structural biology. This project aims to develop advanced graph transformer models for EMA that can robustly assess the accuracy of predicted protein structures without ground-truth data. Leveraging recent innovations in rotation- and translation-equivariant transformer architectures, the proposed methods will capture long-range dependencies within 3D protein structures and provide interpretable confidence estimates critical for downstream applications.

Within a one-year project period, we will design, train, and evaluate two complementary EMA models: one for monomeric proteins and another for multi-chain protein complexes. Model development will use large-scale datasets from the PSBench benchmark, which includes extensive labeled data generated during the CASP15 and CASP16 community-wide structure prediction experiments. Access to NAIRR’s high-performance GPU resources will enable large-scale training, fine-tuning, and benchmarking of these deep learning models.

By advancing the state of the art in protein structure model accuracy estimation, this project will provide the scientific community with reliable, interpretable, and open-source EMA tools, thereby supporting NAIRR’s mission to accelerate scientific discovery through trustworthy and high-performance AI research.

requestTitle: Start-Up: Qingyu Chen, Yale University
Task-Grounded Security for LLMs Toward Secure Instruction Following and Mitigating Prompt Injections
abstract: The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in critical applications is severely hampered by prompt injection attacks, the top-ranked threat in OWASP's LLM security framework, yet current research fails to capture realistic deployment constraints by treating LLMs as generic chatbots rather than task-specific systems. This research program addresses this gap through four interconnected aims: (1) establishing SystemBreach, a benchmark of 50+ real-world tasks that evaluate security based on production-quality system prompts; (2) developing unsupervised defenses via activation monitoring that detect malicious inputs through statistical deviations in internal representations; (3) quantifying the security-utility trade-off by formalizing the "ignoration" phenomenon where models silently discard potentially adversarial data, measured through the novel IgnoreBench framework; and (4) pioneering a security-first architectural paradigm that enforces instruction-data separation by design. Preliminary results demonstrate feasibility with activation-based detection achieving F1 scores above 0.75 across multiple LLMs, while revealing that standard security fine-tuning increases ignoration rates by over 45-fold, highlighting the critical need for architectural solutions beyond reactive patches. This work provides immediate empirical resources and a foundational roadmap for building the next generation of demonstrably secure and reliable AI systems.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot: Extracting Formal Models From 5G Specifications For Security Analysis
abstract:
The project seeks to fill the gap in automated 5G and NextG security analysis by developing novel approaches to extract formal models from large and complex specification documents. 5G is designed by the 3GPP, which designs and maintains technical specifications for 4G/5G and other cellular network systems. These technical specifications comprise natural language descriptions, spanning hundreds of documents with millions of words, which contain ambiguities, complexities, and, in some cases, inconsistencies that often lead to exploitable flaws. 
Nonetheless, it is nontrivial to analyze these unstructured documents for such flaws automatically. Analyzing formal models instead can be a crucial step forward in solving this problem and can be the building block of further security or compliance testing. However, such gold standard formal models are unavailable and building them manually is an intractable problem for complex layered networks such as 4G/5G. While previous research relied on manual interpretation of grammars and rules to annotate specifications and extract formal models, we employ a structured, self-supervised method that automatically provides an error-free, human-involvement-free approach. On the whole, this project advances the state of the art by developing rigorous methods to automatically extract, model, and analyze formal models from complex 4G/5G technical specifications. By integrating NLP, formal verification, and domain-specific knowledge, the work enables systematic identification of vulnerabilities and gaps in cellular protocols that are otherwise difficult to capture manually.

requestTitle: Enhancing the Trustworthiness and Reliability of Cyclone Prediction Systems with Physics-Informed AI
abstract:
Cyclones, such as hurricanes and Nor'easters, pose a significant and growing threat to both life and economic stability. While weather forecasting has improved, predicting the evolution of high-impact storms remains a critical challenge, as existing models often struggle to reliably capture their complex transformations and interactions with other weather systems.

This project confronts this challenge by developing an advanced framework to enhance the trustworthiness and reliability of long-range cyclone prediction. By leveraging a holistic, AI-driven approach, our research aims to identify the subtle atmospheric precursors and initial conditions that lead to the development of dangerous storms. The ultimate goal is to create more accurate and timely warning systems, providing communities with crucial extra time for preparation, which can save lives and mitigate economic damage.

The project will generate new fundamental insights into cyclone dynamics and produce a robust, open-source framework, contributing to the improvement of next-generation weather and climate prediction systems for the entire scientific community.

requestTitle: Advancing Retrieval‑Augmented AI to Deliver Transparent, Trustworthy Insights from Massive Ocean Datasets
abstract: OceanAI is a retrieval-augmented, provenance-aware AI system that makes complex ocean datasets—like sea surface temperatures and tide records—accessible through natural language. By linking large language models to structured NOAA data and curated sources, OceanAI provides transparent, verifiable answers with charts, metadata, and machine-readable output. The platform helps scientists, students, and policymakers explore ocean trends without coding or domain expertise. A working prototype has been demonstrated at the 2025 NOAA Enterprise Data Management Workshop. All tools and findings will be shared openly to support research, education, and environmental decision-making.

requestTitle: Certifying Internal Memory in Efficient LLMs: Robustness and Integrity of the KV-Cache
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) use the KV-Cache to efficiently handle multi-turn dialogue and long-context tasks by storing internal states across interactions. While this improves performance, it creates new security and privacy risks. For example, hidden instructions (prompt injections) can manipulate model behavior across sessions, and cached private data may leak between users. These threats persist beyond a single input, making them harder to detect and mitigate.

This project proposes a systematic framework for certifying the robustness and integrity of the KV-Cache. We will formalize key attack vectors and develop randomized smoothing techniques that track how internal states evolve over time, offering certified protection against injection, leakage, and state inconsistency.

requestTitle: Real-Time Run-to-Run Control of Disturbance Propagation in Additive Manufacturing via Large-Scale Diffusion Models
abstract:
Additive manufacturing often faces high failure rates due to unpredictable thermal behavior. This variability stems from the layer-by-layer process, where each layer’s thermal response is highly sensitive to environmental conditions, material properties, and complex geometries. Unlike point sensors or point clouds that offer limited or costly data, thermal cameras provide detailed, real-time temperature maps, revealing critical insights into heat flow, cooling, and hotspots that affect bonding and internal stresses.

However, most existing control methods reduce rich sensor data to low-dimensional representations or depend on static models, thereby failing to capture complex, evolving disturbances. Even advanced closed-loop systems generally make only coarse, layer-level adjustments. Despite the availability of high-resolution, high-speed thermal imaging, current approaches do not fully exploit this data for real-time, adaptive control. While diffusion models are well-suited to modeling complex spatiotemporal phenomena, they have yet to be integrated into closed-loop control frameworks.

This project closes that gap by developing a new control system that uses thermal imaging as the primary monitor. It preserves the full spatial and temporal structure of sensor data, captures complex dynamics through diffusion models, and ensures robust performance with closed-loop analysis and explicit uncertainty quantification. By turning thermal variability from a challenge into a controllable feature, this work aims to deliver more consistent, higher-quality 3D printing with fewer failures and less waste.

requestTitle: GeoFoundation-Powered Carbon Flux Estimation Using Ground Observations, Remote Sensing Observations, and Reanalysis Data
abstract: Quantifying net ecosystem exchange (NEE) and gross primary productivity (GPP)  is vital for global carbon budgeting but hampered by sparse eddy-covariance towers and vegetation heterogeneity. Satellite remote sensing offers broad coverage but cannot directly measure NEE and GPP or fine-scale land-use changes. Machine-learning upscaling has produced global flux products yet struggles regionally. Emerging geo-foundation models like Prithvi-EO-2.0 and Panopticon excel at capturing detailed spatial patterns, while AI systems such as Aardvark infer dynamics from sparse data. This project will fuse satellite imagery, tower flux data, and reanalysis to produce monthly NEE and GPP estimates at 0.5° resolution from 2001–2024, reducing uncertainty and delivering a public dataset.

requestTitle: Multimodal Learning for Detecting and Tracking Unmanned Aerial Vehicle
abstract:
This project proposes a multimodal sensor fusion framework that integrates RGB and infrared cameras with passive RF sensors. Multimodal learning algorithms will be developed to fuse data across these
complementary sensing modalities, enabling robust detection and tracking of UAVs in complex environments, including low-light and high-interference scenarios. A key emphasis is on the synchronization and calibration of sensor inputs, as desynchronized data can mislead the model and degrade
performance. Prior to integration, individual sensor modalities will be thoroughly evaluated to ensure standalone effectiveness. The resulting system aims to operate in real time, remain cost-effective, and be
deployable on resource-constrained platforms such as other UAVs or mobile surveillance stations.

requestTitle: Understanding LLM Reasoning Failures: Toward Safer and More Reliable AI
abstract: As Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes domains – ranging from education and healthcare to scientific discovery and decision-making – their safety and reliability hinge on our ability to detect when, how, and why their reasoning fails. This project aims to systematically understand and characterize the failure modes of state-of-the-art LRMs by rigorously evaluating their robustness and faithfulness under carefully designed stress tests. We will develop new frameworks for probing reasoning failures and create principled evaluation tools to identify, interpret, and ultimately mitigate these failures in large language models.

requestTitle: Networked Time-Series Foundation Models for Reliable and Resilient Power Systems
abstract:
In power systems, optimal power flow (OPF) aims to determine the optimal generator dispatch, voltage settings, and power flows while satisfying system constraints. Traditional optimization solvers are computationally expensive, e.g., solving the AC-OPF problem for a 192,768-bus system may take 25 to 50 minutes. This motivates exploring modern AI techniques (e.g., foundation models) to improve efficiency. Nevertheless, developing foundation models for power systems involves several key challenges. First, integrating graph-based grid topology with time-series power demand/generation is nontrivial, as neither graph nor time-series foundation models alone can capture this interaction. Second, modeling long time-series and large network presents scalability challenges. Third, foundation models must enforce physical constraints.

To address these challenges, this project aims to develop a networked time-series foundation model for power system monitoring, forecasting, and fault mitigation. The crucial idea is to integrate the graph-based topology of the power grid with time-series data of power demand and generation. More specifically, the project contains three key tasks: (1) designing and pretraining a networked time-series foundation model to enhance real-time system monitoring, (2) fine-tuning the model for accurate short- and long-term forecasting, while analyzing neural scaling laws to understand generalization, and (3) enabling intelligent fault detection and mitigation by integrating the model with real-time AI agents capable of generating control strategies. Expected outcomes include open-source foundation models and research publications to further advance the application of foundation models in critical energy infrastructure.

requestTitle: ARMOR-HAL: Unified Defense for Adversarial Robustness and Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated impressive progress in connecting visual perception with natural language understanding, enabling applications in interactive assistance, decision support, and autonomous systems. Yet, their practical deployment remains hindered by two critical vulnerabilities: exposure to jailbreak attacks and the generation of hallucinated content that lacks visual grounding. Existing methods treat these issues in isolation. On one hand, safety alignment strategies improve resistance to adversarial exploits but often weaken instruction-following and chain-of-thought reasoning, which can, in turn, amplify hallucination. On the other hand, hallucination mitigation techniques strengthen visual grounding but leave models open to jailbreaks and adversarial fine-tuning. To overcome this fragmentation, we introduce ARMOR-HAL (Adversarial Robustness and Hallucination Mitigation in Multi-modal Responses), a unified defense framework that addresses both challenges simultaneously. ARMOR-HAL enhances safety alignment beyond shallow token-level defenses while reinforcing cross-modal grounding to curb hallucinations. Our approach integrates per-token depth-regularized alignment, visual steering, and attention-sink calibration, ensuring that LVLMs withstand jailbreak attempts without compromising semantic fidelity or visual truthfulness. By unifying these complementary defenses, ARMOR-HAL provides a principled pathway toward safer, more reliable, and trustworthy LVLMs for real-world deployment.

requestTitle: Computational Resource Request for Teaching Chemical Data Science with AI/ML Tools
abstract: "CHEM 487/542 — Special Topics in Physical Chemistry: Chemical Data Science" is a newly developed course in the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology at Rutgers University–New Brunswick, scheduled for the Spring 2026 semester. Designed for graduate students and advanced undergraduates, this course integrates lectures and hands-on sessions to provide foundational knowledge and practical research skills in data science and artificial intelligence (AI) as applied to chemistry. Students will learn how to represent chemical data, perform statistical analyses, and build machine learning (ML) models for applications such as molecular property prediction, reaction analysis, and materials design. Each student will also design and execute an independent project that applies data-driven approaches to real-world problems across chemistry, biology, and materials science. Using NAIRR Classroom computational resources, students will gain direct experience running data-driven workflows, training AI models, and analyzing large-scale chemical datasets within GPU-accelerated environments. These resources will greatly enhance the learning experience by exposing students to modern computational practices and scalable AI infrastructure, ultimately preparing them to make meaningful contributions to the rapidly evolving field of chemical data science.

requestTitle: A Knowledge-Guided Multitask LLM for Software Vulnerability Detection, Reasoning and Mitigation
abstract: Software vulnerabilities pose serious risks to real-world systems, potentially leading to crashes, data loss, and security breaches. While various detection techniques such as static analysis and large language models (LLMs) have been developed, these methods still face two challenges: (i) current benchmarks do not cover diverse detection tasks; and (ii) existing LLM detectors overlook domain knowledge. To address these challenges, this project aims to propose a knowledge-guided multitask LLM-based detector that can identify, pinpoint, explain, and fix vulnerability functions simultaneously. Specifically, we first create a comprehensive vulnerability benchmark dataset that covers diverse tasks. Then, we develop a new knowledge-guided multi-task LLM detector based on our created dataset. The resulting detector is expected to advance various downstream security tasks, such as patch presence test, malware detection, and automatic program repair.

requestTitle: Hands-on AI Inquiry: A Participatory and Exploratory Lab Model for Trustworthy AI Education
abstract: As artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) systems become increasingly embedded in society, computing professionals must be prepared to navigate challenges in responsible design, deployment, and use, using both affective and cognitive knowledge. Course materials should provide experiential engagement needed to foster meaningful reflection on values and impact of AI systems in society. This project proposes a participatory, lab-based model for responsible AI/ML education that integrates exploration of values and decision-making with hands-on technical experimentation using a customized, no-code visualization web app and real models trained on anonymized, student-relevant data. Through guided experimentation and reflection, students will analyze model evaluation signals, including robustness, calibration, transparency, privacy considerations, and differences in error rates across subpopulations. They will then map trade-offs, and consider how technical decisions influence different stakeholders, including themselves. We will evaluate the intervention by asking: (1) Does the lab improve students’ understanding of model evaluation methods and AI/ML decision systems? (2) Does it shift attitudes toward professional responsibility and the broader societal implications of AI/ML? (3) How does it affect the quality and depth of students’ reflection on trust, values, and impact? and (4) Do students demonstrate increased communication skills or decision-making courage when discussing AI's pros and cons? A quasi-experimental design will compare a traditional and intervention offering of a required undergraduate responsibility-focused computing course, using pre/post AI Literacy & Responsibility assessments, thematic analysis of reflections and discussions, and think-aloud protocols. The project will produce open-source, adaptable instructional materials that promote affective and cognitive growth in trustworthy AI practice.

requestTitle: Multi-Modal Semantic Routing for vLLM
abstract:
The vLLM Semantic Router (https://github.com/vllm-project/semantic-router)
is an open-source framework for directing user prompts to the most appropriate large language model (LLM). At present, routing is limited to text-only requests, but emerging applications increasingly involve speech, voice, video, and other modalities. Without multi-modal support, developers face fragmentation in building seamless AI workflows.
This project proposes to extend the Semantic Router with multi-modal routing capabilities, focusing on speech-text pipelines and exploring vision capabilities. We will evaluate and fine-tune speech foundation models (IBM Granite, Whisper/WavLM) as the core routing infrastructure, while exploring vision models (FLAVA, BLIP-2, CLIP/OpenCLIP) as secondary capabilities. We will leverage H100 GPUs for large-scale evaluation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The project will deliver: (1) a production-grade multimodal router, (2) systematic evaluation reports comparing routing accuracy, latency, and cost-efficiency, (3) fine-tuned multimodal models, (4) comprehensive benchmarks and datasets, and (5) deployment recipes for OpenShift AI, KServe, and Kubernetes environments. All results will be open-sourced to strengthen the vLLM and NAIRR ecosystems.

requestTitle: Time Series Data Agent: an Agentic System with Foundation Models for Multimodal Data
abstract: This project proposes the development of a Time-Series Data Agent (TS-Agent) under the NAIRR Pilot Deep Partnership, Core AI Track. The objective is to transform our previously developed Abstract Shape Token-Editing Predictive (ASTEP) framework from a passive analysis tool to an active, agentic system capable of multiple time-series tasks, including optimal control. We will develop a unified, token-based architecture where interpretable time series representations are aligned with semantic embeddings from the IBM Granite Language Model. We will also build the overarching TS-Agent, an agentic framework that orchestrates the model’s functionalities. The TS-Agent will be able to utilize appropriate tools, analyze and reason about potential solutions, and deliberate internally before producing a final solution for execution.

requestTitle: Efficient Memory Offloading for Cost- and Energy-Efficient Foundation Model Training
abstract: Foundation model training is often limited by GPU memory, with multi-GPU distribution used as the default workaround despite high communication and energy costs. We propose transparent memory offloading from GPUs to adjacent CPU memory over PCIe as a cost- and energy-efficient alternative. Our preliminary results show up to 15% throughput improvement and reduced network traffic. Using MOC infrastructure, we will extend this study to large-scale workloads, including advanced parallelism and Mixture-of-Experts models. The findings aim to guide future system designs that better integrate GPU–CPU memory hierarchies, lowering infrastructure costs and broadening access to large-model training.
resourceName: IBM & the AI Alliance — Collaboration on Open-Source Cloud Platform, Models and Tools

requestTitle: Evaluating and Improving Applications of Large Language Models to Automated Software Testing
abstract:
Recent advances show that large language models (LLMs) can generate software tests with coverage comparable to traditional methods while producing more readable tests that reflect developer intent. Yet, significant gaps remain between developer-written tests and both traditional and LLM-based automated test generation (ATG) tools, especially in test scope, modularity, and input complexity. These discrepancies highlight the need for evaluation metrics and techniques that capture the structural and semantic qualities developers value.
This project addresses these gaps through three objectives. First, we will examine patterns of redundancy in LLM-generated and developer-written test suites and develop tools to improve efficiency. Second, we will enhance modularity and self-containment by combining static and dynamic analysis with LLM-based code generation. Third, we will develop novel strategies for scenario-based test generation that better capture developer practices. Together, these contributions will improve our understanding of the differences between generated and developer-written tests and will move ATG tools toward producing more meaningful, maintainable, and developer-aligned test suites.

requestTitle: Building Reliability and Transaction Semantics for LLM Agents
abstract: Agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) are unreliable and often take actions that leave their shared operating environment in an inconsistent state. For example, coding agents can make incorrect code modifications, or can create unit tests mismatched with code modifications, etc. This project aims to improve agentic reliability for a wide variety of settings, via a series of new techniques that always that assure the state of the world (e.g., of the codebase, for coding agents) is correct, even if agents execute erroneous actions. In doing so, we take inspiration from “transactions”, which are popular in databases, and incorporate smart “roll backs” of agentic actions into the agentic world. Together these techniques will create a new reliability abstraction for the emerging agentic ecosystems in various domains.

requestTitle: CLEARBOX: Interpreting and Improving Multimodal LLMs
abstract: We propose CLEARBOX, a novel open-source suite of tools for white-box and black-box interpretation and intervention of foundational Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Specifically, we propose to build algorithms and software to mechanistically probe, intervene, and visualize the internal activation patterns. This toolkit will provide researchers with critical infrastructure to dissect internal representations, diagnose cross-modal alignment failures, thereby developing and deploying safer and more robust MLLMs.

requestTitle: Model Merging for Code LLMs: Reasoning Fusion and MoE-Aware Methods
abstract: Model and adapter merging are powerful techniques for integrating task-specific specialist LLMs into a single model, reducing costs and latency while maintaining quality. However, their applicability to software engineering tasks remains underexplored, especially in agentic systems that combine multiple models for different coding tasks. This project advances two key areas in this domain: systematic integration of reasoning-heavy and lightweight models and specialized merging techniques for Mixture-of-Experts architectures, including expert alignment and routing-optimized fusion. We will assess performance across multiple coding tasks in agentic workflows, aiming for single-model (or an optimally small number) efficiency with multi-specialist capabilities.

requestTitle: Adaptive KV-Cache Compression for Agentic AI
abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in long-context and agentic settings, where memory efficiency becomes a critical bottleneck. A key challenge lies in the growth of the key–value (KV) cache, which scales linearly with sequence length and strains memory resources during autoregressive generation. This project introduces an adaptive compression framework for the KV cache that dynamically learns compact representations of token information in real time. The proposed framework tracks the most informative subspaces for keys and values using lightweight updates. To support agentic workloads, where the nature of token streams varies with planning, tool use, and reflection, the method further incorporates mode-specific compression strategies that allocate memory based on contextual importance.

Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning for Discovering Knowledge - Full Proposal
abstract: This project aims to develop scalable post-training algorithms that enable AI systems to autonomously discover novel scientific knowledge, particularly in domains such as mathematics and physics. While recent milestones, such as LLM-based systems achieving gold medal performance at the 2025 International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO), are remarkable, they leave open a critical question: are these systems truly discovering, or merely recombining patterns seen during pretraining? To address this, we propose to design and scale RL-based techniques that promote creative search, systematic exploration, and trial-and-error learning, moving beyond imitation to genuine discovery. We will build on our prior work, e3 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09026), which introduced an RL recipe enabling small-scale, open-source models to solve challenging math problems with state-of-the-art performance.
