requestTitle: Resource Request for Privacy-Preserving Traffic Safety Analysis: A Module on Trusted AI With Real Data from Civic Partners
abstract: This proposal requests computational resources to support an advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) course on trust focusing on privacy-preserving traffic safety analysis. Students will learn machine learning (ML) algorithms and trusted AI practices, and apply them on the real-world problem of traffic. They will work with large volumes of traffic accident and student-driver education data from civic partners in South Carolina. They will process sensitive traffic data, generate privacy-preserving synthetic datasets, and create predictive models for accident analysis. The requested GPU resources will enable students to implement end-to-end pipelines including data synthesis, automated cleaning, statistical correlation analysis, and interactive visualization of traffic patterns. Access to NAIRR Pilot Classroom Resources would give students the computational capacity to work with real-world traffic safety challenges while maintaining appropriate privacy controls for stakeholder data.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot Expansion: FA1- Collaborative EAGER- Multimodal AI-Augmented Empirical Social Research and Training
abstract: In the rapidly growing digital landscape, technological literacy has become a crucial skill for all individuals that enhances critical thinking skills and promotes adaptability in an ever-changing job market. However, traditional technology education has often focused primarily on Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) learners, leaving a significant gap in the technological incompetency among non-STEM major. This classroom proposal will address this gap through two Large Language Models (LLMs) and prompt engineering-focused courses for humanities and STEM students. The humanities course will focus on analyzing LLMs from the lenses of ethics, biases, and privacy with an emphasis on the best practices underlying synthetic data creation while, the technical elective STEM course Machine Learning Security and Privacy (and similar courses) will be taught at The University of Toledo (UToledo), George Mason University (GMU) and Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) in multiple modalities including in-person, hybrid, and asynchronous online.

requestTitle: ThreatGuard: AI-Driven Automated Threat Modeling for Secure Cloud
abstract: Threat modeling is a critical component of secure hardware development, enabling proactive identification and mitigation of security vulnerabilities early in the design process. However, existing tools often lack standardization, comprehensive coverage of system threats, and automation, making them challenging to apply in complex systems containing hardware, software, and applications. ThreatGuard addresses these gaps by leveraging generative AI based Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate and standardize threat modeling for cloud systems. By integrating dynamic vulnerability databases and property-driven formal verification, ThreatGuard not only ensures up-to-date threat coverage but also provides a systematic approach to root-cause analysis. This research aims to systematically standardize the threat modeling process, reducing dependency on domain-specific expertise and increasing the efficiency of cloud security measures. The developed tools and methodologies will have direct implications for securing cloud infrastructure, strengthening system design resilience, and improving the industry's overall security posture.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot Classroom Request For CIS 5190 Applied Machine Learning at the University of Pennsylvania
abstract:
CIS 5190 Applied Machine Learning is a course offered at the University of Pennsylvania that equips students with both theoretical and practical expertise in machine learning. Covering key areas such as supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning, this course emphasizes hands-on experience with real-world datasets. Students will engage deeply with machine learning algorithms, implementing them in various projects that require significant computational resources.

To support these educational objectives, we are requesting access to advanced computational resources via the Vocareum AI Notebook platform. This platform will enable students to effectively train and test machine learning models, particularly in the latter half of the course when they will be tackling complex, data-intensive projects. The requested resources include GPU access, sufficient memory, and storage, ensuring that students have the necessary tools to apply their learning to challenging real-world problems.

requestTitle: Resources for Machine Learning, Programming, and Big data courses for Data Science and Biomedical Data Science Graduate Programs
abstract: The Machine learning and programming courses at the School of Applied Computational Sciences in Meharry Medical College are the foundational and advanced level courses for the data science and biomedical data science master’s and PhD programs. The machine learning course focuses on learning various machine learning techniques and their applications in different data science and biomedical real-world problems. It includes implementing state-of-the-art machine learning and deep learning algorithms and evaluation on real-world datasets. The programming course requires hands-on applications of learned programming skills in real-world datasets. The big data course provides students experience of various Big data tools like Hadoop, Spark to analyze large scale datasets.  The Vocareum AI Notebook platform, can provide access to required computational resources as well as GPUs for the machine learning and deep learning projects. These courses help gain students' necessary skill sets to be prepared for industry jobs as well as help them in presenting their class project work in various conference presentations and publish papers.

requestTitle: Accelerating Participatory Modeling with AI: Translating Large-Scale Interview Transcripts Data into Causal Loop Diagrams via Large Language Models
abstract:
One promising method for understanding complex problems is participatory modeling through the creation of Causal Loop Diagrams (CLDs) in System Dynamics modelling, which is a visualization tool to represent the interactions within a system and provide critical insights for policy and decision-making.
However, constructing CLDs is a time-intensive process that requires significant input from community stakeholders, followed by manual parsing and synthesis of interview transcripts—steps that are labor-intensive and prone to human error and cognitive bias. To address this challenge, this study leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the parsing, synthesis, and modeling of interview transcripts into CLDs, enabling a more efficient and scalable participatory-driven modeling approach. With their ability to process large volumes of unstructured data, LLMs provide faster and more reliable insights. 
This approach will be tested in the healthcare domain, where prompt understanding of complex systems is essential for improving patient outcomes. Specifically, we will use interview transcripts from our NIH study on understanding issues related to alcohol and substance-exposed pregnancies. We will evaluate the feasibility of using LLMs to generate quality CLDs, by defining and implementing evaluation metrics that cater to CLD similarity metrics. These metrics include a) existing natural language processing, b) graph similarity metrics, and c) CLD similarity metrics. 
This approach could significantly reduce the time and resources required for participatory modeling analysis, offering broad applications in fields that face complex problems requiring qualitative data-driven policy decision-making.

requestTitle: Pretraining new LLMs with morphologically aware tokenizers for social media English and historical Latin
abstract:
Pretrained Transformer language models are key to all advances in natural language processing, but the effects of their own initial foundation -- subword tokenization models like BPE or WordPiece -- are still poorly understood.

These methods learn subword segmentations and vocabularies that are dramatically mismatched to the actual units of meaning within words -- morphemes.  We are developing morphologically aware Transformer tokenizers that give much higher quality and more generalizable segmentation information.  To illustrate generality, we focus on two settings: (1) social media English, where we have access to billions of tweets with novel compounds and dialect-specific morphology, whose challenges give rise to racial dialect disparity in NLP systems (prior work: Blodgett et al. 2016, Eggleston and O'Connor 2022); and (2) historical Latin, a morphologically rich language where we have access to both large-scale pretraining data and sophisticated linguistic resources (e.g. LemLat, or our prior work: Hudspeth et al. 2024).

This builds on prior work which has explored some tokenizer variants, but usually within unsupervised segmentation models targeted toward compression tasks, completely multiple literatures including unsupervised information-theoretic models with inductive bias and evaluations targeted for human language morphology (e.g. Morfessor), and our proposed category of blended models where we hypothesize significant potential, by utilizing supervised learning-based morphological segmenter, derived from expert-annotated morphological data, and incorporating as a joint Viterbi decoder along with a core unsupervised model already known to be effective for LLM tokenization, such as the Unigram LM (Kudo 2018).

We will compare alternative Transformer tokenizers, including our novel ones that incorporate morphological supervision.  For each new tokenizer, we will segment our pretraining corpus, train a new Transformer LM (likely with Megatron-DeepSpeed, which we have used for preliminary work), and evaluate performance on downstream tasks.  We will also examine performance disparities across historical or demographically contingent language varieties; for example, our prior work found NLP performance gaps between historical periods in our Latin corpus, and NLP performance gaps for African-American English versus mainstream American English in our social media corpus, both of which we aim to assess from our developed models.

This will be computationally expensive, even with the older class of BERT-style models we have used in preliminary work, and for which the literature has done some exploration of alternative tokenizers.  The ability to conduct many pretraining experiments will be crucial to addressing key research questions; and we may be able to scale up to larger models (e.g. 1B parameters) that are more often used in generative LLM applications.  This compute award would be applied to purchase time on GPU servers for training and evaluation for all these settings.

requestTitle: Towards Multi-modal and Lifelong AI Clinical Agents System
abstract:
Recent advancements in generative models, such as large language models (LLMs), combined with the availability of electronic health record data, have enabled AI systems to collaborate effectively through conversations in areas like diagnostics, patient communication, and medical research. While systems like ClinicalAgent have achieved success in clinical trial outcome prediction, two major challenges remain: (1) the inability to process and integrate multi-modal data (e.g., diagnostic reports, medical imaging, time-series data, and drug history) and (2) the high cost of retraining models, which hinders continuous learning and adaptation to new medical knowledge.  
This project aims to address these challenges by developing a multi-modal and lifelong AI clinical agent system, envisioned as an “AI family doctor.” These agents will integrate diverse modalities to deliver personalized, accurate, and context-aware medical assistance. Their capabilities include early disease detection, improved patient monitoring, and reduced workload for healthcare professionals, promoting equitable and efficient global healthcare solutions.

requestTitle: Certification of Generative Responsible AI Models (C-GRAM)
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs), a type of generative AI (GenAI), inherit biases and misinformation from the human-generated data they are trained on, raising concerns about their safety, ethics, and security. LLMs can produce toxic, biased, hateful, and misleading text, hallucinate, and provide harmful responses to malicious prompts. Businesses struggle to implement responsible GenAI solutions due to a lack of awareness about these risks. Existing AI risk management frameworks, like NIST's, do not quantitatively evaluate these risks. 

Our goal is to develop a certification framework for GenAI models that quantifies the risks of bias, harm, and toxicity, enabling businesses to choose models based on their risk tolerance. This framework, QuaCer-B for bias and QuaCer-C for knowledge comprehension, will provide high-confidence bounds on the probability of unbiased responses. The certification process currently requires significant computational resources, which are insufficient for larger models and multi-modal evaluations. 

The project plan includes setting up the computational environment, testing and revising the certification framework on various LLMs, and extending the certification to other types of harm. The final framework and results will be published in an AI conference and made open-source. This work aims to provide the first reliable certification framework for LLMs, crucial for their safe deployment in public-facing applications.

requestTitle: Advancing AI for Astronomical Discovery through Agentic Benchmarking
abstract: Astronomical surveys routinely observe billions of sources from the cosmos, yet due to the limited number of human experts, only a small fraction of astronomical sources will ever be reasoned and studied in detail by humans, potentially missing many interesting sources. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has sparked significant interest in developing AI agents capable of autonomously conducting scientific research. This agentic approach, where AI systems can plan, design experiments, and interpret results, has immense potential to accelerate discovery and identify scientifically significant sources. However, realizing this vision requires robust benchmarks to evaluate the holistic problem-solving abilities of AI agents tailored for astronomical research. So far, while there is tremendous interest in such agents, AI astronomer advancement faces much difficulty due to the lack of benchmarking efforts to advance this study. In this study, we aim to create the first astronomy-based agentic benchmark extracted from real research workflows in astronomy literature. By carefully curating multi-step reasoning examples that test an AI agent's ability to strategize, write analysis code, and engage in scientific dialogue, this work will provide an unprecedented way to assess and advance agentic astronomical research capabilities. This work aligns directly with key national priorities in advancing AI for scientific discovery and using foundation models to interactively examine complex data, and pave the way for game-changing AI-driven discoveries across the sciences.

requestTitle: Development of Spatial Discretization Operators by Machine Learning Optimization Techniques
abstract: As we encounter a moment of rapid adoption of Machine Learning (ML) as an alternative toolkit for the forecasting of environmental systems, questions remain about the interpretability and physicality of end-to-end ML forecasting engines. In order to continue an effort to bring greater interpretability and adoption of ML techniques, we present a framework for equivalence between Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures and discrete calculus operators on uniform and unstructured grids respectively. We are able to cast numerical differentiation in the context of Symbolic Regression models where constraints and desired properties (improved dispersion) can be directly incorporated into the regression sequence of an ML setup. We present several examples of differencing schemes and other existing discretization methods that are tuned via ML training regression to achieve greater accuracy in approximating derivatives and more favorable dispersion profiles related to transport. This targeted, small-data approach can improve upon existing NWP models in a minimally invasive manner using modest computational resources.

requestTitle: Enhancing LLM Reasoning using Intermediate Solution Steps and Dynamic Data Augmentation
abstract:
Graphs are the underlying data structure for many fields, including protein structure modeling, legal reasoning, social networking problems, and many more and building models to understand graph data has been a core machine learning problem. Despite recent strides in reasoning capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit significant limitations in performing complex, multistep reasoning tasks on graphs. These shortcomings indicate that LLMs are unable to fully understand graph structures, and thus unable to perform graph-based reasoning. LLMs capable of reasoning on graphs would be able to better understand and leverage explicit relationships present in data, which is a critical step towards improving overall LLM
reasoning. Our research aims to bridge this gap by training LLMs to break down complex problems into multiple solvable steps.

requestTitle: Navigating Chemical Reaction Space via Deep Learning
abstract: This research proposal presents a comprehensive framework for navigating and modeling chemical reaction space using deep learning approaches. We address three fundamental challenges in reaction modeling: the lack of accurate molecular-level reaction dynamics models, insufficient integration of 3D molecular information with reaction conditions, and complexity in multi-step synthesis planning. Our approach unfolds in three phases: (1) developing energy-informed models for reaction dynamics that capture molecular conformational changes through transition states, (2) creating a 3D-aware multimodal language model that combines spatial molecular information with experimental procedures for reaction prediction, and (3) implementing a chain-of-thought reasoning system for multi-step retrosynthesis planning augmented with chemical knowledge retrieval. The proposed framework will be evaluated against established benchmarks including Transition-1x and USPTO-50k, with potential applications in drug discovery, materials design, and sustainable chemistry. By bridging the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental outcomes, this research aims to accelerate innovation in chemical synthesis while maintaining interpretability and practical applicability.

requestTitle: Trustworthy multiscale adaptive turbulence foundation models
abstract: This project proposes to develop a trustworthy foundation model for solving multiscale turbulent flows — central to energy generation, earth sciences, and power and propulsion systems. Compared to physics-based simulations, foundation models offer faster solutions, and, unlike single-purpose AI, generalize better across multiple systems. To be operationalized in real-world scenarios, models must be trustworthy, ensuring accuracy and reliability, robustness, and resilience. However, realizing these qualities introduces significant challenges in data, model, training, and deployment strategies, due to the multiscale and multiphysical nature of turbulence. Specifically, 1) data samples for multiscale turbulence are often extremely high-resolution, challenging even exascale supercomputers; 2) data are too sparse to cover the high-dimensional parameter space for effective foundation model training; 3) overconfidence in foundation models can cause users to overlook issues like domain shifts in unforeseen complicated diverse application scenarios. To overcome the challenges and develop a trustworthy foundation model for turbulent flows, we propose an integrated approach to guide model development with four specific aims: 1) design physics-inspired multiscale algorithms composed of multi-fidelity representations and adaptive tokenization to enable training on high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) data, 2) bridge data gaps and enhance trustworthiness by incorporating physics and adversarial techniques, 3) develop a trustworthiness module for measuring and enhancing model alignment to physics, and 4) pretrain the foundation model and illustrate effectiveness in distinct domain-specific fine-tuning tasks.

requestTitle: Towards the World's Largest and Most Advanced Genomics Foundation Model
abstract:
We are applying for 214,000 hours of A100 80GB GPU resource to create the world’s largest and most advanced genomics foundation model (GFM) within 12 months. To generate more direct scientific impact, we plan to open source and deploy the well-trained model through a research coordination network on “Foundation Model for Science" across 21 major research universities in the Midwest region of USA . 

This project is led by the PI Han Liu from Northwestern University and co-PI Zhong Wang from the Joint Genome Institute at Department of Energy. These two PIs have demonstrated strong track record on training genomics foundation models. More specifically, they have created the first encoder-based genomics foundation models DNABERT which has been downloaded for more than 2 million times in the past two years. It is incorporated in NVIDIA BioNeMo as the representative work of genome analysis. Their follow-up work —DNABERT-2— serves as the state-of-the-art genomics foundation model in industry and academia. Their more recent decoder-based genome foundation model — Genome Ocean — features 4 billion parameters and outperforms all the open-sourced competing models in a wide range of genomics tasks. This proposed project will build upon their successful experience and expertise to extend the current 4 billion parameters Genome Ocean model to a 30 billion model with the same architecture on more than 2TB of genomics sequences obtained from real world environmental samples.

requestTitle: Computing-Efficient Training for Large-Scale Vision Transformer Foundation Models
abstract: Vision Transformer (ViT) is a powerful AI architecture for computer vision that is used by most imaging foundation models due to its effectiveness in discerning complex visual patterns across many tasks. However, training large-scale ViT foundation models requires considerable computing resources, leading to a significant energy footprint for training. For example, Open-AI’s SORA video generator model was trained on more than 10,000 NVIDIA H-100 GPUs and the training took more than a month on a supercomputer. The energy consumption for training SORA was equivalent to the total annual energy consumption of 300 US households.  This one-year project aims to improve ViT scaling algorithms computing efficiency, reducing AI development cycle and training time. We will develop a training framework optimized for hardware-conscious scaling and computing efficiency, specifically tailored for large-scale ViT models. The framework will be validated using a pathology cancer imaging segmentation model as a use case.

requestTitle: Trustworthy and Computing-Efficient AI Foundation Model for Earth System Modeling
abstract:
Accurate prediction of Earth system dynamics across various spatiotemporal scales is vital for sustainable socio-ecological systems. Traditional physics-based models, while detailed, are computationally intensive and often struggle to integrate diverse datasets, limiting their predictive accuracy. On the other hand, machine learning models trained on consistent datasets excel in specific tasks but lack the versatility required for broader applications. To address these challenges, we have developed the Oak Ridge Base Foundation Model for Earth System Predictability (ORBIT), an advanced vision-transformer foundation model for climate modeling with up to 113 billion model parameters and incorporates 91 climate variables. ORBIT leverages a novel hybrid tensor-data orthogonal parallelism technique, making it the largest model of its kind—surpassing the size for current climate AI foundation models by a thousandfold. In addition, performance scaling tests on the Frontier supercomputer have shown that ORBIT maintains scaling efficiency between 41% and 85% across 49,152 AMD GPUs, achieving a sustained computing throughput of 1.6 exaFLOPS. However, the model's reliability and predictive power remain largely unexplored across a wide variety of downstream tasks, leaving uncertainties about its performance in diverse climate scenarios. 
This one-year project aims to assess and enhance ORBIT's trustworthiness across diverse downstream fine-tuning tasks. We will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of ORBIT's performance using both standard machine learning metrics and domain-specific climate science criteria. Our assessment will encompass model validation, extreme event prediction, uncertainty quantification, computational efficiency, and physical consistency of predictions.

requestTitle: Next-generation Foundational Model for Biological Sequence Design with Discrete Flow Matching
abstract: In this proposal, we propose to develop a next-generation foundation model for biological sequences based on discrete flow matching to address the limitations of existing language modeling approaches. We propose three main objectives: (1) developing a superior foundational model using discrete flow matching that offers position-independent sampling and highly guidable sequence representations, building upon our successful Statistical Flow Matching (SFM) framework; (2) implementing a hybrid reinforcement learning framework that combines human feedback (RLHF) with automated self-evolution to optimize for crucial biological metrics while maintaining biological constraints; and (3) extending the model's capabilities to handle multimodal conditional generation for diverse applications including drug development, antibody engineering, and biocatalysis. The project will leverage large-scale biological sequence data with evolutionary information from sources such as UniRef, UniProt, SabDab, and Brenda. Our interdisciplinary team brings expertise in generative AI, optimization, and biological molecule design, positioning us to deliver a transformative tool for accelerating therapeutic protein development and advancing precision medicine. The resulting open-source foundation model will significantly impact drug discovery, biosynthesis, and disease treatment while maintaining responsible AI practices.

requestTitle: Accessing OpenAI API by CREDIT Center at Prairie View A&M University
abstract: A multidisciplinary team of researchers and educators from two HBCUs—Prairie View A&M University (PVAMU) and Texas Southern University (TSU)—has partnered with Texas A&M University (TAMU) and NASA collaborators to implement a project titled “DEAP Institute in Research and Education for Science Translation via Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation.” The project’s goal is to build a comprehensive solution that translates non-scientists’ questions into scientific database queries, developing an AI-based system capable of providing interactive, real-time, and user-relevant Earth Science information. This initiative seeks to enhance the discoverability and accessibility of NASA’s scientific data for a wider audience, aligning with the NAIRR Pilot's focus on empowering the public and other stakeholders to utilize scientific data. The core challenge of converting non-scientists' questions into database queries—known as Text-to-SQL—involves transforming natural language into SQL queries. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to innovative approaches to Text-to-SQL, with a particular focus on prompt engineering and fine-tuning. Building on our previous work, the project aims to further improve GPT-based Text-to-SQL systems by conducting extensive validation using large-scale benchmarks, including the BIRD datasets, through the OpenAI API.

requestTitle: Learning Locomotion Through Vegetation
abstract: This proposal aims to reduce the spread of invasive species by deploying a fleet of legged robots to significantly enhance detection and intervention speed, particularly in regions that may prove hazardous for human workers. However, outdoor monitoring tasks like these present an added layer of uncertainty for the robot as these environments are often rough and littered with vegetation and other obstacles. Legged robots are uniquely positioned to thrive in these conditions. Here, we propose to accelerate the learning of an RL-based policy for legged locomotion in vegetation by using a dataset of MPC solutions generated with a specialized leg disentanglement controller from our prior work. We hypothesize that this approach reduces the need to learn from scratch in the absence of accurate simulation, leverages the strength of RL by making the controller more robust compared to a baseline MPC or end-to-end learned policy, and may learn emergent is entanglement behaviors from the provided reference. The result of this project will be an learned controller for legged locomotion in challenging vegetated areas which will enable their use for environmental tasks such as invasive species monitoring.

requestTitle: Effectively Processing Unstructured Data At Scale: With Applications in Building a Statewide Police Record Database
abstract: Analyzing unstructured data has been a persistent challenge in data processing. We are building DocETL, a system that optimizes complex document processing pipelines using Large Language Models (LLMs). DocETL allows users to specify a processing pipeline at a high level, and uses an agent-based framework to automatically optimize them, leveraging novel agent-based rewrites and an optimization and evaluation framework that we introduce. A preliminary version of DocETL has already been used for a range of use-cases, with over a thousand GitHub stars. As part of this proposal, we aim to extend the development of DocETL, and evaluate and deploy it at scale. In particular, we are working with journalists and public defender units to process millions of pages of documents, gathered via public records requests using recent transparency laws, to build the first-ever state-wide public-facing police records database in California.

requestTitle: Leveraging 4D Self-Supervised Deep Learning to Map Mitochondrial Dynamics and Drug Action in Cancer Cells
abstract: This project leverages 4D lattice light-sheet microscopy (LLSM) and self-supervised deep learning to link mitochondrial phenotypes to drug action in cancer cells. Traditional high-content screening approaches are limited to 2D, overlooking critical 3D and temporal dynamics. Our lab has pioneered the use of LLSM for real-time 4D imaging in cancer drug screening, generating a dataset of Cal27 cancer cells under 26 drug conditions. We aim to expand our self-supervised deep learning framework from 2D (x,y) to 4D (x,y,z,t) to derive interpretable latent spaces which reveal how drug action alters mitochondrial dynamics. Achieving this requires high-performance multi-node GPU setups, such as NVIDIA DGX Cloud, to handle the computational and storage demands of our data-intensive contrastive learning models. Successful completion will establish the first latent space mapping 4D drug-induced phenotypic changes, providing a foundational tool for advanced cancer drug discovery.

requestTitle: Qualitative AI Labeling Support (QUAILS): An LLM-Supported Qualitative Thematic Analysis Procedure for Transparency and Safety in Educational Sciences Research
abstract: Qualitative data analysis (QDA) is a widely used family of approaches in the educational sciences that emphasizes identification, labeling, categorization, and interpretation of language meaning from text-based data, such as interviews, documents, surveys, and dialogue. QDA is well known for its high human-resource cost, as it requires people to read and label data over several rounds. This makes large datasets intractable for human analysis due to time and financial costs. The QUAILS study proposes development of a robust LLM-based approach for a type of QDA called thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2012). There is a need for safe, explainable, and transparent AI research if it is to be used for education inference. Therefore, this study also emphasizes transparent documentation of LLM outputs by breaking down LLM steps using emerging chain-of-reasoning and confidence reporting methods, which allows researchers to track and evaluate how models achieve their insights and identify biases. The proposed project will reveal frameworks for design of LLM prompts that mirror qualitative research categorization, labeling, and language analysis tasks for the education sciences. This will increase LLM trustability and safety for educational research and model robust documentation toward better explainability than current AI-based approaches for QDA.

requestTitle: Foundation Models for Long-Context Natural Language Policy Understanding
abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, including language understanding, logical reasoning, and creativity. It is anticipated that in the near future these models will be used alongside human subject matter experts to help analyze the appropriateness of complex policies, determine redundancies and inconsistencies in a web of documentation spread out over an organization, and aid in complex decision making due to superhuman powers of knowledge synthesis. While Transformer is currently the standard architecture for FMs, it does not make the best use of available resources or scale well to the very long context needed for policy analysis. Our Megalodon architecture has been shown to be more resource-efficient to train and more performant on long-context tasks than Transformer, but no public reproducible model has been released. We propose to build public and completely open-access models using our architecture.
resourceName: TACC Vista (NVIDIA GH100 Grace Hopper Superchip)

requestTitle: AudioPuzzle: A Masked Generative Generalist Foundation Model for Audio Intelligence
abstract: We propose to develop a novel generative generalist audio foundation model for unified audio and music processing tasks. Our approach involves developing a unified generative model that integrates multiple audio tasks such as generation, source separation, event detection, music transcription, and captioning. By adopting this unified approach, we aim to improve performance across all audio/music tasks, with particular benefits for low-resource tasks. The resulting foundation model will make advanced audio processing capabilities accessible to researchers, industry practitioners, and the broader scientific community. This project has the potential to advance applications in speech recognition, music technology, environmental sound monitoring, and accessibility services, thereby accelerating advancements in audio AI and its real-world applications.

requestTitle: Request for 250,000 A100 GPU Hours to Develop the NIH-Funded CAMERA Platform for Brain State Prediction and Modulation.
abstract: We seek 250,000 A100 GPU hours over two years on the NSCA Delta GPU to support the NIH-funded Context-Aware Multimodal Ecological Research and Assessment (CAMERA) platform. CAMERA integrates intracranial neural data, physiological signals, and behavioral data with interpretable machine learning to predict human anxiety and memory states. Unique to this project is the collection of intracranial data directly from the amygdala and hippocampus, combined with wearable and environmental sensors, to develop a high-resolution understanding of brain-behavior interactions. GPU resources will enable processing of these complex datasets, training multimodal predictive models, and executing real-time inference for closed-loop neurostimulation, advancing psychiatric neuroscience and translational research.
piInstitution: Columbia University in the City of New York

requestTitle: Advancing Explainable LLM to Bridge the Knowledge-Practice Gap in Healthcare Communication
abstract: This proposal seeks to investigate the extent to which LLMs can: (i) accurately evaluate the quality of healthcare news based on science-informed guidelines, and (ii) effectively communicate actionable feedback to healthcare reporters to enhance the quality of their work.

requestTitle: Enabling Reliable RNA Foundation Models via Biologically-Informed and Efficient Designs
abstract: Despite significant advancements in natural language tasks achieved by language-centric foundation models (FMs), their application to scientific domains of biology presents intricate challenges. These challenges arise due to the complexity and limited availability of biology data. Simply scaling models and datasets is insufficient, as it increases the risk of hallucinated results and reasoning errors in these FMs. A promising approach involves integrating biology-specific knowledge into the designing and learning process to constrain the solution space. Another bottleneck lies in the massive training/inference costs of FMs, which makes them impractical in real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose a biologically informed RNA foundation model that incorporates biological priors into its architecture design. This approach aims to develop more trustworthy and reliable models for scientific applications in biology. Specifically, we suggest enhancing the reliability of RNA FMs by integrating scientific biases and external knowledge graphs, and by developing uncertainty quantification methods to improve trust in RNA FM predictions. Additionally, we focus on enhancing scalability and efficiency across the RNA FM training pipeline by adopting a modular multi-modal architecture and designing systematic methods to eliminate redundancies during training and fine-tuning. Equipped with our developed multi-modal RNA-FM, this proposal plans to conduct validation on a series of single-cell tasks and two novel biology applications of virus detection and de novo design of circular RNA. The successful outcome of this research will result in the dissemination of reliable and efficient RNA foundation models making significant advances in addressing complex scientific biology problems.
piInstitution: University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill
resourceName: TACC Vista (NVIDIA GH100 Grace Hopper Superchip)

requestTitle: SPOT-MH: A Multi-Modal Foundation Model for Detecting Precursors to Failures in Robotic Material Handling
abstract: This proposal develops methods to improve detection of precursors to failures in material handling tasks that use robots for rapid object transportation. The manufacturing industry has been shifting towards high-mix, low-volume production, characterized by a greater variety of goods produced in smaller quantities. This means robots will need to handle a diverse range of materials and tasks, which they can do by relying on sensors to understand the environment. This inevitably introduces noise and uncertainty, and thus increases the risk of failures. To address these challenges, we propose SPOT-MH, a novel multimodal "foundation'' machine learning model for robots in material handling. This model will use data from multiple sensors, such as vision and force. It will first predict the relative motion of an object to the carrier, and then predict whether the current state is a precursor to a failure. We will demonstrate the effectiveness of SPOT-MH on diverse material handling tasks. Implementing SPOT-MH will improve the safety and speed of robotics and automation, and ultimately lead to transformative benefits for material handling.

requestTitle: Building Scalable Multimodal Models for Natural Domain Understanding
abstract: This project aims to advance large-scale multimodal models to seamlessly integrate and analyze images, sounds, and text within natural domains. Although models like CLIP and ALIGN have achieved zero-shot categorization by aligning visual and textual representations, their performance in natural domain tasks is limited due to the insufficient representation of domain-specific data in their training datasets. To address these challenges, we will leverage diverse datasets, including satellite imagery (e.g., Sentinel, Landsat) across the globe spanning decades, millions of geo-tagged images, sound recordings, and observation data from iNaturalist, as well as text from Wikipedia. By employing contrastive learning and scalable architectures, the project seeks to integrate spatial, visual, and auditory information to develop generalizable representations for natural domain tasks, enabling novel applications in ecology, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring.

requestTitle: Functions of Rapidly Evolving Proteins and Their Roles in Pathogenicity
abstract: Rapidly evolving proteins constitute a significant portion of a bacterial proteome. These proteins diverge substantially from their homologs, frequently change functions and locations of active sites, and therefore are more challenging to study. Fast-evolving proteins are nevertheless as crucial as conserved ones for our fundamental understanding of molecular evolution and biomedical applications: pathogenicity factors in bacterial pathogens typically undergo fast evolution due to arms races between hosts and pathogens. Revolutionary advancements in computational protein science now facilitate the efficient investigation of fast- evolving proteins. Advanced artificial intelligence methods such as AlphaFold have produced accurate models of protein 3D structures, which could revolutionize bioinformatics approaches. Now, instead of relying on sequence-based homology searches, which frequently fail to find relatives of fast-evolving proteins, we can use similarity in 3D structures, which tend to be more conserved evolutionarily. Additionally, methods for predicting protein-protein interactions (PPIs) are nearing the accuracy of high-throughput experiments, offering another approach to gain functional insights to a protein by finding a well-studied interaction partner. The time is ideal to capitalize on these developments and tackle challenging problems that were previously impossible to address. In this proposal, I intend to study fast-evolving proteins using state-of-the-art computational methods, followed by experimental validation. First, I have developed methods to recognize domains from AlphaFold models and assign them to an evolutionary context for functional inference. I plan to enhance these methods using deep learning techniques and develop additional methods to predict functional categories. While existing tools are primarily optimized for conserved protein families with deep sequence alignments and extensive experimental data, my methods will cater specifically to fast-evolving proteins. Subsequently, I will apply these tools and my expertise in comparative genomics and PPI modeling to study the fast-evolving and pathogenicity-associated proteins encoded by the pan-genomes of human pathogens. By determining their evolutionary origins, predicting their interacting partners, and inferring their functions, I aim to identify a set of uncharacterized and fast-evolving candidate pathogenicity factors (CPFs). Finally, I will select several promising CPFs and experimentally validate their secretion and interacting partners which are predicted by my computational methods using medium- throughput experiments.

requestTitle: Hydrogem: A Generative AI Framework for Hydrological Data Quality Assurance and Resilience
abstract: The Hydrogem project addresses critical challenges in hydrology by leveraging advanced artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for quality assurance/quality control, anomaly detection, and forecasting of hydrological data. Accurate hydrological data is essential for managing water resources, mitigating flood risks, and understanding climate-driven changes, yet existing datasets often suffer from inconsistencies, gaps, and anomalies. Hydrogem integrates graph neural networks, temporal convolutional networks, and transformers to create a multi-task generative AI model capable of handling diverse hydrological datasets. The dataset, sourced from 3,000 sites across North America, includes over 100–150 GB of time-series data, primarily stage and discharge measurements. By identifying patterns, detecting inconsistencies, predicting future trends, and imputing missing data, Hydrogem enhances the integrity, reliability, and usability of hydrological datasets, supporting better decision-making in water resource management and climate adaptation efforts.

requestTitle: Pre-training Foundation Model for Immunology on ImmPort Open-source Data
abstract: In this project, we aim to pre-train a large-scale foundation model for the immunology field with open-source data from the ImmPort platform. The pre-trained model is expected to significantly improve the embedding performance on cell and bulk levels, which can be used for clustering, classification, etc. The immunology foundation model will be fine-tuned to support a variety of immunology downstream tasks, including oncology, transplantation, infection, etc.

requestTitle: Accessible Plug-and-Play AI: A Medical-informed Foundation Model for Consistent Lung CT Analysis
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have introduced foundation models (FMs) as powerful tools for a wide range of applications. However, general-purpose FMs sometimes fall short to address the unique challenges of medical imaging, such as variabilities in reconstruction kernels, field-of-view (FOV), and spatial alignment, particularly in lung CT analysis. This project aims to develop a medical-informed foundation model (MIFM) that transforms lung CT images into standardized outputs with the desired kernel, FOV, and spatial alignment. Our MIFM is designed for plug-and-play usability, enabling immediate deployment across diverse clinical and research settings. Using high-performance computing resources, we will train the MIFM on medical-specific tasks, including image registration, kernel harmonization, and FOV extension. These tasks are integrated into a unified model that captures domain-agnostic, meaningful data representations, going beyond conventional autoencoding methods. The success of this project will democratize access to advanced AI tools, allowing institutions with limited resources to process and analyze large-scale datasets.

requestTitle: Multi-agent Code LLMs for Parallel Software Development
abstract: The Parallel Software and Systems Group (PSSG) at the University of Maryland is currently pursuing several research projects aimed at advancing AI research in the context of parallel and high performance computing.  We have three primary scientific goals. Our first research goal is to evaluate and improve the use of Code Large Language Models (Code LLMs) for parallel and high-performance code synthesis. The second research goal is to investigate the use of LLMs for automating portable software development and performance optimization.  The third goal is to improve the hardware performance of model inference, which is important for the first two goals.  We intend to increase throughput (token/s), decrease latency, and reduce memory utilization, while maintaining accuracy on downstream tasks.

requestTitle: DCL 24-093 NAIRR Demonstration Project: Multimodal AI Socratic Instructor for Smartphone (MAISIS)
abstract: The proposed AI system called MAISIS (Multimodal AI Socratic Instructor for Smartphone) will use verbal, affective, and embodied motion inputs as well as information on the student’s self-generated attempts to correctly match motion graphs from the motion app to prompt and guide thinking and learning in a way that foregrounds the construction of a causal conceptual model of motion. The AI will create a multi-dimensional cognitive model of where the learner is in understanding kinematics. This AI model will give nuanced feedback that will predict, explain, and respond to the progressively more complex challenges that the app presents based on how the user is performing in real-time. The need for this AI model has emerged from our studies on the app use with middle school and high school students over the past two years.

requestTitle: NAIRR Request to Support NSF-2321851: Collaborative Research: CISE: Large: Executing Natural Instructions in Realistic Uncertain Worlds
abstract: This request asks for resources to support our NSF-2321851 CISE Large project which will design and develop a novel integrated framework for embodied AI agents that is comprised of synergistic advances in computer vision, language understanding, world modeling, planning, and control. The research will study new ideas in 3D vision and language understanding , as well as approaches to low-level full-body control for robot skills, inspired by recent successes in language modeling, that facilitates both modular skill learning and knowledge sharing.

requestTitle: Evaluating Privacy and Surveillance Risks of Large Language Models
abstract: This proposal seeks to evaluate and mitigate the privacy and surveillance risks posed by Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision Language Models (VLMs), and AI agents. With the increasing integration of these technologies into critical infrastructures and applications, concerns about user profiling, targeted advertising, and real-time surveillance are mounting. The research will explore three core areas: (1) LLM-driven Surveillance Capitalism, where chatbots use AI to personalize ads and profile users without their awareness; (2) AI Shoulder Surveillance, where smart glasses and VLMs enable automated shoulder surfing attacks that capture sensitive data from smartphone screens; and (3) Real-Time VLM Surveillance, where VLMs embodied in camera sensing platforms can be used to surveil people and device users' behaviors in the wild. By developing privacy evaluation frameworks and open-source datasets, this research aims to push the boundaries of AI safety and privacy, encouraging the creation of anti-surveillance measures in future AI systems, and providing end users with tools to educate themselves on such privacy risks.

requestTitle: Developing a Foundation Model for the Tree of Life  with over 200 Million Images to Accelerate Biology and Ecology Research
abstract: The HDR Imageomics Institute is at the forefront of defining the emerging field of imageomics: the science of connecting images to biological traits. One of the Institute’s major projects is developing the BioCLIP model, which is being used for a wide range of biology and ecology tasks such as biodiversity monitoring, rare species identification, and species delineation. The first iteration trained a vision transformer using 10M images spanning the tree of life aligned with autoregressive text labels of taxonomic hierarchies. The next phase in this project’s development aims to significantly expand the model's capabilities by enhancing our multimodal data and model training approach in several key ways. For the data, we are scaling up the quantity by more than 20x to over 200M images sourced from independent aggregators and primary data providers. For model development, we will test additional model architectures within the ViT framework, compare multiple objectives including CLIP and SigLIP, and scan across multiple image resolutions and hyperparameter settings. Our scientific goal of this proposal is to revolutionize the way diverse biological data is interpreted by scaling BioCLIP to an unprecedented magnitude of biological data and biodiversity coverage. This will achieve the most capable open-source foundation model for organismal biology, which will serve as a basis for scientific discovery in order to address ecological and biodiversity aspects of earth, environmental, and climate challenges.

requestTitle: Datasets and Generative Models for Photorealistic Inverse Rendering
abstract: Indoor scenes involve visible and invisible light sources interacting with spatially-varying material and shapes through a complex light transport. Inverse rendering seeks to recover shape, spatially-varying material and lighting from a single or few images, which is a severely ill-posed problem. We propose to develop novel diffusion models for inverse rendering in indoor scenes, with a particular focus on lighting estimation. This will be achieved through (a) the creation of a large-scale synthetic training dataset and (b) fine-tuning of image-to-image diffusion models to yield spatially-varying lighting in the form of light probes. This will enable novel applications in augmented reality, image editing, interior design and robotics, through the ability to insert virtual objects or edit scene properties with a high degree of photorealism.

requestTitle: Feasibility Study of Generative AI in Construction Safety
abstract: The goal of this project is to explore the feasibility of generative artificial intelligence (i.e. ChatGPT-based conversational AI) in construction safety research. This project will develop a web-based platform that can answer questions from construction stakeholders (e.g., workers, project managers, and engineers) based on safety regulations. Firstly, the project team will input the construction safety regulation (Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)) into a structured database. Then, a ChatGPT-based web application will be developed to allow users to query the OSHA handbook. The project team will test the developed platform in various construction safety scenarios including (struck-by, electrocution, work-from-height, and catch in/between) to validate the feasibility of generative AI in safety. This project will improve the construction workplace safety.

requestTitle: Uncovering Brain Biotypes and Clinical Outcomes with a Neuroimage Foundation Model
abstract: This project will develop and open-source a NeuroImage Foundation Model for the analysis of neuroimaging data, leveraging large-scale public datasets and complementary data from Vanderbilt University Medical Center. By employing a vision transformer-based architecture and self-supervised training techniques, the NIFM will learn high-dimensional, transferable representations that can flexibly handle diverse neuroimage modalities. The resulting framework will reduce data and computational burdens in subsequent analyses, thereby accelerating the development of imaging-based biotypes and advancing AI-driven neuroimaging research. Aligned with the goals of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), this effort will directly support ongoing National Institutes of Health (NIH)-funded projects, including the development of late-life depression risk stratification tools (R01MH12160) and the optimization of existing neuroimage processing pipelines (R01EB017230).

requestTitle: Domain-Informed Foundation Models for Reliable and Interpretable Event Analysis
abstract:
Understanding how events materialize, unfold, and evolve is crucial for various domains, including healthcare, finance, and social sciences. With the availability of large-scale publicly accessible data from sources like social media and news, machine learning models have been developed to analyze, infer, and predict events. However, large-scale models such as deep neural networks often lack interpretability, making it difficult to understand and trust their predictions. Most state-of-the-art works for interpretable ML focus on static analysis in object detection or language models. 

This project aims to develop interpretable methods for dynamic environments, with applications of predicting events of varying scopes using heterogeneous and multi-source features. By leveraging hierarchical, relational, and complex evidence, we seek to enhance the models’ ability to understand time and changes, leading to robust and improved prediction accuracy. Additionally, we will explore several types of explanations, including causal factors and circuit analysis, to provide deeper insights into the models' decision-making processes.

requestTitle: State-Of-The-Art Multimodal Foundation Large Language Models evaluation
abstract: The foundational large language models have remarkable capabilities that can be beneficial in building precision monitoring applications provided their knowledge base is sufficiently large and diverse. It is not clear, however, to what extent these models will be able to recognize the species that are rarer or not commonly observed in nature. Put differently, one challenge of working with large language models or large vision language models is the knowledge of what type of objects/scenes or the level of granularity may be out of scope. This project seeks to evaluate the large language foundation models such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet or Claude Opuse (Anthropic) https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-5-sonnet,  GPT-4o (OpenAI), and Gemini 1.5 Flash or 1.5 Pro (Google) with respect to their capability to accurately describe the images that feature different plants and animals in their naturally occurring environments. More particularly, we would like to use the image captions that the models produce to parse the category of the object (plant or animal) in the picture as well as scene attributes such as, whether the image was taken during night or day, whether the image depicts indoor or outdoor environment, weather conditions in the image, are the objects in the image appearing in a group or individually and whether they are wild or domestic species. These attributes can be helpful with deductive reasoning about images.

requestTitle: A New Course on High Performance for Machine Learning at an HSI
abstract:
This graduate-level topics course in 'High-Performance Computing for Machine Learning' integrates in-depth study of literature on foundational and cutting-edge parallel and distributed deep learning research with hands-on experimentations. Through collaborative, team-based projects, students will address real-world scaling challenges such as optimizing training throughput, memory efficiency, and communication overhead for billion-parameter models utilizing systematic performance analysis and iterative optimization strategies.  

Weekly paper discussions will delve into breakthrough techniques in model parallelism and distributed training. The students will master the theoretical advances, understand the research landscape and outstanding open research challenges, ML training optimization workflows, encompassing performance profiling, bottleneck identification, and systematic debugging, while using industry-standard tools: PyTorch, TensorFlow, Dask for model development, CUDA for GPU acceleration, SLURM for resource management, and MPI/Horovod for efficient communication and scaling. Through hands-on experience with large-scale AI workloads, students will learn to navigate challenges in infrastructure management, deployment, and system optimization.  

Assessment will focus on understanding of research literature, presentations and discussions, and a final project presentation. This course fosters an environment where theoretical advancements are systematically translated into practical solutions, equipping students for exploring further research and technical leadership roles in AI infrastructure optimization and preparing them for diverse career paths in the rapidly evolving field of high-performance machine learning.

requestTitle: Trustworthy Embodied 3D Vision-Language Question Answering with Situational Encoding
abstract: Achieving the integration of multi-modal information and logical reasoning represents a significant milestone in developing conversational and human-centered embodied AI. Although recent research has demonstrated considerable progress in linguistic understanding and image comprehension using natural language commands or dialogues, the ability to perceive and reason in real-world 3D embodied environments still falls short of human expectations, due to limitations in 3D reasoning capabilities and interpretability. This project aims to explore 3D embodied scene comprehension, wherein an agent is required to understand its situation and surroundings within a dynamic, egocentric environment and subsequently perceive, reason, answer, and act accordingly to complete complex tasks.

requestTitle: Addressing HPC I/O Issues with Enhanced, Trustworthy Large Language Models
abstract: This project aims to design enhanced and trustworthy large language models (LLMs) to tackle complex I/O performance issues in high-performance computing (HPC) systems. These I/O issues may stem from problematic programming practices or inefficient interactions with various distributed HPC I/O stacks. The core idea is to leverage LLMs to analyze I/O logs generated by applications, providing interactive guidance to help users identify and ultimately resolve I/O performance issues in their scientific applications.

requestTitle: Frameworks and Platform using Large Languauge Models to Predict Epileptogenic Zone Based on the Descriptions of Seizure Semiology
abstract: Seizure semiology, which focuses on the systematic study of signs and clinical manifestations observed during seizure episodes, plays a pivotal role in understanding and localizing the epileptogenic zone (EZ)—the specific brain area responsible for initiating seizures.   With recent advancements in large language models (LLMs), there is a promising opportunity to enhance the accuracy of EZ localization by leveraging LLMs to interpret complex seizure descriptions. The descriptive nature of seizure semiology aligns well with LLMs' capabilities in processing and understanding nuanced language.  By training LLMs to map seizure semiology descriptions directly to specific brain regions associated with EZs, we can potentially improve the speed and precision of localization in clinical settings. To achieve this,   Fine-tuning the LLMs using masked data and other specialized training methods can further enhance their ability to interpret seizure semiology and yield better localization results. Our prelimenary result and platform (aiepilepsy.stevens.edu) showed the great value of LLMs to accurately predict EZs.

requestTitle: A Foundation Model for Hematopathology: Advancing Diagnostics for Blood Disorders
abstract: Hematological malignancies present unique diagnostic challenges due to their morphological complexity and heterogeneity which contributes to diagnostic variability among pathologists.  This project aims to develop a generalist hematopathology foundation model trained on high-volume digital slide images which can automate a diverse set of diagnostic assessments. We anticipate this model will enhance diagnostic accuracy, support laboratory hematopathologists, and improve patient outcomes by providing reliable analyses.

requestTitle: Unified Multimodal Discrete Diffusion
abstract: The ultimate aspiration of artificial intelligence (AI) is to create machines capable of reasoning and acting through diverse, multimodal experiences, much like humans do. Current Natively Multimodal models are dominated by autoregressive models, which model tokens in a left to right order. These models process image, text, video, audio jointly for doing a variety of tasks such as image captioning, question answering, image generation etc.  Although autoregressive models have dominated in the text domain, they have been found to be suboptimal for images, video and audio.  With the recent success of discrete diffusion in text generation, we believe it to be the right candidate for the next generation of unified generative models. Discrete diffusion models offer several advantages over autoregressive models, including better control over quality versus diversity of samples, simultaneous inpainting in multiple spaces (e.g., image and text), ease of alignment and guidance with multiple objectives, and flexibility in generation order. With these benefits in mind, we aim to develop the first Universal Non-Autoregressive (diffusion) model capable of jointly processing text, image, video, and audio to perform various downstream tasks.

abstract: The ultimate aspiration of artificial intelligence (AI) is to create machines capable of reasoning and acting through diverse, multimodal experiences, much like humans do. These models process image, text, video, audio jointly for doing a variety of tasks such as image captioning, question answering, image generation etc.  Although autoregressive models have dominated in the text domain, they have been found to be suboptimal for images, video and audio.  With the recent success of discrete diffusion in text generation, we believe it to be the right candidate for the next generation of unified generative models. Discrete diffusion models offer several advantages over autoregressive models, including better control over quality versus diversity of samples, simultaneous inpainting in multiple spaces (e.g., image and text), ease of alignment and guidance with multiple objectives, and flexibility in generation order. With these benefits in mind, we aim to develop the first Universal Non-Autoregressive (diffusion) model capable of jointly processing text, image, video, and audio to perform various downstream tasks.

requestTitle: Building Trustworthy Language Models: Benchmark, Metrics, and Training Method
abstract: Preventing misinformation is a key goal in safety training for language models (LMs). However, current techniques primarily concentrate on refusal training, which may miss opportunities to provide helpful responses without compromising safety. To address these limitations, we first construct a benchmark to quantify LMs' resilience against creating misinformation or disinformation while remaining helpful. Moreover, current training mechanisms conflate harmlessness and helpfulness into one reward, leaving safety unguaranteed. We propose a multi-objective reinforcement learning approach that uses lexicographic ordering to prioritize safety, followed by truthfulness and helpfulness. This ensures LMs to be resilient against false information without compromising their usefulness.

requestTitle: Development of Large Language Models for Pediatric Type 1 Diabetes Management
abstract: This proposal seeks computational resources to support the Health Informatics Practicum II course at Nova Southeastern University’s Dr. Kiran C. Patel College of Osteopathic Medicine (NSU-KPCOM). The course provides students with hands-on experience in applying advanced AI techniques to solve real-world health informatics challenges. Students will collaborate with Nicklaus Children’s Hospital and the NSU-KPCOM medical school on a project focused on fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for pediatric type 1 diabetes management. This initiative addresses a critical healthcare challenge: while many consultations are basic and repetitive, they are time-consuming and constitute the majority of provider requests, leaving less time for complex cases. To develop a support tool for physicians in clinical consultation, the fine-tuning process will rely on curated datasets from PubMed, clinical guidelines, and de-identified consultation data, offering students the opportunity to work with diverse and domain-specific data. The project aims at develop a multilingual LLM, capable of generating responses in English and Spanish,  so to satisfy the needs of South Florida's diverse population. Computational resources will be used during class time and for independent project work, allowing students to gain technical proficiency in deploying and evaluating AI systems. This application supports the development of future health informatics professionals while contributing to innovative applications of AI in healthcare.

requestTitle: EAGER: NAIRR Pilot Expansion: FA1 Generative AI and Black digital archives
abstract:
With this work, we will connect AI and computing scholars with scholars who work in the study of Black digital archives and culture for mutual training, co-creation of new AI-based digital artifacts, and re-imagining of how AI systems can and should be created to interact with Black cultural and archival practices. NAIRR resources will be used for research training workshops for co-creation with Black and archival study scholars, as well as initial research related to and development of artifacts for that workshop. We will explore the implications of current dominant uses of AI (particularly generative) systems for Black digital archives and will develop new designs and early prototypes of possible systems based on the needs of those working in Black digital archives. Training on and using tools provided by NAIRR will be key for the mutual learning and co-design needed for this project.
As researchers work together to create contextualized and relevant AI systems using resources provided by NAIRR, a particular emphasis will be placed on using a multi-level framework for ethical engineering of AI systems that is currently being developing as a part of current NSF CAREER award. We will study impacts across individual, organizational, and social levels as we engineer AI systems so that we can better understand Black digital archives, to understand how we can extend and augment current archives and ways of knowing amongst relevant communities, and to understand what generative AI systems mean for the future of Black digital archives. Our work will integrate several disciplinary perspectives, especially those from AI, computational cognitive science, sociology, and Black studies to study these impacts across levels of behavior and analysis.

requestTitle: Assessing the Sensitivity of Prompt Framing for Political Information
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) organizations and government institutions aim to build trust among users in efforts to scale AI technology for public good. Yet, research in the realms of political science and social psychology suggests trust is multidimensional and subjective, making it challenging to determine what is a good and for whom. Prior work on political information and motivated reasoning further indicates people tend to self-select into online information environments; however, research has yet to fully explore how users' experiences with AI technology can differ depending on how they seek out information. In this proposed work, we posit that people's trust in AI technology may be conditional on their own experiences with (and/or the judgments of trusted political elites about) these tools and aim to examine whether and the extent to which outputs produced by AI technology are sensitive to the framing of prompts about political information. Using prompts culled from existing literature on partisan framing effects, the use of search engines for political information, nationally-representative survey data, and salient political topics around the November 2024 general election, we will assess whether and in which political information domains existing models are sensitive to prompt framing. We will also examine whether there are differences in prompt sensitivity across models with various capabilities, in models subject to fine-tuning, and across a variety of political information areas consistent with NAIRR objectives, e.g., energy, the environment, technology, health and safety outcomes, and education. Whether or not users receive substantively different information based on a prompt framed in certain partisan/ideological terminology, the capability of a specific model, and the moderation and/or timing of a prompt all have important implications for trust among users and developers, as well as how these tools might be used for political aim. In exploring the real-world applications of AI technology, this work can further help to inform users, developers, and policy makers of the capabilities and limitations of these tools. In doing so, this proposed work can help to inform strategies for mitigating deficits in trust, enhancing use of AI technology, and improving democratic health.

requestTitle: Towards Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success due to their exceptional generative capabilities. Despite their success, they also have inherent limitations such as a lack of up-to-date knowledge and hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a state-of-the-art technique to mitigate these limitations. The key idea of RAG is to ground the answer generation of an LLM on external knowledge retrieved from a knowledge database. Existing studies mainly focus on improving the accuracy or efficiency of RAG, leaving its security largely unexplored. In this project, we aim to perform a systematic study on the security vulnerabilities of RAG systems and develop robust RAG systems against attacks.

requestTitle: Evaluating and Mitigating Biases in LLM through Causal Reasoning
abstract: The proposed project seeks to enhance the fairness of large language models (LLMs) through advanced causal reasoning methodologies. While LLMs have achieved significant advancements in recent years, their responsible deployment and usage are often a public concern due to inherent biases. This research aims to assess and mitigate these shortcomings by evaluating biases of existing LLMs and developing effective strategies to mitigate biases. Specifically, we will employ causal prompt engineering, data-efficient fine-tuning, and ad-hoc model modifications to elevate fairness metrics and facilitate more responsible model behaviors.

requestTitle: Scientific Foundational Model Development for Supporting Trustworthy Scholarly Writing
abstract: Scholarly writing is a complex cognitive task requiring continuous decision-making, extensive working memory, and multitasking. Developing effective scholarly writing assistants is challenging due to the issue of non-factual responses from large language models (LLMs) and isolated assistance at different stages of writing. Our project aims to develop scientific foundational models that provide reliable, multimodal support for the entire writing process, including text, images, code, social media discussions, and peer reviews. We will enhance trust by marking original reference sources in generated content and linking references across modalities. Upon completion, we will release two open-source models: a pretrained LLM identifying reference sources in outputs, and a fine-tuned VLM for vision-language tasks. All data, model weights, and training details will be openly shared to promote scientific transparency. These models are expected to enhance scientific discovery and contribute to the development of reliable, safe AI across various fields.

The models and data will also be used by the PI to teach a STEM course (Computational Methods in Water Resources) at Clemson University.

requestTitle: Multi-Directional Conditional Generative Models as Efficient Surrogates for Large-Scale Spatiotemporal Simulations
abstract:
Large-scale spatiotemporal simulation systems are important for real-world decision-making and policy applications, such as alleviating traffic congestion and vehicle pollution, optimizing supply chain logistics, controlling disease spread, and shaping international trade policies. These simulations allow stakeholders to evaluate the outcomes of various decisions or policy options, ultimately helping to identify optimal solutions. However, two significant challenges arise when using such systems: (1) calibrating the simulation models from sparse, noisy real-world data, and (2) both calibration and optimal decision identification require running repeated, computationally expensive forward simulations.

This project aims to tackle these challenges by developing innovative multi-directional conditional generative models that serve as efficient, powerful surrogates for both forward simulation and inverse inference (calibration). These models will significantly reduce computational costs, while enabling accurate predictions and robust uncertainty quantification across various contexts.

The research will focus on three key tasks: (1) designing a multi-functional  generative modeling framework that captures the spatiotemporal functions relevant to the simulation, (2) designing an novel denoising training method that allows flexible, multi-directional conditioned sampling for both forward and inverse prediction, and (3) developing an efficient training and sampling algorithm that accelerates sample generation and supports uncertainty quantification.
