requestTitle: Toward Large Scale Graph Foundation Models
abstract: The rapid growth of graph-structured data in various fields, from social networks to biological systems, demands the development of scalable and versatile Graph Foundation Models (GFMs). This project aims to create large-scale GFMs that can efficiently handle diverse graph-based tasks, such as node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. By focusing on the design and integration of a robust graph vocabulary, we will enhance the generalizability of these models across different domains. Our approach leverages cutting-edge machine learning frameworks and distributed training techniques to ensure that the GFMs are both powerful and adaptable.

requestTitle: Developing Engaging AI Chatbots to Enhance Senior Well-being
abstract: This research aims to enhance the mental well-being of the elderly by developing a Large Language Model (LLM)-empowered AI chatbot designed to engage seniors in meaningful, multi-turn dialogues. The proposed system will not only support cognitive functions but also aid in detecting early signs of Mild Cognitive Impairment and dementia. However, challenges such as quantifying conversational engagement, overcoming the opacity of proprietary LLMs, and addressing data heterogeneity and privacy must be addressed. To tackle these, we propose three research thrusts: formulating objectives for long-term engagement, model-agnostic adaptation of black-box LLMs, and developing personalized, decentralized AI chatbots.

requestTitle: Allocation for NDIF Pilot on Delta and Delta AI
abstract:
This NAIRR pilot proposal is a request for the necessary computational resources to conduct a 90-day pilot test of the National Deep Inference Fabric (NDIF) with a non-time-limited (90-day) job on the GPU nodes needed to develop and test the NDIF inference service on benchmark and real-world research traffic on an open-parameter 405b parameter LLM model.

The National Deep Inference Fabric (https://ndif.us) is a research-oriented inference service that is being designed to keep large neural network models preloaded and available to be efficiently shared for scientific inference experiments that inspect or alter the internals of those models.  Its novel architecture is designed to provide a unique combination of transparency and efficiency, to enable researchers to study the internals of important large-scale research targets such as trillion-parameter LLMs that would be infeasible without NDIF, reducing costs by efficiently sharing resources between researchers.

We emphasize that although science will be performed during the test, the purpose of this allocation is engineering: our primary goal is to gather the experience needed as part of our work to develop and test a new type of infrastructure for efficiently allocating GPU resources to AI research.  The 90-day test period is designed to pave the way for an architecture that provides very efficient access to a much larger set of scientific studies by eliminating set-up time overhead and sharing the underlying models.

requestTitle: A Dialogue-Based Protein Language Model
abstract: Protein and chemical synthesis are pivotal in biotechnological and biomedical innovation. Despite significant advancements, the field faces challenges in predicting and generating novel proteins and chemicals due to their inherent complexities. This project aims to improve protein and molecule design by developing a dialogue-based model built on the pre-trained LLaMA-3 model. The goal is to generate high-quality de novo proteins and chemicals, enhancing drug discovery, enzyme engineering, and synthetic biology. The model will offer precise control over conditions by integrating human-like conversational instructions, including 3D structures and functional properties. We will collect and preprocess a large dataset, including protein sequences, 3D structures, and chemical SMILES representations for model training. The LLaMA-3 model will be pre-trained on this dataset, followed by instruction tuning to refine its performance. Evaluation metrics such as accuracy, sequence diversity, and structural quality will ensure the model's reliability.

requestTitle: Towards Efficient Fine-tuning of Large Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), such as OpenAI ChatGPT and Google Gemini, have revolutionized Natural Language Processing and empowered many real-world applications. Efficient hyperparameter optimization is one of the most critical challenges in fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs), which significantly impacts model performance and resource consumption. Existing practices either demand extensive computational resources or fall short of finding optimal settings, thus hindering the development of more accurate and efficient LLMs. This project aims to investigate Efficient Fine-tuning techniques for LLMs (EFT-LLM) to facilitate the adoption of Large Language Models for domain-specific applications. The long-term goal of this project is to broaden access to large foundation models, enabling more researchers, developers, and organizations to develop LLM-powered real-world applications through efficient LLM fine-tuning techniques across various sections, such as healthcare, finance, and education. This one-year project will develop a framework prototype, EFT-LLM, with core hyperparameter optimization capabilities to facilitate efficient LLM fine-tuning. Concretely, we will investigate the following two fundamental research questions: (1) how to leverage past hyperparameter optimization experiences to develop an open-source foundation model for hyperparameter optimizations, and (2) how to automate the hyperparameter optimization process for LLM fine-tuning. The research findings of this project will also improve the content of various courses at FIU in the areas of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems.

requestTitle: Differentially Private LLMs via Distillation
abstract: Differentially private SGD (DPSGD) enables training large language models (LLMs) on private data with a worst-case guarantee on data leakage, but this guarantee comes at the cost of model utility due to added noise. We propose a novel approach that leverages DPSGD and knowledge distillation together to produce differentially private LLMs that have higher utility and produce more fluent, consistent tests. Our preliminary results show our method improves output quality and reduces hallucinations. We request $25,000 in OpenAI API credit to enable a complete evaluation of our novel approach.

requestTitle: Retrieval Augmented Conformal Inference for Reliable Prediction with Foundation Models
abstract: Foundation models are extensively trained via self-supervised learning on vast datasets, which equips them with the ability to adapt to a wide range of applications in a "zero-shot" fashion. Their notable success has transformed public perception and utilization of AI systems, making them integral to user-facing applications in various domains, including critical sectors such as medicine. The adaptability of foundation models enables their application to novel user-specified downstream tasks, but the opacity of their training data and limited access to internal parameters can undermine trust in their predictions in these tasks. To ensure responsible use of foundation models, it is necessary to scrutinize their predictions by quantifying and communicating uncertainty with the end users. The goal of this project is to develop a “universal” method for estimating uncertainty in predictions generated by foundation models in zero-shot (user-defined) tasks. Specifically, we will develop a novel approach for quantifying uncertainty in the zero-shot predictions of foundational vision-language models that can seamlessly adapt to new tasks without requiring access to the model's training data or internal parameters. Our proposed approach involves augmenting foundation models with calibration data retrieved from external knowledge bases relevant to the user-specified task at hand (e.g. the open web), and employing conformal prediction techniques to calibrate the model's predictions using the retrieved data. As part of this project, we will develop an open-source web-based “wrapper” tool that enables on-the-fly calibration of any foundation model in user-specified downstream tasks.

requestTitle: Domain-Specific Generative Models of Human Hand Skills
abstract:
Generative image models have seen significant advances in the last several years, and recent advancements in diffusion models have enabled synthesis of images that are nearly indistinguishable from reality. However, the capabilities of generative image models come with some disadvantages.
In particular, they seem to inexplicably fail for certain common articulating object categories. For example, users of popular generative image models have reported that these models struggle to generate human hands, an important category given the applications in robotics, mixed reality and art.
Similar problems have also been observed with generative video diffusion models for human body motion and interaction. The goal of this proposal is to build domain-specific generative image and video models to faithfully reconstruct articulating human hand interactions and skills.

requestTitle: Pilot NAIRR Project: Multimodal Generative Model for Synthesizing High-Quality Small Molecules with Desired Properties of Few Real Examples
abstract: This project aims to develop a novel multimodal generative model for synthesizing high-quality small molecules with desired properties from few real examples. By leveraging large language models, graph neural networks, and vision transformers, the proposed model will learn from limited data and integrate information from molecular graphs, images, and text descriptions. Through self-supervised pre-training and fine-tuning using prompt-based learning, the model will capture relationships between different modalities and generate diverse, valid molecules that exhibit target characteristics. This approach has the potential to revolutionize drug discovery and molecular design by efficiently navigating the vast chemical space and accelerating the identification of promising candidates.

requestTitle: Machine Learning for CS Undergraduates
abstract: In primarily undergraduate institutions with limited computing resources, gaining access to AI-capable resources is challenging, and it is even more difficult to develop contemporary course materials. I propose to expand a machine learning course to scale up to larger computational resources, using Jetstream2 as an educational platform that provides access to GPUs, Jupyter notebooks, and components for student submissions, feedback, and evaluation. This approach will enable students to learn about current AI developments, including machine learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and large language models (LLMs).

requestTitle: A Foundation Model for the EMIT Instrument
abstract: Towards accelerating technical innovation and scientific discovery it has been of great interest in the machine learning for Earth Observation (EO) literature to develop so-called “foundation” models. Foundation models produce a representation that enables future models which utilize this representation rather than the to achieve superior performance with less human data annotation compared to models trained from scratch. Foundation models are trained in a self-supervised or unsupervised manner that requires no human effort outside of the algorithmic design and validation, but require a large corpus of unlabeled data to be effective. EO instruments generate massive amounts of data that are prohibitively expensive to manually label by humans. The EO setting thus presents a strong value proposition for self-supervised learning and the construction of foundation models. The large quantity of unlabeled data available from EO instruments is an ideal setting for self-supervised learning, and foundation models can serve as the engine that powers few-shot learning. The goal of our project is to build a foundational model for shortwave infrared radiances measured by the EMIT instrument. Primary tasks of interest for EO are segmentation and detection tasks in which regions of the input are identified as containing an object or property of interest. We will build the foundation model by pre-training on a dataset of publicly available EMIT radiance data (L1B). To validate the effectiveness of the foundation model measure the performance of a model trained on the representation yielded by our foundation model for the task of methane source detection.

requestTitle: Pre-training a Large Tabular Model
abstract: The rapid advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have showcased their immense potential across various domains, yet their capabilities in processing structured tabular data remain underexplored. This proposal aims to address this gap by pre-training a foundational model designed specifically for both tabular and text modalities. Leveraging extensive pre-training and a robust neural network structure, this model aims to enhance performance in critical tasks such as table classification, regression, synthetic data generation, and data imputation across fields like finance, healthcare, and marketing. Our research will utilize a public dataset, Tablib, consisting of 627 million tables, and involve significant computational resources, including high-performance GPUs and substantial storage capacity. Through this effort, we aim to create an open-source resource that can significantly enhance the automation and efficiency of tabular data tasks, driving innovation and productivity in data-intensive domains.

requestTitle: Accelerating Few-Step High-Quality Generation in Diffusion Models: A Novel Adaptive Approach for Efficient AI-Driven Content Creation
abstract: This project aims to enhance the efficiency of diffusion models in generating high-quality image and video content from text inputs. By developing adaptive few-step generation techniques, we seek to significantly reduce the computational steps required while maintaining or improving the diversity and quality of the generated content. This initiative will leverage advanced GPU resources to accelerate research and contribute novel methodologies to the field of generative AI.

requestTitle: Certifiable Attribution and Secure Training of Generative AI Models
abstract:
This NAIRR proposal supports the compute needs for the PIs' continuing effort from NSF#2101052 in developing certifiable attribution and secure training methods for generative AI (GenAI) models. This project responses to the focus area of “Accelerating societally-relevant research on AI safety, reliability, security, and privacy”. 

For certifiable attribution, we seek watermarking methods that enable a public attribution service that correctly and robustly distinguishes between GenAI and natural contents, and attributes GenAI contents to their user-specific models. Attribution facilitates GenAI content regulation. 

For secure training, we seek training protocols that balances training cost and training data privacy in collaborative training sessions where semi-honest servers may participate. Secure training facilitates privacy-guaranteed collaboration among data providers.

Our 12-month study will be a continuation from the currently supported efforts, leveraging the existing team and developments. Our prior contributions have been disseminated through top AI and cybersecurity venues, yet we face a bottleneck in compute while scaling up our efforts to real-world datasets, models, and application settings. Therefore, we request a total of 160k GPU (>A100) hours and prefer parallel GPU access to accelerate computational experimentation.

requestTitle: Advancing AI for Understanding Implicit Language in the Courtroom
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have great potential to transform workflows in contexts where social knowledge of language use is critical. But such domains also contain difficult uses of implicit and indirect language that current methods are not equipped to handle.  This project aims to apply LLMs to detecting implicit language, focusing on the  challenging social context of courtroom language, an area marked by extensive use of implicit and subtle linguistic cues. The courtroom is a domain with huge potential impact, as LLMs can assist with unsupervised discovery and annotation tasks and help discover bias in the legal system. And the algorithms we develop can also play a role in helping interpret implicit language at scale in many other domains, and help us understand better how LLMs generate and interpret covert meanings.

requestTitle: Enhancing Understanding of Diabetes-Related Kidney and Pancreas Conditions through Genomic and Imaging Analysis
abstract: Diabetes is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and chronic pancreatitis (CP), both of which progressively impair organ function. Despite ongoing research, effective biomarkers for predicting these diseases remain elusive. Advanced techniques such as spatial transcriptomics (ST), proteomics (SP), and Hematoxylin-and-Eosin (H&E) stained whole-slide imaging (WSI) are being used to elucidate the microenvironments that contribute to disease progression. These methods have refined cell type segmentation and identification, improving diagnostic processes significantly. A key aspect of this project involves the integration of genomic and histopathological data using machine learning (ML) to enhance diagnostic accuracy. Techniques like Vision Transformers and unsupervised ML are employed to analyze and integrate data from comprehensive repositories like the Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) and the Human Pancreas Analysis Program (HPAP). This integration aims to develop novel diagnostic and treatment strategies, thereby advancing nephrology and introducing innovative therapeutic options for managing diabetes-related kidney and pancreas diseases.

requestTitle: Extending the Computational Reach of Noisy Quantum Computers through AI-assisted Noise Mitigation and Modeling
abstract: Quantum computation has surpassed classical computation in certain applications like cryptography and physics/chemistry simulations. However, practical quantum advantage is hindered by the noisy nature of near-term quantum devices. Quantum error correction (QEC) is impractical due to high qubit demands and technical challenges. This proposal focuses on quantum error mitigation using AI-assisted approaches to model and mitigate noise in quantum computers. Current research relies on analytical methods that are limited in scope, while AI-based approaches can address complex noise factors. The proposal aims to develop advanced machine learning models and create comprehensive datasets for error mitigation, benefiting the research community.

requestTitle: Geometry Effects on Iterative Learning for Multiscale Modeling of History-Dependent Metamaterials
abstract: A key question in advancing AI methods that enable scientific discovery is to understand what kind of data is necessary to obtain an accurate surrogate. We explore this question for history-dependent elastic-plastic behavior of architected metamaterials. We introduce an iterative approach where we use a rich arbitrary class of trajectories to train an initial model. We then iteratively update the class of trajectories with those that arise in large-scale simulation and use transfer learning to update the model. We investigate the convergence and transferability of the learned surrogate models. Furthermore, we propose to study fundamental issues in advancing AI methods that enable scientific discovery by specifically investigating fundamental questions that arise in the multiscale modeling of history-dependent metamaterials with an iterative learning approach: (i) Explore the effect of sample geometry at large scale on the convergence of the iterative learning approach; (ii) Study sampling strategies with consideration of geometry; and (iii) Understand the effect of unit cell structures on the iterative learning approach.

requestTitle: Accuracy and Unbiasedness of AI-Generated Synthetic Medical Images
abstract: When training Machine Learning (ML) models for domain-specific tasks, the paucity of high-quality annotated data for the domain is a prevalent challenge. While there are general-purpose, large-scale ML datasets such as ImageNet or LAION, as well as various pretrained “foundational” models, the performance of these models for domain-specific downstream tasks after finetuning still depends on the availability of the high-quality annotated data from the domain. An example of a domain-specific task is skin disease diagnosis from images. Previous studies have investigated the potential of ML models using relatively large datasets of skin images. However, existing skin disease datasets consist of mostly individuals with light or medium skin tone from developed countries, which are not representative of the wide range of skin diseases and populations grouped by race, age and sex. The paucity of annotated high-quality examples for rare diseases or groups is a frequent challenge in ML-based medical diagnosis. In this work we propose to explore the use of generative AI/ML to synthesize images that help reduce distribution shifts, data imbalance, and biases in existing limited datasets. Preliminary results from our current project using diffusion models finetuned with skin images showed visible improvements in the accuracy of skin disease classification when the original data is augmented with synthetic data. However, experiments were performed in a few limited settings due to the high computational cost of diffusion model training and inference. Through the grant we will perform comprehensive evaluations of synthetic skin image generation and showcase the power of generative AI for medical research.

requestTitle: Model-Parallelism Infrastructure for Large-scale Deep Learning by Gradient-Free Optimization
abstract: This project is to investigate a radically new pathway toward model parallelism infrastructure for large-scale DNNs based on optimization methods that do not rely on backpropagation for training. This project plans to address the challenges of training very large and very deep neural network models that require huge amounts of high-dimensional data. The project will develop new optimization techniques and distributed DNN training software infrastructure to enable wider applications and model parallel deep learning training deployment. This project focuses on proposing and developing a suite of new model parallelism optimization algorithms and system infrastructure for training large-scale DNNs, especially for image processing of massive datasets for geospatial scientific research. To enable model parallelism in training, new gradient-free optimization methods are proposed to break down the whole problem of DNN optimization into subproblems, which can then be solved separately in parallel (by many GPU or Lambda serverless function workers) with high efficiency and high scalability.

requestTitle: Detection and Recognition of Euphemisms
abstract: Detecting and interpreting figurative language is a rapidly growing area in Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, the processing of euphemisms in NLP has been largely underdeveloped thus far. This project addresses two main issues: 1) the design of algorithms for detecting and interpreting euphemisms, and 2) enhancing the interpretability of black-box neural models by creating new datasets and tasks. These explore the embedding space of transformer language models for euphemism recognition. We find a way to quantify several aspects: 1) euphemistic expressions and their paraphrased counterparts differ in the strength of the sentiment they convey; 2) the interpretation of euphemistic and non-euphemistic expressions is context-sensitive; 3) euphemisms are vaguer than the taboo expressions they replace. The experiments test which linguistic properties of euphemisms are captured by deep learning approaches and why. The developed algorithm can detect new euphemisms, not previously recorded in dictionaries, without human intervention. Computational work on euphemisms is crucial for advancing our understanding of how strategic language use can bias perceptions of significant, contentious actions, and it may help in developing methods to de-bias language models. This research on euphemisms also sheds light on what topics are considered controversial or sensitive in specific cultures. Applying the algorithm to diachronic data to detect changes in euphemism usage provides insights into cultural shifts. The corpora produced are valuable for addressing questions at the intersection of AI, linguistics, cultural anthropology, and social psychology. The range of languages studied offers a natural way to make interesting linguistic observations about euphemisms. Since euphemisms constitute a form of verbal behavior, finding ways to detect and interpret them automatically may lead to a broader understanding of human behavior overall.

requestTitle: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning for Improving University Student Retention
abstract: The goal of this project is to develop privacy-preserving machine learning models, using technologies such as PySyft, to help generalize efforts at universities to improve student success and retention. Many universities collect extensive data on their students, including academic performance, demographics, financial aid information, campus involvement, and more. Applying advanced machine learning techniques to this rich data has the potential to uncover valuable insights that could help identify at-risk students early in their academic journey and enable targeted interventions to improve their likelihood of success and ultimately boost retention rates.

requestTitle: An artificial intelligence platform to discover emerging drugs of abuse
abstract: Every year, dozens of new drugs of abuse emerge on the illicit market, causing overdoses and fatalities and fuelling a national drug crisis. Whereas much attention has focused on conventional drugs of abuse, such as fentanyl or methamphetamine, the emergence of totally new drugs has received comparatively less study. This is partly because novel drugs are extremely challenging to identify in patient samples such as blood or urine. The possibility of using artificial intelligence to overcome this gap by detecting previously unknown drugs of abuse in clinical and forensic samples is largely untapped. This project will address this gap by adapting and deploying cutting-edge artificial intelligence technologies, including chemical language models, to detect emerging drugs of abuse in patient samples and seized materials.

requestTitle: Scalable and Representation Learning-Capable Adaptive Resonance Theory and Reinforcement Learning Neural Networks for Robust Lifelong Learning
abstract: Representation learning and scalability are important challenges in continuous learning, also known as lifelong learning or lifelong learning machines. Adaptive Resonance Theory is an important approach to these challenges in unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning also offers important capabilities with respect to these challenges.  This project seeks to enhance and combine unsupervised and reinforcement learning capabilities by designing hybrids for more compact and explainable AI. The research team has made significant contributions to real-time AI, which will be enhanced by combining these contributions with more computationally intensive approaches that will be able to be deployed in more compact architectures after training. The described approach is essential to achieve cost-effective lifelong learning.  The project will make lifelong learning more broadly available, particularly in applications with embedded or real-time requirements. It will enhance workforce development through active efforts at broadening participation.

requestTitle: Multimodal Generative Models for Wildfire Smoke Detection
abstract:
Research has shown that climate change creates warmer temperatures and drier conditions, leading to increases in the frequency, extent, and severity of wildfires.  Given the danger posed by wildfires to people, property, wildlife, and the environment, there is an urgent need to provide automated tools to provide early notification of wildfires for effective wildfire mitigation. The task of wildfire smoke detection proves challenging in real-world scenarios given the transparent and amorphous nature of smoke; faint, small, or dissipating smoke plumes; and false positives from clouds, fog, and haze.  Since smoke is shapeless and has no clear boundaries, wildfire smoke detection in an open environment is a much more difficult exercise than the typical object detection problem, and is still an ongoing challenge.
 
This project will investigate the use of multimodal generative models for the task of detecting wildfire smoke plumes from camera images.  Specifically, the goal is to determine whether multimodal generative models can be used to develop a general approach  that can work for potentially any geographical location, camera type, and weather condition with minimal labeled data. This research will build upon our previous work on smoke detection to deepen our knowledge of effective deep learning-based approaches for detecting wildfire smoke plumes from camera images. More specifically, we expect that this new approach will allow us to build models that can generalize to out-of-distribution inputs, leading to a general approach  that can work for diverse geographical locations, camera types, and weather conditions without requiring a large amount of specific, labeled training data, which is difficult, expensive, and time-consuming to obtain. The findings of the proposed research will have important implications on the scope of problems that multimodal generative models can be effectively applied to out-of-the-box.

requestTitle: Elucidating protein-protein interactions with deep learning
abstract: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) is fundamental to biology and medicine. Identifying interacting partners of targeting proteins through experimental approaches is typically time-consuming and often challenging. Accurately predicting PPI through computational approaches has long been a grand challenge due to the enormous search space. Here, we plan to develop an efficient and effective deep learning system for PPI prediction, which may transform our understanding of protein interaction and complexes.

requestTitle: Hallucination-Free Multimodal Models
abstract: The last year has seen a revolutionary advance in AI, with the introduction of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), such as GPT-4, Gemini, or Claude that can reason in terms of images and language. This has spurred a significant activity in the academic community, towards the development of public domain LMMs such as LLaVA, Qwen-VL and CogVLM. While these models can perform tasks that were not conceivable a few years ago, they are well known to be prone to hallucinations. This is a significant problem for all models but particularly acute for the public domain models, which tend to be much smaller and trained on much smaller datasets. The  goal of this project is to augment the models with capability to detect hallucinations and omit an answer or correct it when an hallucination is detected.

requestTitle: MD/MS in AI Dual Degree Program UT Health San Antonio
abstract:
Abstract:

The University of Texas Health Science Center San Antonio (UTHSA) and the University of Texas San Antonio (UTSA) have collaboratively developed the first MD/MS dual degree program in Artificial Intelligence for medical students. This innovative program combines a one-year didactic training at UTSA with three AI-focused elective courses at UTHSA, providing students with a comprehensive education in applying AI techniques to healthcare-related problems. The courses, Capstone I, Capstone II, and FHIR for Medical Students, are designed to equip students with the skills to conduct independent research, write up findings for publication, and leverage healthcare data using the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard.

To support the growing computational needs of the program, UTHSA is requesting funds to purchase a high-performance Nvidia H100 GPU. This additional resource will enable students to conduct more complex research projects, including convolutional neural networks, deep learning, computer vision, digital imaging processing, and generative AI preprocessing and finetuning. The GPU will be integrated into UTHSA's existing infrastructure, which includes CPU servers, storage, and data security measures that comply with HIPAA regulations.

The project team, led by Dr. Ronald Rodriguez, consists of experienced educators and researchers in medicine and AI who have a strong background in AI methodologies and have previously worked with similar computing resources. The team is well-prepared to utilize the new GPU immediately upon acquisition. With the addition of this powerful computational resource, the MD/MS in AI dual degree program will be well-equipped to provide students with hands-on experience in applying cutting-edge AI techniques to healthcare, ultimately contributing to the development of more accurate, reliable, and impactful AI solutions in the medical field.
piInstitution: University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio

requestTitle: Course on Deep Learning and Modern Applications
abstract:
The University of Illinois Chicago (UIC) seeks support from the NAIRR Pilot for the Fall 2024 course "Deep Learning and Modern Applications," led by Dr. Theja Tulabandhula. This course aims to educate 30 students on advanced machine learning techniques, focusing on deep learning architectures and reinforcement learning frameworks. Key topics include CNNs, LSTMs, VAEs, GANs, Transformers, and AI ethics. Students will utilize resources primarily through VScode IDEs and Jupyter notebooks.

The course requires resources for training models, analyzing data, running simulations, and for supporting the educational objectives of hands-on learning and application of advanced techniques.

Public datasets like those from Kaggle, Hugginface and the UCI Machine Learning Repository will be used, and necessary software includes Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib. The requested resources will be used during class, for assignments, projects, and assessments.

requestTitle: Development of a AI-guided Neuro-Oncology Patient Navigator (BrainGPT)
abstract: The primary aim for this project is to generate a AI-guided patient navigator aid to remove hurdles and barriers brain tumor patients when interacting with the health care system. Ultimately, this tool will facilitate patient education and ease scheduling/coordinating care visits. Given the overwhelming nature of a brain cancer diagnosis, patients can struggle to manage the immediate onslaught of provider visits, laboratory tests, imaging appointments, and simultaneously comprehend the complex health information given to them. Moreover, the fragmented and complex health care system in the United States makes navigating this maze of information even more challenging, especially for patients who are of advanced age, have neurological deficits, or limited mobility. Finally, the long-term monitoring and management of brain tumors requires frequent visits and assessments for many years after the initial diagnosis, highlighting the ongoing need for assistance with patient navigation during periods of disease monitoring and ultimately disease prognosis. All these visits and interactions with health care providers require significant resources, and identifying support resources and removing patient-specific barriers to receiving high quality care is needed to guide patients through these difficult-to-navigate healthcare environments. The neuro-oncology patient population represent a prime opportunity for an AI-enabled patient navigator (BrainGPT) that can integrate with the electronic medical record and help patients coordinate their upcoming visits, answer questions about their test and imaging results and educate if any questions arise before or after provider visits.

requestTitle: LLM Training and Evaluation for Pandemic Prevention and   Response
abstract: This project will train and evaluate a pandemic-related large language model (LLM) using a large corpus of documents on infectious diseases and epidemic-prone priority pathogens from trusted public sources. This LLM will be used to analyze on-line posts of emerging disease outbreaks, and extract features for downstream categorization and prioritization. Further, the model will help analyze clinical practice guidelines for emerging infectious diseases to assess their completeness, consistency with the latest practices, and identify gaps and inconsistencies where updates are needed.

requestTitle: Investigating the Use of Deep Learning Algorithms for Generating Synthetic Molecular Dynamics Trajectories
abstract: Molecular dynamics have been used for the examination of the properties of molecules. Depending on the size of the system and other relevant parameters, a regular molecular dynamics simulation can be time consuming and costly since it needs to solve Newtonian equations of motions for a large number of atoms and simulation time steps. In this study, the time-lagged autoencoder (TAE) algorithm and the long short-term memory (LSTM) algorithm will be used for generating a large number of synthetic trajectories based on molecular dynamics simulation. As opposed to the numerous calculations involved in traditional molecular dynamics, the TAE and LSTM algorithms offer significant time savings. We have examined the working of the algorithms by varying different parameters involved in the TAE and LSTM algorithms such as the number of nodes and layers, and the amount of points in each data set that have a significant impact on the performance of the algorithms. This proposed that novel use of the TAE and LSTM algorithms provides a straightforward method of using deep learning in amplifying rare events in biomolecular systems.

requestTitle: LLMaven: An AI Powered Tool library for Scientific Discovery
abstract:
This project's scientific goal is to create open, transparent and useful AI-based software for scientific research. We propose building a tool library, named LLMaven, using a Generative AI approach, specifically Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) based LLM. We will use RAG as a means of extending LLMs for data that has privacy/IP concerns that is cost 
effective for individual researchers who do not have the resources to develop their own models. The motivation for LLMaven is based on the current landscape of inequity in Generative AI based technology for science.

requestTitle: Pioneering Training of RNA Foundation Models at the Trillion-Data Scale
abstract: Accurate RNA structure prediction remains a critical challenge in molecular biology, with current learning-based models achieving only modest success due to limited structural data. Recent experimental breakthroughs have enabled high-throughput collection of chemical probing data at unprecedented scales, opening new avenues for deep learning approaches. We propose training a large foundation model on a dataset of 100 million RNA sequences with corresponding chemical probing profiles. This model will learn rich internal structural representations of RNA, enabling fine-tuning for downstream tasks such as tertiary structure prediction and de novo RNA design, accelerating the development of RNA-based therapeutics.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot: Democratizing Fine-tuning for AI Alignment
abstract:
Safety fine-tuning to align AI models with human needs is crucial for developing safe, secure, and trustworthy AI. However, the conventional safety fine-tuning approach demands an immense amount of GPU memory, which is beyond the reach of many research groups and organizations, hindering their efforts to improve AI alignment. 

To address the memory challenge, previous methods have included offloading computations and memory to the CPU and using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). However, these methods either suffer from poor training efficiency due to limited CPU-GPU bandwidth or achieve sub-optimal training accuracy because of overly constrained optimization spaces.

In this project, we aim to reduce the memory requirement of safety fine-tuning by combining offloading with PEFT. Initial studies in a single GPU setting show that, compared to state-of-the-art offloading frameworks, our approach increases fine-tuning throughput by up to 3.33 times and reduces end-to-end fine-tuning time by 33.1% to 62.5% while achieving the same accuracy.

We will leverage the diverse hardware configurations available in the Delta GPU cluster to extend our approach to a distributed setting. Our goal is to build an end-to-end distributed, memory-efficient fine-tuning framework that greatly reduces safety fine-tuning costs without sacrificing model quality.

requestTitle: Asclepius AI: Pioneering Adaptive Medical Intelligence for Enhanced Healthcare Delivery
abstract: Our team is developing Asclepius AI, an innovative generalist medical AI assistant designed to revolutionize clinical decision-making and healthcare workflows. This groundbreaking project aims to advance medical AI through three novel approaches: enhancing broad-spectrum accuracy across diverse medical tasks and imaging modalities, implementing real-time interactivity for dynamic feedback integration, and achieving adaptive versatility via an agent-based framework. By integrating cutting-edge techniques such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation and In-Context Learning, Asclepius AI has the potential to significantly improve healthcare delivery efficiency and quality across various clinical settings, paving the way for more personalized and effective patient care.

requestTitle: Cross-modal Distillation with LLMs and Continuous-time Transformers for Blood Glucose Forecasting
abstract:
Blood glucose management is pivotal to treating diabetes, a condition affecting millions worldwide. Traditional methods for predicting blood glucose levels primarily rely on analyzing time-series data from continuous glucose monitors (CGMs). However, these methods often overlook contextual influences such as dietary intake, physical activity, and medication adherence, which are typically recorded in daily logs or electronic health records (EHRs) in non-standardized textual formats. Additionally, while CGM data provide a continuous record, other methods like fingerstick tests are performed at irregular intervals, leading to non-uniform data that present further analytical challenges. Existing models primarily designed to process numerical data from regular time intervals struggle with these irregularities, often resulting in less accurate or reliable blood glucose forecasts. Furthermore, the failure to integrate textual data from EHRs means that current models do not capture the nuanced interplay between lifestyle factors and glucose levels. Integrating both numerical and textual data from EHRs into a unified model represents a significant advancement in personalized diabetes management, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding and prediction of glucose level dynamics.

To bridge these gaps, we propose to develop a predictive model using cross-modal distillation with Large Language Models (LLMs) and continuous-time transformers. This model aims to enhance the accuracy and reliability of blood glucose forecasts by effectively processing both irregular glucose monitoring data and textual information. This work represents the first comprehensive effort to integrate textual and numerical data for diabetes-related data. This integration is expected to significantly improve the accuracy and personalization of diabetes management predictions.

requestTitle: Hubble: a suite to advance the study of LLM memorization
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) memorize vast amounts of information from the pre-training corpora, including copyright-protected information and personally identifiable information (PII). The ability to exactly reproduce this information could lead to privacy violations and copyright infringement. 
We propose the creation of Hubble, a suite of models trained on data with randomized interventions to answer several key questions about LLM memorization related to copyright and privacy concerns. 
We will measure how well LLMs of different sizes memorize different types of data, including PII-like strings and copyrightable materials. 
We will also study how memorization is affected by document duplication and the presence of related texts on the web.
In addition to these questions about memorization, the Hubble suite will also provide artifacts for researchers studying membership inference, copyright takedown methods, and mechanistic explanations for memorization, among other topics.

requestTitle: Enhancing Collective Communication for Machine Learning with Machine Learning
abstract:
Large-scale artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and traditional scientific computing on distributed memory systems are all heavily dependent on collective communication.   Collective communication is a higher-level abstraction than pairwise communication that achieves a shared algorithmic goal across a set of computing elements.   Because it is so critical to numerous areas, there has been growing interest in improving collective communication performance and scalability at the algorithmic and other levels.  We have contributed to such work, including on the largest scale distributed memory systems, exascale computers.   The proposed work will extend our efforts to  complex heterogeneous nodes, for example those with numerous GPUs with complex intra-node topologies, we have been limited by access to hardware that contains a sufficient number of such nodes.   

We will study an approach to collective communication that combines the mechanisms of extensive algorithm choice and parameterization, with machine learning techniques to select algorithms and parameters.   Our approach, if successful, will enable high performance, scalable collective communication without synthesis and other expensive elements.   Additionally, we will study whether the flexibility of this approach is sufficient to ameliorate the effects of scheduling, potentially allowing less expensive resources to be used for applications.

requestTitle: Language Model Customization for Safe, Secure, & Trustworthy AI
abstract:
Language models have emerged as one of the most impactful artificial intelligence technologies. Though widely deployed in products, they are still not well understood scientifically, with new studies coming out every day seeking to better characterize their abilities and limitations, and also contributing new improvements to their accuracy, interpretability, efficiency, and customizability.
The proposed project includes two research studies, to be carried out in parallel, to advance our fundamental understanding of language models. The first study continues our work on core algorithms to improve the accuracy, interpretability, efficiency, and customizability of language models through document retrieval. GPU time is requested to train language models to behave as search engines over their own pretraining data, enabling new forms of attribution when answering questions and improving the trustworthiness of the model in many applications. The second study extends our work on decoding-time customization to new domains, such as code generation and multimodal applications. GPU time is requested to fully compare new decoding-time model customization techniques, which we have developed in prior work, to existing high-performance methods which are far more expensive. Decoding-time customization will help to make language models more secure and trustworthy for their users by allowing patches for newly discovered security vulnerabilities and enabling use with sensitive data that a user wishes to keep private.

requestTitle: Optimizing Model Pruning for Enhanced Robustness
abstract: This study focuses on optimizing Large Language Models (LLMs) by reducing their size while preserving high performance. Although LLMs have demonstrated success in various tasks, such as general question answering, summarization, and specialized medical and legal tasks, their large size comes with storage and processing overheads. Our objective is to fine-tune LLMs to maintain performance based on general metrics such as perplexity and task-specific metrics by implementing pruning techniques and adjusting pertinent components. We will evaluate these changes against adversarial attacks that target text misclassification and gauge the robustness of the pruned models. The refined LLMs are expected to be more compact, yet resilient against attacks and able to maintain high performance, closely resembling the original model's capabilities. This work will benefit both academic and industry experts, empowering them to develop more efficient models with broader applicability for end users globally.

requestTitle: Network-aware Multi-omics Large Language Model for Disease Progression Prediction
abstract: We propose a network-aware multi-omics large language model (LLM) to fully harness multi-omics data's potential, addressing challenges in current methodologies. Our approach involves continuous training of a unified backbone encoder using diverse omics datasets, aligning multiple omics via contrastive learning, and handling noisy and sparse data through imputation and cross-modal translation. By integrating network guidance into the pre-training phase, our model aims to enhance the understanding of multi-omics landscapes, improving disease progression prediction and biomarker discovery. This method incorporates three sub-tasks: (1) developing a unified framework for multi-omics data integration using transformer architectures, consolidating representations from various omics despite limited datasets; (2) enhancing noisy and sparse data through data imputation and cross-modal translation, improving data quality and multimodal learning; and (3) pre-training the model with biological insights from gene regulatory networks, leveraging joint self-supervised tasks to understand gene-gene interactions. This comprehensive approach addresses the limitations of existing large language models in analyzing single-cell multi-omics data, aiming to provide more precise insights for precision medicine.
piInstitution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University

requestTitle: Toward Virtual Bioinformaticians: Empowering Scientific Discovery in Genomics with LLM-Based Agents
abstract: The rapid growth of transcriptomic data and its associated processing challenges necessitate advanced solutions to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of bioinformatics tasks. In response, we propose the development of the Rational AI-Operated Bioinformatics Assistant Team (ROBAT) system, an innovative team of AI-powered agents designed to automate foundational yet laborious bioinformatics tasks. The system will be comprised of large language model (LLM) agents specialized in three primary areas: gene expression data processing, differential gene expression analysis, and gene network analysis. Thrust 1 will focus on developing AI agents capable of preprocessing gene expression data, imputing missing values, and correcting batch effects. Thrust 2 will advance the automation of differential gene expression analysis through robust statistical tools and machine learning solutions to ensure precision under complex biological conditions. Thrust 3 will involve the development of AI agents that utilize co-expression and pathway analysis tools to decipher and model gene interactions and pathway dynamics

requestTitle: OpenChemLMM: A Multimodal Foundation Model for Advancing Chemical Research and Education
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown success in various scientific domains, but often struggle with domain-specific tasks due to lack of fine-tuning and outdated knowledge bases. Recent studies show that domain-specific fine-tuned models can greatly enhance performance. In chemistry, such LLMs have the potential to push the boundaries of research by serving as an intelligent assistant, guiding complex syntheses and accelerate drug discovery, yet current models often fail to handle the complex, multimodal nature of chemical data (including literature jargon, chemical entity representations, spectroscopic data, etc.). By developing a powerful and practical foundation model for chemistry, we aim to unlock similar advancements and enable chemists to leverage AI for complex problem-solving and decision-making in real-world scenarios. To this end, we propose OpenChemLMM, a multimodal foundation model tailored for chemistry. By integrating diverse data modalities such as natural language description in publications and textbooks, figures of chemical structures, reactions, and synthetic paths, spectrum and characteristics of compounds, and other historical, experimental and simulated data, OpenChemLMM aims to thoroughly enhance the understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs in chemistry, ultimately accelerating research and education in the field. Furthermore, we believe this model will lower the barrier of entry for many non-experts, broadening and diversifying the participation and opportunities from students and researchers.

requestTitle: Accelerating LLM use for One-on-One Personal Tutoring in CS Education
abstract: We aim to develop reusable infrastructure for LLM-based tools in two computer science courses (a programming course and a proof-based theory course), determine the highest-impact uses of LLMs for student learning, and produce a general-purpose open source framework for quantifying the performance of LLM tutors.

requestTitle: Towards Efficient Multimodal Edge Wildlife Monitoring
abstract: The explosion of IoT sensors in industrial, consumer and remote sensing use cases has come with unprecedented demand for computing infrastructure to transmit and to analyze petabytes of data. Concurrently, the world is slowly shifting its focus towards more sustainable computing. For these reasons, the `TinyML' community is actively proposing methods to save communication bandwidth and excessive cloud storage costs while reducing algorithm inference latency and promoting data privacy. Such proposed approaches should ideally process multiple types of data, including time series, audio, satellite images, and video, near the network edge as multiple data streams have been shown to improve the discriminative ability of learning algorithms, especially for generating fine grained results. Incidentally, there has been recent work on data driven conditional computation of subnetworks that has shown progress in using a single model to share parameters among very different types of inputs such as images and text, reducing the computation requirement of multi-tower multimodal networks. Inspired by such lines of work, we explore similar per patch conditional computation for the first time for mobile vision transformers that will eventually be used for single-tower multimodal edge models.

requestTitle: Active Semantic Navigation and Mapping
abstract: Exploration of the world must balance the introduction of new information and the quality of localization, structure, and semantic estimation. The proposed approach leverages Fisher Information to balance the dual objectives of maximizing the information gain for the environment while minimizing the cost of localization errors. The balance of this information is critical to ensure that the internal state remains consistent and does not degenerate beyond recovery. Expanding upon this concept, visual language models (VLMs) provide a common sense for a task on top of the objectives to minimize localization errors and maximize information gain. Experiments of this larger scale would be aided by the NAIRR initiative to properly train and evaluate the proposed methods on large-scale 3D simulation environments with promising simulation-to-reality transition performance. Equally intensive compute is required to retrain visual language models that will guide the task-conditioned exploration of the scene.

requestTitle: Distributed Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning with Serverless Computing
abstract: In recent years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms have found widespread applications in areas such as scientific simulations, swarm robotics, autonomous driving, and video games. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is particularly crucial for modeling scenarios where multiple agents interact within an environment, mirroring real-world situations involving cooperation and competition. However, MARL is computationally intensive due to the exponential increase in state and action spaces, making training slow and resource-intensive. Traditional server-based DRL frameworks like Ray's RLlib often lead to resource inefficiencies. Serverless computing, or Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), offers a promising solution by dynamically allocating resources only when needed, reducing waste. Previous research on serverless training frameworks for single-agent reinforcement learning (SARL) has demonstrated significant resource savings and accelerated training. However, applying serverless architecture to MARL presents additional algorithmic and systematic challenges. This project aims to design and implement the first serverless training framework for MARL, optimizing training speed and resource utilization by understanding agent heterogeneities and similarities. Experimental validation on large-scale clusters will further enhance our framework and contribute valuable insights for the development of efficient distributed MARL algorithms.

requestTitle: Development of a Large World Model (LWM) for Enhancing Safe Human-Robot Collaboration in Lunar Missions
abstract: This project is to develop a robust Large World Model (LWM) that seamlessly integrates non-declarative memory data with existing LLM/LMM architectures. This integration aims to significantly enhance the safe interaction capabilities between humans and robots. The application domain will focus on the lunar south pole—an emerging hub of scientific and economic activity with human astronauts and robots, which PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) forecasts will grow into a $170 billion market by 2040.

requestTitle: Deep Learning and Experimentation for Property-Controlled Molecule Generation
abstract: The focus of this proposal is on molecular biology instantiation. The rapid growth of publicly-available small molecular databases has spawned much research and interest recently in deep learning treatments of in-silico molecule design and optimization. While many of the existing deep learning methods demonstrate their ability to generate chemically valid molecules, they are currently limited in their ability to inform wet-laboratory studies aiming to exert control and answer the following question: can your informatics model generate molecules that are constrained to these specific regions of a landscape of biological properties of interest? We seek to advance this question both broadly and specifically on quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs), small disinfectant antimicrobial compounds. The objective of this proposal is to advance property-controlled molecule generation by bringing together novel generative deep-learning models that are capable of learning over molecular data with experimentation that is capable of guiding models to desired regions of the biological space.

requestTitle: Robust Visual Navigation with Efficient 3D Semantic Mapping and Vision-Language Models
abstract: Exploring emerging 3D technologies is essential to overcoming the challenges in computer vision and navigation. Recent studies have shown promising results in reconstructing complex 3D scenes from 2D images using advanced methods like Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) and Gaussian Splatting, while Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled machines to understand and interact with their environments more effectively. Combining LLMs with 3D reconstruction offers a unique opportunity to enhance computational models' understanding and interaction with the physical world. A recent approach has integrated language into NeRF by optimizing embeddings from a vision-language model like CLIP within 3D scenes. However, leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for real-time 3D reconstruction in navigation systems remains challenging due to resource constraints and slow speeds. Our research addresses these limitations by developing an advanced LLM-Vision method to reconstruct environments accurately and efficiently at a frequency of at least 20 Hz, using state-of-the-art neural network architectures and advanced sensor fusion techniques. This scalable solution aims to bridge the gap between theoretical models and practical applications, with plans to extend it to real autonomous vehicles.

requestTitle: Providing GPU Resources for Deep Learning at NC State
abstract: The neural network and computer visions courses at NC State are foundational courses for Electrical & Computer Engineering and Computer Science students. Several hundreds of students sign up for them every Spring semester. Currently, the instructors do not have access to a computing platform with the GPU resources needed to support their activities. Access to such platform would standardize resources to students that rely on free cloud computing, and would allow the implementation of common development environments and automatic grading tools.

requestTitle: Generative models of neuroimages for personalized assessment of risk for Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and multiple sclerosis afflict over 6 million US adults. Those affected by these diseases often require prolonged care, which places strain on families and healthcare. With early detection, treatment and care may be avoidable through timely intervention and management. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) maps brain features enabling clinicians to monitor AD disease risk. We aim to develop a generative model (GM) that harnesses deep neural networks (DNNs) to predict participants’ future T1-weighted (T1w) brain MRIs. By utilizing DNNs, which can determine intricate patterns beyond human perception, predicted MRI scans could assist in forecasting early signs of disease before symptoms. In asymptomatic patients, the ability to predict personalized future MRI scans can help to identify AD-related neuroanatomy changes at baseline clinical examination, long before cognitive changes due to AD. Additionally, doctors could monitor the effectiveness of treatments and even refine them to reduce the need for unnecessary interventions. We will first train an unconditional GM that generates patients’ MRIs without age as a guide. We estimate a month to achieve this, including initial setup. We will add age conditioning in months 2-3 and fine-tune hyper-parameters in months 4-5. In the last month, we will analyze results and publish findings.

requestTitle: Supervising Calibration for Safe and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence Systems
abstract: Model confidence crucial feature in safe and trustworthy AI systems, as it allows users to decide how much to trust a model. However, confidence scores are only meaningful if models are calibrated, i.e. their confidence corresponds well with their actual accuracy. While past work has focused on extracting calibrated confidence scores from frozen models, we propose to shift the paradigm and train models to be better-calibrated, overcoming the limitations of existing methods. We propose two novel modules for estimating confidence and a new training regime for automatically correcting and calibrating confidence scores based on past decisions.

requestTitle: AI-Based Predictive Model for Hurricane Genesis
abstract: Between 2013 and 2022, there were 165 hurricanes in the Northern Atlantic region alone (https://ibtracs.unca.edu). These extreme weather events cause loss of life, property and infrastructure damage, population displacement, economic downturn, environmental and habitat damage, health and economic risks for susceptible populations, and negative psychological impacts (Pielke and Landsea 1998, Cutter, Emrich et al. 2006, Greening, Doering et al. 2006, Letson, Sutter Daniel et al. 2007, Lee, Ce et al. 2008, Mitchell Christine, Esnard et al. 2012, Jonkman, Godfroy et al. 2018, Lavelle Francis, Mizzen David et al. 2023). Hurricane occurrences and intensities have increased over the last several decades (Vecchi, Landsea et al. 2021, Mann 2024). Research has demonstrated that these changes will only increase as a function of anthropogenic climate change (Balaguru et al. 2023), including the recent suggestion that a new category of hurricane will be needed to account for the increasing strength of storms (Wehner and Kossin 2024).

requestTitle: Enhancing Large Language Model Alignment through Diffusion Generated Soft-Prompts
abstract: We introduce a novel method to better control and align the behavior of large language models (LLMs) using "soft-prompts" generated by smaller latent text diffusion models. The key innovation is leveraging the iterative, controllable generative process of diffusion models to create semantic proposals that guide more powerful LLMs during text generation. These soft-prompts fundamentally align model outputs with desired attributes that persist even as systems scale up.

requestTitle: TrinityAI: Trust, resilience and interpretability of Foundation Models
abstract: This project aims to develop a framework to evaluate trust, resilience, and interpretability of foundation models for detecting out-of-distribution inputs, identifying out-of-context inputs, causal factorization for understanding their failure models, and characterizing the reasoning power in LLMs.  The current generation of foundation models including LLMs and VLMs face critical challenges including a lack of assurance, insufficiently precise specifications, and limitations in the interpretability of their response. The project aims at developing a test and validation framework for design-time and runtime analysis and monitoring of the large foundation models to ensure their safe deployment.

requestTitle: An AI-enhanced Analysis Workflow for Human Neural Connectivity
abstract: New machine learning and artificial intelligence technologies are paving the way for future neuroscience research. We propose to develop the next generation of MaPPeRTrac, a comprehensive neuroimaging analysis workflow that simplifies cluster computing for in vivo human brain connectivity research. The study of white matter connectivity or the “connectome” in human brains can reveal the physical communication network underlying both healthy brain functioning and neuropsychiatric pathologies. The structural connectome can be derived non-invasively, linked to clinical outcome and can advance the diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of diverse brain disorders. Successful connectome requires quality images that can be achieved with comprehensive correction of imaging artifacts and removal of noise. Recently, the Swin-Unet transformers model has shown promise in diffusion MRI denoising in a variety of datasets. We propose to develop a Swin-Unet denoising module for the state-of-the-art connectome analysis pipeline, MaPPeRTrac, that has a high-throughput parallel computing framework for computing clusters. The proposed AI-enhanced MaPPeRTrac would incorporate Swin-Unet transformers and several additional machine learning-based features to power the next generation of structural connectome analysis, to offer improved precision and biological interpretability, hence bringing benefits to the broader research and clinical community.

requestTitle: Principled Quantification of Training Data Influence on Generative AI Models
abstract: This research aims to quantify the influence of individual training data points on generative AI models. This quantification will help address AI safety issues concerning privacy, copyright, and hallucination. We focus on two key challenges: 1) establishing a principled definition of "influence" and 2) enhancing the computational efficiency of influence estimation techniques. Current methods rely heavily on model retraining, leading to ambiguity in evaluation metrics and high computational costs – especially for large models. Our approach recognizes the non-deterministic nature of non-convex AI models within the training process. We will conduct research to understand and effectively simulate the randomness inherent in training dynamics, which will allow us to develop more efficient techniques to accurately measure training data influence.

requestTitle: Personalizing Large Language Models In-situ and at Scale
abstract: Large language models (LLMs), such as GPT-4 and LLaMA, have significantly advanced natural language processing applications like chatbots and autonomous driving. With the increasing demand for private, safe, and trustworthy AI, as well as resilient service without Internet access, there's a rising trend of deploying LLMs on accessible local platforms. This proposal aims to facilitate pervasive in-situ LLM inference and personalization for small organizations and end-users, by improving model efficiency with learned sparsity. It ensures better privacy and trustworthiness by avoiding the data collection inherent in existing cloud-centric deployments.
resourceName: TACC Vista (NVIDIA GH100 Grace Hopper Superchip)

requestTitle: Global Counterfactual Explainability of Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful graph-based deep-learning techniques that have been applied to solve a wide range of real-world applications, including drug discovery, recommendation systems, and natural language processing. However, combining feature information and graph structures has led to complex non-linear models of GNNs. Consequently, this increases the difficulties of understanding the GNN’s working mechanism as well as its prediction accuracy. This project is to address this challenge by creating an efficient and comprehensive framework that explains the behaviors of GNNs. Explainable GNNs not only improve the model’s security but also enhance the trust in the model’s recommendations. In sharp contrast to the existing works that mainly focus on local and instance-specific non-counterfactual explanations, we take a global approach that generalizes counterfactual reasoning across several graphs in this proposal. This project will be a contribution towards explainable AI research.

requestTitle: Training a unified Large Language Model that explains first via visually-grounded caption and then decide
abstract:
Large Language Models are pervasive but notorious for (1) hallucinating unfaithful explanations, after the decision; (2) failing many visual reasoning tasks; (3) do not generate references or evidence that led to the final answer.
In this work, we propose to finetune LLaVA to work on many image-text tasks (e.g.  image classification, image-difference captioning, visual questioning answer) using a single unified model. This model would first scan the image and generate visually-grounded caption, and then predict the final answer in the format of the downstream image-text task.
Project aims to improve both trustworthiness and explainability of LLMs in the image domain.

requestTitle: Detecting Misalignment and Ensuring Robustness in LLMs
abstract: We propose to address open challenges for safe and trustworthy AI via three main research thrusts that center on testing and evaluating LLMs and ensuring that these systems have improved reliability and robustness and are better aligned with possibly competing social value. Our proposed research has three main thrusts: (1) Develop and test red teaming strategies for LLM reward functions to detect misalignment, (2) Extend and test our newly developed techniques for detecting reward hacking/policy over-optimization behaviors in LLMs, and (3) Scale and test our newly developed robust RLHF algorithms to enable LLMs to better optimize multiple, possibly competing, reward functions. We have already developed the basic theory and algorithms in prior work, but our prior work did not consider LLMs. Our goal with this proposal is to scale our efforts to LLMs and perform large scale evaluations using the large GPU clusters provided through NAIRR to study the scalability of our AI safety and robustness techniques.

requestTitle: Uncertainty Quantification and Anomaly Detection with Evidential Deep Learning
abstract:
Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) is an uncertainty-aware deep learning approach designed to provide confidence (or epistemic uncertainty) about test data. It treats learning as an evidence acquisition process where more evidence is interpreted as increased predictive confidence. This project will utilize computational resources in the NAIRR Pilot to study the trustworthiness of predictions from AI models used in particle physics data using EDL and computing with Bayesian methods. We will also exploit the connection between uncertainty quantification (UQ) and anomaly detection (AD) to study EDL-based AD using One-Class Classifier methods and compare with the traditional Variational Autoencoder approach to AD. provide a brief overview of EDL for uncertainty quantification (UQ).

The project will explore applications in high-energy particle physics, including object-level and event-level classification and regression tasks. It focuses on developing Deep Learning (DL) models for High Energy Physics (HEP) research, specifically in the context of categorizing proton-proton collision events at the LHC. The objectives include creating DL models that predict classification probabilities and detect anomalous events while also studying their interpretability. By incorporating uncertainty and anomaly-awareness, these models provide a comprehensive understanding of the classification problem, enabling the identification of potential new physics signatures. Additionally, the project aims to develop low-complexity, low-latency, and interpretable variants of these models for trigger-level applications and online analysis, enhancing their practical usability in the field of HEP. This project expects to use 3000 GPU hours on the A100x4 nodes with an estimated storage requirement of 3 TB over the next 6 months.

requestTitle: Explainable vision-language models for pancreatic cancer radiology imaging analysis
abstract: Consistent, accurate, and nuanced interpretation of medical imaging data is crucial for clinical decision making in oncology, particularly for rapidly progressing diseases such as pancreatic cancer. Interpreting external images for referral patients is critical for reliable case management, however, it requires separate billing procedure to in-site radiologist and requests are frequently not handled in time for clinic appointments and timely patient care. Our proposal aims to avoid clinical inefficiencies that occur due to unread external medical images through the development and application of multimodal models to augment the clinical workflows of trained radiologists.

requestTitle: Safe Recovery from Robotic Failures
abstract: Learned robot policies in real households will encounter many unfamiliar or corner cases that are not covered within the training distribution, or novel scenarios caused by distribution drift such as when there are new appliances or utensils in a kitchen.  Failures in learned perception and policies are inevitable in these real-world complex tasks and environments. We develop methods to deal with such failures during execution, either in perception or policy components.  Our key idea here is that timely detection can help contain the failure of individual components and recover from them to avoid task failure. To permit this, we propose continuous monitoring during execution. We propose strategies for online monitoring of the visual classifiers and the RL policy components to detect imminent failures, that can then trigger interventions that permit recovery such as by moving the camera to improve the confidence of visual predicates and policies, and verification behaviors at intermediate checkpoints that allow the robot to check and correct its work before proceeding.

requestTitle: Testing and evaluating a machine learning model for protein function prediction
abstract: Proteins are the fundamental components of living systems and are responsible for a wide variety of important functions within cells. It is essential to have a solid understanding of the functions of proteins to have a complete comprehension of the biological processes that occur within an organism. However, due to labor- and time-intensive nature of finding protein functions experimentally, computational methods to predict protein function have become popular. In this project, we will develop and deploy a ML platform for automatic protein function prediction. We will evaluate the ML model over thousands of classes using publicly available primary (sequence), tertiary (structure), and PPI attributes of the proteins in Arabidopsis thaliana, human, and mouse.
