requestTitle: Addressing Backdoor Attacks in Large Models
abstract: Very large AI models are trained on vast amounts of data but are susceptible to backdoor attacks, where an adversary can manipulate model predictions by inserting a small trigger into a very small subset of training data (referred to as “poison”). We have found that it becomes more challenging for state-of-the-art “cleaning” methods to remove poison from large models as they become better trained. Our goals are to study why this occurs and to develop improved strategies that utilize the combined powers of cleaning objectives and data selection.

requestTitle: The LLM-Augmented Human Knowledge Project
abstract:
We propose to advance interpretability and trustworthiness of LLM technology with a novel LLM (Large Language Models)-Augmented Cognition System (LLM-CSys) architecture that uses an LLM optimized for knowledge skills, with software-based executive control, grounded in external knowledge corpora, and augmented with formal reasoning software such as theorem provers. We have created a Knowledge Engine that can be applied to different corpora to process and curate knowledge at scale. This proposal requests the much-needed computational resources to further the research on the Knowledge Engine and to apply it to create an open Knowledge Center and to discover knowledge in biomedicine and education. 

With our Knowledge Engine, we will create an open Knowledge Center that can provide trustworthy answers, with complete citations for transparency and interpretability. Besides providing open domain knowledge, our focus of diabetes management can serve as a first example to improving patient education in general. We pioneer a new form of deep search where users can get full articles on topics of interest with complete citations and a comprehensive bibliography. With AI augmentation, it is now possible for human experts to create curated content efficiently on the ever-growing amount of online knowledge. Moreover, it is the first time that we can take down language barriers so we can learn about different cultures and perspectives directly from media and literature in the native languages. Such exposure can foster a more informed and nuanced global perspective. We will apply our generic knowledge discovery methodologies to derive new insights and knowledge from a large collection of documents. Our two target applications, drug discovery and scenario planning in career choice, can have a significant impact on human welfare.

requestTitle: Stand-off Triage with Real-time Advanced Physiological Signatures to Effectively Manage, Monitor, and Adapt Deployed AI capabilities and Effective C2 in a Distributed Environment
abstract:
Autonomous triage requires breakthrough innovations to noninvasively identify and classify human injuries in the field, with no physical contact. Advances in sensing and autonomy are also needed to take these measurements. Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh have assembled an experienced team to compete in this life-saving technology challenge. 
Access to a set of advanced computing resources accelerates the research & development of novel AI-based and distributed capabilities, the government can scale support to other domains to achieve a strategic decision advantage, where AI becomes a key and prevalent component to future command and control systems (C2). C2 principles help in coordinating the efforts of various responding agencies, including emergency medical services, hospitals, public health departments, and non-governmental organizations. Through effective command and control, these entities can work together cohesively, supporting information management, avoiding duplication of efforts, and ensuring that resources are used where they are most needed. C2 systems can facilitate the rapid collection, processing, and dissemination of information regarding the emergency's scale, affected individuals, available medical resources, and status of ongoing operations. This ensures that responders have timely and accurate data to inform their actions.
With the rise of AI-based applications also comes new challenges to include the ability to effectively manage, monitor, and adapt deployed AI capabilities and effective C2 in a distributed and or contested environment.  Distributed operations is a critical component of next-generation C2 whether the response is to disasters, pandemics, or other crisis. Key to transitioning from a single monolithic C2 node to multiple distributed C2 nodes is the ability orchestrate operational processes, while optimizing for limited resources. Through the development of distributed C2 capabilities the government can achieve an agile, fully mobile, distributed, and virtualized C2 operational capability to enable C2 anywhere and anyplace.

requestTitle: Request for NAIRR Pilot Classroom Resources - Vocareum AI Notebook for Machine Learning in Cybersecurity Course
abstract:
The "Machine Learning in Cybersecurity" course at the University of Southern Mississippi prepares students to address modern cybersecurity challenges using advanced machine learning techniques. Students engage with real-world problems, developing practical skills by implementing and evaluating machine learning algorithms.

Utilizing the Vocareum AI Notebook platform, the course provides access to computational resources, including GPUs for deep learning tasks. This enables students to work with large datasets and sophisticated models in a Jupyter-based environment, crucial for data science and cybersecurity research.

Students work on projects simulating real-world scenarios, such as detecting network intrusions and classifying malware, using current industry practices and publicly available datasets. This course equips students for careers in cybersecurity and encourages further academic pursuits, with opportunities for conference presentations and scholarly publications.

requestTitle: Building AI-enabled data visualization interfaces
abstract: ESPM 157: Data Science for Global Change Ecology, introduces upper-division undergraduates across a range of disciplines to cutting-edge data science methods in an experiential context.  In this new AI-focused unit, students will leverage GPU-enabled compute through NAIRR to build a data exploration tool that uses open-weights LLMs such as llama3 to translate natural language queries to SQL in python-based visualizations using ollama, langchain, and streamlit.

requestTitle: Machine Learning for CS Undergraduates
abstract: In primarily undergraduate institutions with few computing resources, gaining access to AI-capable resources is challenging, and even more difficult to build contemporary course material. I propose to expand a machine learning course to scale up to larger computational resources, ideally using Vocareum as an educational platform that provides GPUs, Jupyter notebooks, and components for student submissions, feedback , and evaluation. In this way, students will learn about current AI developments, including machine learning, RAG, and LLM tools.

requestTitle: Reliable Large Language Model via Uncertainty Quantification and Alignment
abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into critical decision-making processes highlights an urgent need for these models to accurately understand and articulate their uncertainty, ensuring reliability and trustworthiness across various applications. Current LLMs, while adept at executing tasks with high precision, often fail to quantify or express the uncertainty inherent in their outputs, leading to potential misalignments with human expectations and preferences. This project outlines a comprehensive framework aimed at addressing these challenges by employing Conformal Prediction (CP) and adjusting Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) objectives. By bridging the gap between LLM capabilities and the complex patterns of human judgment, our framework sets the foundation for more responsive, adaptable, and inherently trustworthy LLMs.

requestTitle: Creating and Evaluating Trustworthy AI for Cardiovascular Medicine
abstract:
Our investigator team appreciates these timely opportunities afforded by NAIRR; we are looking to employ foundational models on two challenges in cardiovascular (CV) medicine. Our projects align with the central theme of NAIRR on “Creating Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI”, emphasizing the need for rigorous testing and validation of AI models. Our first project aligns with the aim of “testing, evaluating, verifying and validating AI systems” and our second project aligns with the aim of “increasing the interpretability of learned models”. Briefly: 1) We will evaluate the ability of AI models to effectively transfer knowledge across different data modalities and domains. Our workflow is designed to evaluate the ability of these models to analyze structured biomedical data (single cell omics in CV medicine); 2) We aim to improve the interpretability and reliability of learned models in CV medicine, which is essential for their deployment in highly sensitive healthcare environments. We will train a domain specific foundational model for electrocardiography (ECG) annotation that prioritizes clinical significance. 

The technical viability of our proposed work rests on the impressive potential of foundational models, characterized by their ability to learn from extensive, unlabeled datasets and their versatility in performing a diverse array of tasks. This is further bolstered by our team's extensive experience in biomedical informatics and AI-centric research. Our experience working with deep, large scale neural networks, machine learning projects in biomedical research, as well as natural language processing will facilitate a streamlined and efficient development process. The extensive computational requirements for model training, fine-tuning, and inference underline our necessity for advanced research computing resources offered through this call.

requestTitle: Reliable, Safe and Trustworthy AI \\for Generation of Medical Reports from Scans
abstract: Modern generative AI techniques are leading to transformative changes. However, despite tremendous empirical success in applications many existing approaches rely on poorly understood heuristics. Therefore it is difficult to assess the validity of the generated results in safety critical applications such as healthcare. This project focuses on medical image analysis and reasoning using AI and increasing its reliability, trust and safety.

requestTitle: Exploring the Possibility of Zero-Shot Object-Level Out-of-Distribution Detection
abstract:
Out of distribution detection in the real-world setting is crucial for ensuring the reliability and safety of automated systems, particularly in scenarios where these systems are expected to make decisions or take actions based on their understanding of the environment. Majority of existing research has focused on training specific machine learning models for the out of distribution detection task on custom datasets. However, this paradigm becomes increasingly challenging as machine learning models continue to scale and be provided as black-box cloud services or pretrained models, without access to their training data. This motivates the problem of zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. 

In this proposal, we explore the possibility of performing OOD detection with off-the-shelf pretrained models in object detection. The core idea of our approach replaces detected objects with inpainting. Our OOD detection algorithm conditions the inpainting process with the predicted in domain (ID) label, drawing the input object closer to the in-distribution domain. As a result, the reconstructed object is very close to the original in the ID cases and far in the OOD cases, allowing us to effectively distinguish ID and OOD samples. We aim to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it with algorithms that require additional training on a diverse set of datasets. We also plan to shed light on the interpretability of our approach through qualitative visualization.

requestTitle: Building Trustworthy Digital Health Solutions: A Comprehensive Approach Through Data Collection, Ensemble Learning, and Temporal Adaptation Techniques
abstract: We will build a mobile, cloud-based system for data generation and AI model development at scale. This system will address current limitations in building trustworthy and fair health AI by (1) demonstrating that crowdsourcing and mobile health applications can be used to collect quality controlled and diverse datasets, (2) utilizing fair and robust modeling approaches like ensemble learning for more accurate, practical, and therefore trustworthy predictions of child development and developmental delays like autism, and (3) producing novel methods for mitigating individual model biases and assessing the “power” of AI models that will in turn help scientists, health professionals, and end-users of AI technology understand model performance and increase trustworthiness.

requestTitle: Calibrated, Robust Image Classification
abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems are being used in important applications, such as military settings and healthcare settings. Unsafe ML systems can cause avoidable human casualties. Despite researchers' acknowledgements of the importance of safety, it is often unclear what issues should be given priority or how to proceed. Robustness, monitoring, alignment, and systemic safety are four issues that have recently been identified as needing attention to advance ML safety. However, the success and emerging capabilities of contemporary ML systems require the development, evaluation, and availability of novel approaches to the long-standing problem of ML robustness.  We propose to extend our recent work on robust AI for image augmentations, noise, and/or distribution shifts with uncertainty quantification by utilizing NAIRR GPU resources for training adversarial and generative models.

requestTitle: GenAI for Social Good: Bridging the Gap in Generative AI for Senior Citizens and Other Digitally Underrepresented Groups
abstract:
The digital content contributed by senior citizens and other digitally
underrepresented groups is inherently lagging, making it challenging to re-train LLMs and Image Generative Models to fill the generation gap. In this project, we propose to fill this gap by developing novel concept learning techniques leveraging description logic to enable compositional reasoning and learned concept evolution. It will essentially enable the auto-adaptation of LLMs and Image Generative Models toward targeting digitally underrepresented groups, reducing the bias in deployed AI models that are more attuned to the digital behaviors of younger generations, reducing the chance of leaving senior citizens feeling marginalized or underserved in the digital landscape. The project has two phases: 1) concept evolution and adaptation technology development; 2) through a close collaboration with ASU foundation, we will validate our methods by providing trials to the senior citizens in the lifelong learning institutes with ASU, leveraging on the ASU institutional commitment to meeting the needs of learners across the lifespan.

requestTitle: Evaluating Large Language Models for the Measurement of Complex Social Phenomena
abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used as algorithmic measuring devices to extract information from language, but as others have shown (Ziems et al. 2024), they tend to excel at common tasks that appear frequently in pre-training data (such as sentiment analysis of movie reviews), but not at complex social constructs.  In this pilot project, we will examine their performance at three complex measurement tasks (measuring income inequality, measuring the representation of race in narratives, and measuring the relationships between characters), while also exploring the degree to which LLMs capture information about language dialects and style.  We will examine the performance of open-source LLMs through both prompting and fine-tuning on supervised data, and the chart the ways in which LLMs can help generate new knowledge about culture and society.

requestTitle: Towards Safe, Controllable, and Interpretable Multi-modal Generation
abstract: Multi-modal generative AI models such as DALLE-E, Imagen, Stable Diffusion, and Sora successfully generate photo-realistic model images and videos from text descriptions. However, large amounts of paired data and training auxiliary modules are required to enable controllable generation like ControlNet. This project aims to develop a scalable framework that utilizes the interpretable knowledge in the learned representations of multi-modal generative models to achieve safe and controllable generation. The proposed method will discover the editing direction in the hidden space and distill the interpretable knowledge for controllable generation. This approach will enable fine-grained control over various aspects of the generated content, including style, semantics, and safety, and bring AI alignment with human preferences and societal values.

requestTitle: Enhancing Protein Structure Prediction with Advanced Variational Autoencoder and Diffusion Techniques
abstract: This work presents a novel approach to protein structure prediction, an essential process in bioinformatics that can lead to significant breakthroughs in medical science, drug discovery, and our understanding of life at a molecular level. By combining the power of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and diffusion models, we aim to significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of computational protein structure predictions, thereby contributing to the development of safe and trustworthy AI systems in scientific research.

abstract: Our project aims to advance the thematic focus of Safe, Secure, and Trustwor- thy AI by developing an autonomous Unmanned Aerial System (UAS) capable of safely navigating through smoke in cluttered environments, such as those encountered in wildfires. This initiative will push the boundaries of autonomous navigation and decision-making in hazardous conditions, offering a pivotal step towards deploying AI- driven systems that can provide reliable support during wildfire incidents and be- yond.

requestTitle: An adaptive large language model for socratic case based learning in medical education.
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) excel in information retrieval and synthesis, and have been transformative in various fields that require these elements (Romano et al., 2023). In the realm of education, a sector inherently dependent on these processes, LLMs have shown promise in personalizing instruction and improving learning outcomes (Extance, 2023).
Medical education frequently incorporates case-based learning, which is an approach that emphasizes example-based repetition of simulated scenarios (Donner & Bickley, 1993). This pedagogy is excellent at developing critical reasoning and diagnostic skills in medical students (Stalmeijer et al., 2009), especially when multiple, distinct cases for a given learning objective are presented within a course (Mylopoulos et al., 2018) (Lessing et al., 2022). Medical case-based learning, especially if designed to train adaptability in diagnostic reasoning and recognition through multiple cases per disease, necessitates a rich repository of scenarios that mirror the complexity and variability of real-world medical cases. However, the creation of each detailed and nuanced case is time-consuming and labor-intensive. Educators often draw on their experiences to craft these scenarios, a method that can inadvertently introduce personal biases and limit the diversity of cases presented to students.
Recognizing the potential for LLMs to revolutionize this aspect of medical education, we aim to explore the ability of LLMs to serve as trustworthy tools in medical education. Through a set of specific aims, we will develop, implement, and validate a socratic AI clinical case tutor for medical trainees. By grounding generated cases in the published literature, the model will generate a comprehensive and factually accurate array of clinical cases. By extending the model further with real-world demographic data from the electronic medical record, we will measure and directly mitigate demographic biases that emerge from the historical literature and baseline LLM model. We will validate performance in an educational setting using factual audits by expert clinicians and randomized comparison against traditional clinical static case studies.  Our goal is to create a scalable, efficient methodology for case-based content generation that upholds the educational standards necessary to prepare students for the diverse scenarios they will encounter in their medical careers.

requestTitle: Enhancing Driver State Estimation through Advanced Computer Vision and AI Technologies
abstract: The project aims to enhance an already built system for driver state estimation in autonomous and intelligent driver assistance systems through state-of-the-art computer vision and AI technologies. We aim to address the challenges posed by low-resolution and noisy video data in naturalistic driving environments through a comprehensive AI platform for data management, synthetic data testing, and advanced detection techniques. Our innovations include improved face detection at acute angles and recurrent network-based driver state estimation, which have shown promising results, including an 11% accuracy improvement in head orientation models. Utilizing the Synthetic Driver Dataset (SynDD), we aim to leverage the compute power offered by the Supercomputers through this project to enhance the already existing environment for developers to efficiently train, build, and test models. This initiative promises to significantly advance the precision and reliability of driver assistance technologies, contributing to safer driving conditions.

requestTitle: A Multilingual Foundation Model for Protein Science
abstract: Biochemical information flows from DNA, to RNA, and then to proteins, which drive biological processes. Modern protein design seeks to reverse this process by generating novel protein sequences based on specified functional characteristics. The ability to generate proteins from a desired function has applications not only in medicine but also in industrial settings, such as for plastic degradation, carbon capture, and the creation of new materials. However, the current methods to create novel proteins involve laborious, slow, and expensive laboratory experiments. Computational experimentation provides the opportunity to drastically increase the rate at which novel proteins can be designed. This project develops M3, a novel language modeling architecture that you can interact with, like chatGPT, to produce protein sequence information.  These sequences can then be used to make proteins that suit different applications. The M3 model framework is more efficient and is extendable to enable the addition of other protein information, such as drug-protein interactions.

requestTitle: Generalizable AI for clinical language understanding using nationwide datasets
abstract: Generative AI language models like chatGPT are transforming virtually every aspect of our modern economy, yet their impacts on healthcare remain slow and uncertain. One potential reason is that these general-purpose models may lack the domain knowledge to interpret medical language with the necessary nuance and precision. One of the most promising ways to clinically educate these models is to train them on physician notes, such as those captured in electronic health records systems. A bottleneck to doing this is the fact that these models require large quantities of data from multiple centers, and data sharing is complicated by the critical need to protect patient privacy. In this pilot study, we will use the unique computing resources provided by NAIRR to test a new technology capable of training these advanced models without requiring data sharing, thereby protecting the privacy and security of patient data. We will validate this method, called virtual pooling, by adapting the open-source LLaMA2-chat model to medical language using physician notes from MIMIC-III, the largest open-source dataset of its kind. If this pilot proves feasible and scalable, our next step will be to train one of the first multicenter clinical language models of its kind, sourcing data from multiple hospitals across the US. The potential impacts of such a language model could be tremendous: the ability to recognize the earliest signals of disease earlier than physicians, to help optimize and personalize treatment regimes, and to improve the recruitment of patients into trials of new therapeutics.

requestTitle: Machine Learning-Aided Multiscale Computational Design of High-Entropy Functional Alloys
abstract: The project aims to design high-entropy functional alloys (HEFAs) for energy applications, particularly thermoelectrics, by integrating graph neural networks (GNNs), feedforward neural networks (FNNs), density functional theory (DFT), and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.  The key tasks involve: (1) using GNNs to select elements and determine compositions of HEFA candidates with a solid solution phase; (2) performing DFT calculations to investigate the electronic structures and electrical conductivity of these candidates; and (3) developing machine learning-based interatomic potentials using FNNs trained on DFT data, enabling MD simulations to compute thermal conductivity of HEFAs.  This multifaceted approach leverages the strengths of different computational techniques to overcome challenges in accurately modeling and predicting the properties of these complex multi-component alloys.

requestTitle: AI Foundation Model for Space Weather Applications
abstract: Foundation models (FM) are large-scale, pre-trained models designed to serve as the basis for various processing tasks. The foundation models based on transformers in the domains of vision and language exhibit remarkable potential for effectively adapting to diverse downstream tasks. The deployment of deep learning (DL) models often depends on specialized hardware accelerators because these models demand substantial computational power. The motivation for designing a foundation model using the Helio dataset stems from several critical factors relevant to advancements in heliophysics and space weather forecasting.  Firstly, the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) spacecraft provides unique, high-resolution data that is unparalleled in its detail and scope. This dataset includes extensive solar observations spanning over 14 years, offering a robust foundation for deep analysis through machine learning techniques. Furthermore, there is a notable uncertainty in space weather predictions, such as solar winds, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and solar flares. These phenomena can have significant implications for satellite operations, communication systems, and even power grids on Earth. The application of machine learning models can improve the accuracy and reliability of these predictions, providing earlier warnings and better mitigation strategies. In this context, the Helio dataset's unique attributes—comprehensive coverage, high resolution, and extended duration—make it an ideal candidate for developing a foundation model in heliophysics. This model aims to not only enhance space weather forecasting but also push the boundaries of what is currently possible in predicting and studying solar activities and their effects on space weather. This project is particularly suited for support from the NAIRR. We also envision NAIRR to facilitate advanced research and collaboration opportunities and help impact broader communities.  We also plan to utilize NAIRR to publish the large scale ML-ready datasets and to train the community to use and fine-tune the foundation model. The project is a joint collaboration between existing NASA and NSF-funded efforts. This project will follow open science principles and all artifacts will be made openly/publicly available.

requestTitle: Statistical Inference through Data-Collection and Expert-Knowledge Incorporation
abstract: Our project seeks to improve the inference of complex systems through systematic data collection. Accurate modeling is crucial for understanding behavior, diagnosing issues, and making predictions. Current approaches are often heuristic, fail to account for uncertainty, and are not scalable. This project integrates advanced statistical learning with reinforcement learning to manage uncertainty systematically. These methods will be pre-trained to handle various scenarios in real systems, requiring substantial computational resources for simulation and training.

requestTitle: Exploring Robust Transformer Architectures for Foundation Models
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is currently undergoing a paradigm shift with the emergence of foundation models, exemplified by large language models (LLMs). These models are becoming integrated components of modern computing systems, driving the need for their secure, robust, and resilient operation. However, their susceptibility to adversarial attacks introduces unpredictable behaviors that undermine the security and trustworthiness of these systems. In this project, we propose to investigate robust transformer architectures for foundation models. Specifically, we propose a novel approach to design intrinsically robust transformers with robustness as the pivotal inductive bias by leveraging rigorous mathematical foundations in robust statistical theory and numerical algorithms. The anticipated outcomes of this project will unprecedently improve the safety and robustness of foundation models, ensuring the reliability of AI systems to perform reliably under diverse conditions and to properly handle exceptions, anomalies, or unexpected inputs.

requestTitle: Large scale neural network pre-training for aneurysm detection in 3D brain scans
abstract: Manual detection of intracranial aneurysms in computed tomography (CT) scans is a complex, time-consuming task even for expert clinicians, and automating the process is no less challenging. Critical difficulties associated with detecting aneurysms include their small (yet varied) size compared to scans and a high potential for false positive (FP) predictions. To address these issues, we developed a 3D, multi-scale neural architecture that detects aneurysms via a deformable attention mechanism that operates on vessel distance maps derived from vessel segmentations and 3D features extracted from the layers of a convolutional network. Nevertheless, limitations exists associated with the use of the limited available annotation data. By leveraging resources as part of the NAIRR pilot, we aim to use unannotated 3D scans of the human brain to pre-train a model before carrying out targeted fine-tuning for aneurysm detection and (potentially) other relevant tasks using the same kind of data.

requestTitle: Enabling Advanced Reasoning and Scientific Text Understanding in Language Models
abstract: Finetuning Language Models (LMs) has been shown to improve their usability in a wide range of tasks including information assistance, brainstorming and even creative applications. A lot of this progress is due to the availability of high quality training and evaluation datasets. Whether for obtaining training data for aligning models with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or for evaluating trained models, human labels are often seen as the gold standard relative to other methods of preference collection. However, collecting human data is often expensive and prone to high variance, especially in domains that require expert knowledge such as understanding scientific texts.  Our earlier work has shown great progress in using  synthetically generated data in improving language model capabilities in general domains. However, such data shows less gains for expert domains such as scientific text understanding that require high-quality, complex annotated data. We propose to investigate novel methods for human-AI collaboration to efficiently collect high-quality data for expert domains. Our focus will be on efficient expert supervision and design of reliable evaluation procedures through effective collaboration between human experts and LMs. We will publicly release the training datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and trained models along with publishing the novel research supporting those artifacts.

requestTitle: Accelerating Multi-Messenger Astronomy with At-Scale Machine Learning
abstract: The field of gravitational wave astronomy has grown significantly since the first direct detection of gravitational waves from a binary black hole merger in 2015, to the point that there are now nearly 100 confident detections of compact binary coalescences (CBCs). The fourth observing run (O4) of the International Gravitational-wave Network (IGWN) is well underway, and the increased discovery of gravitational waves now and into the future will enable follow-up observation of events across other cosmic messengers, such as electromagnetic radiation and cosmic neutrinos. Mergers of binary neutron stars (BNSs) and neutron star-black hole (NSBH) systems have the potential to produce these messengers, and the insights we gain in this era of multi-messenger astrophysics will directly correlate with the volume and diversity of data we are able to collect. Therefore, it is desirable to produce alerts with as low a latency as possible to allow other instruments to maximize their observation time. Our goal is the development of a machine learning (ML) algorithm that is capable of detecting these events faster than the traditional, computationally-intensive, matched filtering methods.

requestTitle: HaBiT: Human Behavior and Translational Artificial Intelligence Labs for the Community
abstract:
HaBiT (Human Behavior and Translational Artificial Intelligence Labs for the Community) supports artificial intelligence (AI) "in the wild" to interpret the role of environmental factors on human biology from cells-to-systems, and provides a world-class user-facility that automates testing of technologies to augment human resilience to environmental stresses. Six months of NAIRR compute support is requested to advance beta-testing and initial comparisons of AI models developed through HaBiT.
 

Overview of HaBiT Labs
Greater than 40% of dementia cases are blamed on environmental and lifestyle factors. More directly, environmental causes lead to 25% of early deaths. Light and air pollution, limited safe walking trails, lack of green space, isolation, and severe climate are among the environmental factors that have been shown to dramatically negatively impact human behavior within urban areas. City-wide initiatives like the “Blue Zone Projects,” New York’s “Walk to a Park Initiative,” and “dementia villages” in the Netherlands, aim to either ward-off chronic disease or address the care of chronic diseases by community infrastructure and programming that focus on socio-environmental influences on behavior. However, these projects have been limited in their implementation, reproducibility, and often, scientific basis. Conversely, in vitro and in vivo assays have elucidated potential mechanisms of how organisms respond to environmental stresses in highly controlled situations that rarely translate to natural habitats. A key challenge has been the lack of systematic ways to translate observations of human behavior ‘in the wild’ to testable hypotheses underlying cellular and molecular mechanisms as a function of the environment, and vice versa. New biotechnologies are needed to monitor environmental changes, assess behavior, and identify ways to augment health as a function of a changing environment. Concomitant with this technology gap, a tremendous need exists for infrastructure to evaluate human-augmentation technologies and environmental countermeasures before they are deployed. To address these needs, we are building HaBiT Labs to provide the research infrastructure, training, and translational support to standardize, test and deploy technologies that augment human resilience to environmental stresses.

HaBiT’s research resources consist of (1) HaBiT Labs where living systems are engineered to test biotechnologies that alter environmental response; (2) an AI infrastructure to collect and interpret data on human behavior ‘in the wild’, and (3) digital twins that bridge in vitro to behavior and enable HaBiT users to remotely design experiments. We will engage our community partners, including San Antonio Parks and Recreation, Southwest Research Institute and the MATRIX Consortium of AI researchers, to provide a common testbed for new AI and hybrid AI-cellular systems technologies aimed at augmenting resilience of the community (Objective 1). In Objective 2, HaBiT will launch its research programs including in-house technology projects to optimize human circadian activity in response to the environment. Example projects include smart luminescence materials, cellular models of brain regions governing circadian control, and AI tools to detect city park usage and foster physical activity. HaBiT resources will open to the community, enabling researchers worldwide to develop and test technologies at HaBiT that vertically bridge scales of biology: from intracellular signaling to population-level resilience (Objective 3).

abstract: This project proposes an approach to applying Large Language Models (LLMs) as a foundation model for the analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data with a particular focus on its interpretability. More importantly, the proposed framework emphasizes enhancing the interpretability of models for analyzing scRNA-seq data, aiming to make the model's decision-making process transparent and trustworthy, while also identifying and correcting any potential errors or biases.

requestTitle: Parallel Training of Large Foundation Models and Graph Neural Networks on Graphs with Rich Semantics
abstract:
Graphs, with their inherent ability to model complex relationships and structures, are pivotal in numerous disciplines and applications. These structures often include nodes linked by edges, with nodes frequently annotated with textual data, resulting in what is known as text-attributed graphs (TAGs). TAGs are extensively utilized across a diverse range of domains, from analyzing social networks and enhancing information retrieval to advancing a myriad of natural language processing tasks.

The integration of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) offers a robust solution to effectively handle TAGs. GNNs excel in capturing structural information through a message-passing paradigm, while LLMs, like GPT-4 and LlaMA 3, provide deep, context-aware textual understanding. However, this integration introduces significant computational challenges. The size of LLMs and the expansive nature of data required for GNNs' message passing creates a scalability bottleneck, especially evident during joint training scenarios where each node's computation may depend on a large, dynamically sampled neighborhood.

Additionally, the need for extensive computational resources, like substantial GPU capacities even for modestly sized mini-batches, compounds these challenges. This proposal aims to explore parallel and distributed computing techniques to overcome these barriers, enhancing the feasibility and efficiency of applying sophisticated GNN and LLM models to large-scale TAGs.

requestTitle: Empirical Differential Privacy: Beyond Auditing Differentially Private Deep Learning
abstract: Recent advances in auditing implementations of differentially private machine learning models have provided a powerful tool -- the hypothesis testing approach to deriving the empirical lower bound of epsilon, i.e., the practical privacy threat in terms of the specific dataset and model. We find the empirical lower bound can be applied to two new problems: (1) understanding the meaning of a theoretical privacy budget to a specific dataset and model to guide the selection of a utility-friendly privacy budget; and (2) determining whether an unlearned example in machine unlearning should be processed immediately or at a particular time later, e.g., multiple correlated removal requests coming. These studies will involve GPU-intensive modeling steps. We will use the requested resources to conduct the preliminary studies for these projects.

requestTitle: Model Fusion: Merging Domain-specific with General Purpose Foundation Models
abstract: We are seeking computational resources to train foundation models to accelerate the design and discovery of materials for energy storage applications. To do this, we propose a novel methodology: fusing MIST, our foundation model for molecular property prediction, with existing LLMs to seamlessly merge domain-specific knowledge with LLMs' general knowledge and reasoning abilities. We will benchmark four LLMs (GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama 3, and Gemma) on cheminformatic question-answering tasks from the SMol-Instruct and Mol-Instructions datasets. By providing a simple chat interface, the model will make quantum-level accuracy calculations accessible to computational scientists and the broader scientific community. This will help accelerate our ongoing efforts to develop energy storage and conversion systems needed to enable widespread electrification of transportation, including the heavy-duty and aviation sectors.

requestTitle: Exploring Heterogeneous Datacenter Design for Sustainable AI Deployment
abstract: As we aim to advance the study of Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI, we must do so in a sustainable and efficient manner. The computing industry is forecasted to consume as much as 7-20% of global energy consumption by 2030 – a trend that is only accelerating given that ML models are becoming larger and more complex. Recent proposed legislation aimed at understanding the carbon footprint of AI encourages quantification of the designing and deploying AI at the datacenter-scale from an environmental perspective. While a plethora of novel hardware platforms have recently sought to accelerate AI workloads, there is a high cost to determining the optimal hardware and configuration for a given model, including a large sustainability footprint. To this end, we propose to construct a model to allow for the sustainable and efficient allocation of resources onto an array of novel AI accelerators. To do so, we will utilize the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF) AI Testbed to construct a performance model that will allow researchers to predict the optimal hardware configuration for their workload. We will leverage the diversity of AI accelerators available in the ALCF testbed, including Groq and Cerebras, to measure how given workloads perform while constructing our model. We then aim to explore how to effectively schedule workloads across an array of heterogeneous accelerators, optimizing for both performance and carbon footprint.

requestTitle: A Metric-learning Paradigm for Verifying Origination of Textual Contents
abstract: Breakthroughs in Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistant systems that can provide quality information with conveniences. An issue is paralleling the advantages, however. LLM generated contents are problematic in that they are seemingly indistinguishable from that of human, which cause many issues in areas like science, education, information security, etc. Furthermore, approaches in AI synthesized content detection are either computationally expensive or need accesses to the LLMs' internal computations, both of which hinder their public access. Specifically, the detection is performed through evaluating the similarity metric between the given text to an equivalent example generated by LLMs and through that determining the former's origination. Being able to utilizing the LLMs themselves externally, computational resources will be less demanding in the detection model side. Overall, research components of this project include 1) developing metric models that measure similarity among AI and human texts, 2) developing models that reconstruct contexts for input texts, 3) adapting the framework to use cases including long documents, emails, and conversations, and 4) adapting models to unknown LLMs.

requestTitle: Towards Trustworthy Biomedical Models via Robust Imbalance Learning
abstract:
The project aims to enhance the robustness of biomedical Large Language Models (LLMs) against data imbalances in health datasets. Recognizing the criticality of addressing skewed disease categories, demographic sizes, and symptom frequency, this research focuses on improving model reliability across diverse and uncertain environments. The real examples' shortcomings in adapting to new data distributions underscores the urgency for developing models resilient to imbalance challenges, particularly those arising from heterogeneous sources like clinical records and social media.

With a six-month timeline, the project intends to scrutinize LLMs' robustness against various imbalance scenarios and devise methods to bolster model robustness through novel domain adaptation techniques. The research will leverage the expertise of the lead PI, Dr. Xiaolei Huang, in NLP and health informatics, and Co-PI Dr. I-Chan Huang’s background in epidemiology and cancer control, with a focus on pediatric oncology at St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. The project's phased approach includes an initial examination of imbalance effects on model performance and fairness, followed by the development and evaluation of imbalance adaptation methods.

The team is prepared to promptly utilize NAIRR Pilot Project resources upon access, with all members compliant with necessary regulations. The project's commitment to open-source practices and educational integration promises widespread benefits to the research community, reinforcing its potential for significant contributions to the field of computational healthcare.

requestTitle: GraphNarrator: Natural Language Generation From Large-Scale Open- Domain Knowledge Graph
abstract: The GraphNarrator project, led by Dr. Chengkai Li and his team, focuses on generating natural language descriptions for fragments of large-scale knowledge graphs. These descriptions aim to help users understand complex graph data more easily. The project trains narration models using pre-trained language models like BART, T5, and LLaMA on a dataset comprising 8.7 million pairs of Freebase graph fragments and corresponding Wikipedia sentences. The key challenge addressed is the problem of information hallucination in existing graph-to-text models, where generated text may contain fabricated facts not present in the input graph. The project proposes a novel approach to mitigate hallucination by trimming generated text using dependency parse trees to eliminate portions not represented in the input graph. This approach aims to bridge the gap between graph-to-text models and real-world applications, enhancing the reliability of generated descriptions.

requestTitle: TEA: Two-Player LLM Games with an LLM Referee
abstract: Our project focuses on Large Language Models (LLMs), which are a rapidly advancing model of Artificial Intelligence. Our goal in this project, at a high level, is to design methods to increase the “performance” of an LLM, reduce its susceptibility to adversarial attacks, and also introduce metrics to measure its performance. In more detail, we aim to measure and enhance the performance of a “Target LLM” through its interactions with two other LLMs. One of them, the “Attacker LLM”, has a competing objective with the target, and the other one, the “Evaluator LLM”, evaluates the performance of both the Target and the Attacker and provides feedback. Our setup is designed so that the test of the performance or the improvement of the target LLM happens automatically without any human supervision. In particular, we plan to consider the interaction between the Target, the Evaluator, and the Attacker (TEA) in a game-theoretic setup.

requestTitle: NAIRR Pilot: Computational Foundations for Tractable Deep Generative Models
abstract:
Probabilistic circuits represent joint distributions as deep computation graphs. They move beyond other deep generative models and probabilistic graphical models by guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference for certain classes of queries: marginal probabilities, entropies, expectations, causal effects, etc., can all be computed exactly and efficiently, often in linear time. As such, probabilistic circuits provide an alternative, more capable and trustworthy architecture for the future of generative AI.
Recent developments have ensured that probabilistic circuits are now also effectively learned from data at scale. Moreover, tractable deep generative models are used to control the behavior of intractable deep generative models such as transformers and diffusion models. This way, probabilistic circuits achieve state-of-the-art results in constrained sampling from large language models, natural image distributions, and offline reinforcement learning models.Nevertheless, the computational investments made so far to develop tractable deep generative models is negligible compared to more traditional architectures.To bring the dream of tractable deep generative models to fruition, we propose this pilot project which will build a solid foundation by scaling up tractable model learning and its applications.

requestTitle: Evaluating and Mitigating Biases in Clinical Decision Models
abstract: The digitization of clinical records and the improvement of large language models enables the clinical decision models to intervene the clinical operations with predicted diagnosis decisions and foreseen outcomes. The safety and fairness of the clinical decision models are crucial for developers, hospitals, clinicians and patients. We propose to conduct a comprehensive evaluation with counterfactual data generation techniques to evaluate whether the clinical decision models treat patients of different demographic groups with various behavioral patterns fairly. We further propose to amplify the hidden bias in clinical decision models with in-context influence tracing and then optimize the clinical decision models to mitigate the negative influence of these hidden biases towards downstream tasks. With our proposed method, we would obtain the first comprehensive bias evaluation results across multiple bias sources and various clinical operation components. The bias mitigation method is expected to reduce the hidden bias without the need for additional human annotations.

requestTitle: Scaling Resilient and Adaptable Decentralized Learning to Large Dynamic Networks
abstract: This proposal addresses the challenge of deploying resilient  federated learning (FL) for distributed model training and inference on highly dynamic edge networks. We aim to develop methods that leverage pre-trained models to achieve robust performance under changing network conditions, including extreme device failures and adversarial attacks. Our research focuses on the vertical federated learning (VFL) setting, where edge devices contribute features of the same data points. Prior work by the authors requires training from scratch and has not been scaled beyond 49 devices. We propose to address these limitations by: (1) Investigating challenges in deploying pre-trained models (PMs) in dynamic environments with extreme faults. (2) Developing advanced methodologies for integrating PMs, including models like ResNet and efficient versions of large models. (3) Designing scalable and reliable FL methods for thousands of edge devices. This research will enable the development of robust and efficient VFL for real-world edge computing applications.

requestTitle: Quantification of Mask Efficacy in Large Population
abstract: Airborne transmission of many viruses is possible through virus-laden fluid particles evicted from the mouth of an infected person to be inhaled by a healthy person. Using a facemask with proper fitness is an effective method to diminish the airborne transmission of pathogenic agents. To protect against the virus, mask fit on the wearer's facial topology and effective mask fabric are two critical components.  Here, we leverage new machine learning algorithms along with theoretical physics-based mathematical models to form predictive metrics about mask efficacy in a very large cohort of subjects and diverse daily activities such as talking. By determining realistic measures of mask efficacy in a large diverse population, we pay the way to specify how effectively one can evaluate the practical impact of mask usage on the transmission of respiratory diseases during early stages of potential respiratory diseases.

requestTitle: Improving the Reliability of Large Multimodal Models for Radiology with Confidence Estimates
abstract: Our project aims to advance artificial intelligence (AI) assisted radiology report generation for chest X-rays and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans by developing a system that not only performs state-of-the-art clinically accurate medical report generation but also integrates calibrated confidence estimates for each individual statement in its output. This effort addresses the critical issue of automation bias, where the over-reliance on AI-generated reports could lead to diagnostic errors. By benchmarking and rigorously evaluating various confidence estimation methods, our project aims to minimize these risks. Incorporating confidence scores at the level of individual statements is key to enhancing AI-assisted reporting workflows, allowing radiologists to identify claims needing further scrutiny more efficiently. This strategy is expected to improve the accuracy and reliability of AI-supported radiology reporting.

requestTitle: Integrating Logic Reasoning with Vision Language Models
abstract: The goal of this project is to study Video monitoring based situation recognition in a variety of environments. In the past we have very successfully integrated explicit logic reasoning (using run-time event calculus) with traditional computer vision (TCV) for several applications. We would like to bring the emerging video language models (VLMs) into the mix not only for additional, high-level description, but also to automate the formulation of logic assertions from those descriptions with the help of TCV and compatibility/consistency across multiple versions of VLMs that are fine-tuned with correlated events. One significant application of the technique is in our ongoing NSF project to study student engagement in virtual classrooms, where we believe that VLMs could helpful in generalizing the results obtained through TCV techniques.

requestTitle: Bayesian Nonlinear Intrinsic Dimension Learning in ImageNet
abstract: In statistical literature, there is a plethora of research which assumes that a high dimensional dataset (ambient space) usually sits in a lower dimensional manifold (intrinsic) such that the lower dimensional manifold can capture bulk of the statistical properties in the original high dimensional data. In this project, we intend to develop a Bayesian nonlinear approach to learn the intrinsic dimension of huge datasets like ImageNet. Nonlinear learning allows one to explore intrinsic spaces of the data which sit in a nonlinear transform of the ambient space.  The Bayesian approach provides the overall uncertainty quantification in joint estimation of the intrinsic dimension and the nonlinear map to the intrinsic space. The proposed method can be exploited to learn compressed products of large image datasets that are easier to deploy for future downstream tasks.

requestTitle: Massive virtual screening of small molecules for high-affinity ASGPR ligands in MoDEs
abstract:
Accurate prediction of binding affinity of a drug ligand bound to a target molecule such as a protein is of central importance in early drug discovery. Development of advanced computational tools has enabled better prediction of ligand-protein binding affinity with applications to high-throughput drug screening or virtual screening. To maximize the power of existing tools in a synergistic and scalable way with less model-specific bias, we recently developed a meta-modeling framework of ligand-protein binding affinity prediction by ensembling structure-based classical docking tools and sequence-based deep learning models, achieving state-of-the-art performances compared to exclusively structure-based deep learning models. On the other hand, a novel therapeutic modality has been recently advancing by targeted protein degradation technologies based on hetero-bifunctional compounds. One of them is a molecular degrader of extracellular proteins or MoDEs, which recruits an extracellular protein of interest for lysosomal degradation by exploiting the asialoglycoprotein receptor or ASGPR.

The goal of this proposal is to improve our sequence-based meta-models using larger training datasets to advance more trustworthy AI and carry out virtual screening of 51,000 compounds from the Therma Fisher Maybridge Screening Library to identify high-affinity ASGPR ligands. In a preliminary study, our pre-trained meta-models was validated against a benchmark set of 96 experimentally validated ASGPR ligands with a Pearson correlation of up to 0.52. We aim to improve accuracy, validity, and reliability of model performance, while controlling model-specific bias and vulnerability through our meta-modeling framework. The potential impact of this proposal will be discovery of optimal MoDEs as effective drugs in broad therapeutic applications.

requestTitle: Auditing data provenance for fine-tuned language models
abstract:
The data used to train a language model is one of  the most valuable pieces of information we can have when assessing the performance and behavior of the model. Pre-trained models, especially large base models like GPT, BERT, and T5, along with their more recent successors like LLaMA 2, Mistral, and GPT-4, are trained on vast amounts of data taken from all across the web, and there is little to no transparency about what data is used and how. 

On the other hand, fine-tuned models make use of smaller and more customized data sets in order to tune a model for a specific task, such as breast cancer diagnosis from mammography images, customer reviews analysis for sentiment, and enhancing utility in dialog applications. Many of these data sets are well-known: the Data Provenance Initiative lists over $1800$ such data sets used in fine tuning, and provides detailed information about the data sets and their origin. It is therefore far more plausible that we can determine what data sets were used to fine-tune a model. This is also much more valuable information because the data set used for fine-tuning has a much more immediate effect on model behavior and thus helps us understand more clearly why models might produce the prompt responses that they do. 

The goal of this research project is to develop tools that given a dataset d and a fine-tuned model m, can determine whether d was used in fine-tuning to produce m either wholly or partially.

requestTitle: Development of Foundational Large and Multimodal Language Models for Hydrology Research and Education
abstract: This project aims to revolutionize the field of hydrology by developing a Hydrological Foundational Large Language Model (LLM) and a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM). These advanced artificial intelligence models will be capable of processing and generating hydrological knowledge from both textual and non-textual data sources. The initiative seeks to enhance data accessibility, analysis, and the generation of insights for stakeholders in hydrology, including researchers, educators, practitioners, and policymakers. By leveraging vast datasets, including academic literature, sensor data, satellite imagery and maps, the project will train new models to support a wide range of applications. These applications include facilitating research hypothesis generation, creating dynamic educational materials, and informing water management and policy decisions. The development process involves data collection and preprocessing, model training, integration testing, and the creation of user-friendly interfaces, culminating in the public release of the models and findings. This endeavor is expected to significantly advance the understanding and management of water resources, promoting innovation and collaboration across the hydrology domain.

requestTitle: Scaling layer-wise feature shaping for robust deep networks: next-generation architectures inspired by communication theory
abstract:
The exponential growth of AI is driven by rapid and continuing innovations in deep neural networks (DNNs). The ability to use massive amounts of computation and training data has led to stunning advances in a diversity of areas, including well-established applications such as recommendation systems and computer vision as well as emerging applications such as generative AI and scientific discovery.  However, AI researchers remain well aware that, despite their runaway success, DNNs lack robustness against noise, natural data distortions and adversarial attacks (the latter are small perturbations to the input designed to disrupt DNN performance).  The common approach to increase robustness in DNNs is data augmentation: the data used for training the DNN is augmented by the kinds of distortions that we wish to be resilient against.  However, it is difficult to scale this approach to enhance general-purpose robustness against a wide variety of distortions, including ones that we do not anticipate.

We have recently developed an approach for next-generation DNN architectures that draws upon ideas from communication theory, which forms the basis for today’s wireless cellular and WiFi systems.  A DNN processes the data in multiple layers, and the key idea is to modify the training objective so as to enhance the “signal-to-noise ratio,” a common measure of resilience in communication systems, at each layer.  This is done by adding layer-wise training objectives to shape the features extracted by each layer, in addition to the conventional end-to-end training objective.  We also modify the inference path of the DNN in accordance with communication-theoretic principles, introducing nonlinearities that attenuate distortions and perturbations.  Preliminary results on standard image datasets, based on modifying a single DNN layer using our approach, demonstrate significant gains in robustness with and without data augmentation.

The goal of this NAIRR project is to use the available computational resources to scale our experiments to larger datasets, replacing more layers using our approach. The goal is to provide comprehensive design guidelines and larger-scale proofs of concept of our approach, in order to establish this approach as an essential component of the DNN design toolkit.  We plan to engage the AI R&D community by continuing to open source our code, and by publishing our work in high-profile conferences and workshops.

requestTitle: Networking and Compute for Next Generation Low-Earth Orbit Satellites
abstract:
The next generation of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, dedicated to Earth observation, seeks to enable a compelling vision: frequent high-resolution monitoring of the Earth to track humanity scale events. These satellites operate in low orbits, less than 1000 Km above Earth, and democratize access to Earth imagery for multiple applications: precision agriculture that improves farm yields and incomes, disaster management such as early detection of forest fires, modeling the spread of diseases, geo-political analytics, and climate monitoring. As such constellations scale to hundreds of satellites, traditional architectures for space-Earth connectivity fail to meet their needs. Specifically, these constellations generate hundreds of terabytes of data every day that must be transported to the Earth, while the satellites travel at fast speeds with respect to ground stations on the Earth. Therefore, the data download process experiences day-level delays and is prone to failures due to bad weather or hardware errors. The goal of this proposal is to design a new paradigm for space-Earth connectivity that removes these bottlenecks and enables fault-tolerant networks that generate near-realtime (minute-level) insights from data collected by these satellites. The proposed research will remove networking and compute bottlenecks for LEO satellites and enables novel commercial, academic, and national security applications. Some example applications include early response to aircraft intrusions, forest fires, and geopolitical events. 

The proposed research designs new algorithms and architectures for networking and edge computing on satellites and ground stations. Specifically, the proposed research includes: (a) a new distributed ground station architecture that is robust to transient failures, agile to traffic variations, and enables low latency data download from satellites, (b) an edge computing framework that extracts insights, schedules data transfer, and prioritizes important imagery for networked transfer while being scalable to multiple applications, and (c) design and analysis of interconnects between communication and Earth observation satellites for opportunistic routing. The proposal takes an end-to-end systems level approach to large-scale space-Earth networks, which is essential for their robust, fault-tolerant, and high-performance operation.

requestTitle: Building Trustworthy Multimodal Models for Oncology Applications
abstract: Trustworthiness, safety, and reliability of AI systems are fundamental requirements for any meaningful application of these systems in healthcare. However, developing such models using multimodal data modalities such as radiological images, multi-omics data, pathology images, and clinical notes is challenging. This project explores an innovative approach centered on building embeddings using a deep Bayesian approach for diverse modalities, facilitating the creation of scalable and trustworthy multimodal machine learning models. By harnessing the power of embeddings and Bayesian deep learning, our methodology seeks to effectively fuse information from disparate sources, enabling a holistic understanding of the patient's condition in a trustworthy and safe way. By developing scalable models based on the Bayesian Transformer architecture, our approach aims to enhance the accuracy, efficiency, and trustworthiness of oncological diagnoses and treatment strategies, ultimately contributing to improved patient outcomes.

requestTitle: Efficient approaches for specializing large language models for domain specific text
abstract: Our team is planning to apply the latest large language models to analyze domain specific-text, e.g., clinical notes. Recently, there are various new approaches to efficiently fine-tune the models for domain specific text, ranging from LoRA (training small “modifier” weights based on low rank adaptation) to model merging (merging parameters between models for enhanced performance). We aim to explore other machine learning approaches for effective adaptation/specialization of the models. One example is our recent work, Co-LLM, that trains a base LLM to collaborate with other more powerful assistant LLMs. We plan to extend our work and investigate other efficient approaches for fine-tuning LLMs on domain-specific text.

requestTitle: Privacy Preserving Tutoring System for Health Education of Low Literacy Hispanic Populations
abstract:
This project will implement a computer tutor for low literacy Hispanic breast cancer survivors. Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Hispanics, and although research has shown that education can greatly mitigate stress and improve quality of life, few educational interventions for this population exist. The computer tutor resulting from this project will mimic a human tutor that teaches about breast cancer survivorship skills and about breast cancer in general. Because tutoring involves conversation with the survivor, it is possible that they reveal sensitive personal information; therefore, it is important to encrypt the information in the tutoring session to prevent any privacy breaches. And for the tutoring component to be effective, special attention must be paid to the utilization of natural language processing models as well as models of behavior that are observed in the target population when tutoring and/or interacting with technology. For the privacy component to be effective, techniques that can encrypt and decrypt data at high speeds will be explored to make the interaction fluid. To date, computer tutors that converse with their students have been tried mainly with a highly literate population in college settings, so their impact on low literacy Hispanics is unknown. Therefore, this project will advance our understanding of the impact of designing artificial intelligence powered tutors to address diversity and disparities in the access to information by a subset of low literacy individuals, as well as our understanding of privacy preserving algorithms that work in real-time with complex natural language processing models. More broadly, project outcomes will facilitate access to information for minority populations and will serve to build research capacity and train minority students in the participating teaching-oriented institutions.

The project will be carried out with two objectives in mind. First, development of a novel intelligent computer tutoring system that is customized so that it can effectively query and interact with Hispanic breast cancer survivors by adapting existing content that was created for this population in prior research. Because it has been shown that both the language of many adult Hispanics, and target population interactions with technology, are more nuanced than previously thought, our first objective also involves training natural language algorithms and designing interactions that model those of Hispanic breast cancer survivors. The second objective is to develop privacy-preserving algorithms that utilize robust end-to-end encrypted communication and can encrypt and decrypt distributed data in real time at a speed that does not hinder the interactions with the computer tutor. The contributions of this development process will be threefold: (1) to understand the role of culture and education in the interaction between low literacy Hispanic breast cancer survivors and intelligent tutoring systems; (2) to develop a framework that facilitates the implementation of intelligent tutoring systems for minority populations; and (3) to develop accurate and low latency privacy preserving mechanisms for NLP model training and dialogue interfaces.

requestTitle: Large spatial network generation, transformation, and interpretation
abstract: Spatial networks are complex networks whose nodes and edges are embedded in space. Spatial network data has been experiencing a fast increase recently, ranging from micro-scale (e.g., protein structure) to middle-scale (e.g., biological neuron network) to macro-scale (e.g., mobility networks), where the spatial and network topology jointly determines the network formation, evolution, and function. Modeling and understanding the generation and transformation of spatial networks are long-standing and challenging research domains crucial to broad applications such as medicine signs, mental disease early diagnosis, and societal event synthesis, whose underlying principles are largely unknown yet. On the one hand, existing spatial network generative modeling methods heavily rely on human-predefined principles but cannot automatically learn new ones. On the other hand, deep generative models can learn new underlying principles from the data but are not good at incorporating external principles, which is indispensable to ensure valid space and network topology of the generated spatial networks. Motivated by the above complementary strengths and drawbacks, this project aims at a new framework that can: 1) automatically learn new generation and transformation processes of spatial networks, 2) embed user-specified principles to constrain and regularize the generated spatial networks, and 3) pursue the model interpretability and automatically distill new understandable principles of network process. The research approaches include the development of: 1) Novel spatial and spectral graph decoders for large spatial networks, 2) Deep generative modeling and optimization with spatial and topological regularization, 3) A variety of novel spatial- and spectral-graph transformation strategies, and 4) A novel system for interacting predefined and distilled principles between human and models.

requestTitle: Cloud Computing Credits for Studying Deep Generative Models
abstract: The objective of this project is to design an intelligent deepfake detector that will be capable of assessing the integrity of digital visual content and automatically detect falsified images or videos. requestTitle: Socially-Aware Language Technologies To Support People in Supporting Others for Better Online Communities
abstract:
My research goal is to support people in better supporting others and  accomplishing their tasks by providing them with assistance through building scalable socially aware language technologies, with a special focus on online peer support groups.  How do people support others in need in online support groups?  How can we build social computing systems to support people who are supporting others? Supporters are the key to the success of online peer support groups, which are used by millions of people with health concerns. However, online supporters often do not receive rigorous training and tailored feedback, which might lead to unsupportive or even negative helping behaviors.  Existing mechanisms of training or scaffolding largely rely on human supervision,  making it hard to scale up to help the large number of supporters who  support millions of people in need of care.  This work will fill these gaps and accomplish the vision of supporting people in better supporting others  in several representative text-based online peer support groups  by: (1) developing innovative natural language processing techniques to predict supporters' helping skills and examining how helping skills related to positive outcomes; (2) designing contextualized language generation approaches that provide tailored assistance for supporters by highlighting which helping skills are needed in a given situation and suggesting example responses with actionable feedback; 
and (3) creating an open-source and human-in-the-loop tool to empower supporters and evaluating how the tool can be used for both training and real-time scaffolding via lab studies, field experiments, and real-world deployment.

requestTitle: Advancing the Accessibility of STEM Online Learning by Using Generative AI
abstract: Videos are a popular medium for online learning, but research has found that accessing these materials is challenging for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) learners. This project aims to develop and evaluate effective Q/A mechanisms and interaction designs that enable both DHH and hearing students to collaboratively access STEM videos. Specifically, we propose creating deep learning models capable of generating questions that are relevant and inspiring, thus prompting students' curiosity and encouraging them to explore the learning materials more deeply. Our project will be conducted in two phases: the development of video question generation models and pipelines, followed by a large-scale user study to evaluate their effectiveness in a real-world setting. The team boasts expertise in Human-Computer Interaction, Natural Language Processing, and AI-augmented learning technologies. Evaluation sites include Gallaudet University, the world’s only liberal arts institution dedicated exclusively to the education of Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing learners, and the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, which is committed to fostering an inclusive learning environment.

requestTitle: Accelerating Fusion Energy Research with Physics-Guided Deep Learning
abstract: In order to find the global optimum design of future fusion reactors, it is important to develop fast and accurate models of the heat and particle losses due to turbulence in magnetically confined plasmas. To accelerate the training and validation of physics-guided deep learning models trained on multi-fidelity simulation data of turbulent heat and particle fluxes, we propose using the ALCF AI Testbed's dedicated machine learning platforms. Our project will benefit tremendously from SambaNova's advanced AI-focused hardware. This platform, with its unique dataflow architecture and substantial memory capacity, promises to significantly reduce our model training times and accelerate our adaptive learning workflows for the design of a fusion pilot plant.

requestTitle: Towards Open-World Jailbreaks for Large Language Models
abstract:
As the cornerstone of a new era in AI, generative AI (GenAI) such as GPT-4 promises to catalyze a profound transformation across numerous sectors of society, from education and healthcare to entertainment and commerce. These models, with their unparalleled ability to comprehend and generate multiple data types — including text, images, and audio — at a human-alike level, signify a paradigm shift, unlocking applications previously considered unattainable. However, alongside their vast potential, these models are prone to critical challenges, including the generation of erroneous or harmful content. 

This proposal zeroes in on the critical examination of the robustness of Large Language Models (LLMs). Specifically, through the novel technical designs in ensemble attacks and optimization, we aim to advance the transferability of jailbreaking LLMs, ensuring their effectiveness even in open-world setups. By proactively and adversarially identifying these vulnerabilities, we aim to understand the specific ways in which LLMs break down, providing insights that will be pivotal in steering the evolution of GenAI systems towards greater safety and reliability.
